The Supplement on the Compendium of Indicators (1) (Together with a Commentary).
First Chapter.

In this work, *Jñāpakasaṃgraha*, statements found in the Bhāṣya that were not collected by Nāgeśa are compiled and explained here. *Jñāpakasaṃgraha*: 1. *ṭa eoṅ*; *aiauc*. 2. The mention of the word "prior" (*pūrva*) in the rule *ami pūrvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.107) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that when a [single substitute] occurs for two [sounds], it is of the same nature as the preceding one. 3. In the context of the statement that a long vowel (*dīrgha*) does not occur for a *saṃprasāraṇa* [vowel] by this [rule], the sūtra *halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.2) is the indicator.

The mention of "form" (*rūpa*) is an indicator that the form of the subsequent element is of the same nature as the form of both [the preceding and the subsequent]. Regarding the rule *ādguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87) and other such sūtras prescribing single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) operations, the Vārttikakāra stated that the term "long" (*dīrgha*) must be explicitly mentioned; its purpose is to ensure that when a *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, or similar substitute occurs in place of both the preceding and the subsequent elements, it shall consist of exactly two morae (*mātrā*), and not three or four morae in accordance with the original substituends (*sthānin*). To this, the Bhāṣyakāra replies:

He argued that the mention of the term *dīrgha* (long) need not be made, because the desired result is established through the division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) alone. One rule is: *akaḥ savarṇe*; its meaning is that when a vowel homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with an *ak* vowel follows, there is a single [substitute]. Then there is a second rule: *dīrghaḥ*; its meaning is that in the case of what has been indicated by the phrase "one [substitute] for both the preceding and the following," that which is [the substitute] becomes long—that is, it consists of two morae (*dvimātra*). Thus he demonstrated.

Regarding this, one might suspect that in the case of *paśum*, *viddham*, and *pacanti*, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would likewise be of two morae (*dvimātra*); anticipating this, a resolution is stated by means of an explanatory indicator (*jñāpaka*). He says: *ami pūrvaḥ*. This is the intention: in the case of *paśum*, where *paśua-am* has been reached, there is a concern that when the preceding *u* and the following *a* are replaced by a single substitute, the preceding *u* would become a substitute of two morae, provided that the term *dīrgha* (long) were not mentioned. If the substitute here were indeed of two morae, [the author] would not have employed the mention of the word *pūrva* (preceding).

Since the desired result is obtained simply by the recurrence of the term *pūrvasavarṇa* from the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*, the fact that [the author] employs the mention of *pūrva* (the preceding) indicates this: that which is of the same nature as the preceding element is indeed what occurs in place of both. Thus, in the case of *paśum*, the single substitute is of the same nature as the preceding—namely, of one mora (*ekamātra*)—which is the solution.

Regarding the form *viddha* in the word *tathā viddham*, when the suffix *kta* is added to the root *vyadh*, the semivowel undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa*, resulting in the stage *vi adh ta*. At this point, there arises the doubt that by the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca* (Pāṇini 6.1.108), the single substitute for the preceding and following sounds (*pūrvarūpa*) would become a long vowel consisting of two morae (*dvimātra*). If it were indeed a long vowel of two morae, then the rule *halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.2) would not have prescribed the lengthening of a *saṃprasāraṇa* vowel following a consonant, because the desired result would already be established by the two-moraic *pūrvarūpa* itself.

Therefore, that sūtra indicates by means of the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca* that the resulting single substitute (*pūrvarūpa*) is not long (*dīrgha*). Hence, there is no fault; this is the resolution. Similarly, regarding the form *pacanti*: when *pac-a-anti* is established, there is the apprehension that the subsequent single substitute (*pararūpa*) might be long by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97). However, because of the inclusion of the term *rūpa* in the expression *pararūpam*, it is indicated that the substitute in place of both [elements] must be of the same nature as the form of the subsequent element.

Therefore, the resolution here is that there is only one single substitute. [The objection is: Since the rule *jhrjñā.paṭa* (Pāṇini 6.1.73) prescribes the insertion of a *tuk* after a long vowel before the suffix *cha*, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a rule dependent on a short vowel does not apply when a long vowel is present. [The opponent objects: On the view that parts of letters (*varṇaikadeśa*) are included under the term "letter" (*varṇagrahaṇa*), in forms such as *ālūya* and *pralūya*, the letter *u*—which is a part of the long vowel *ū*—would also be included by the mention of the "short vowel. Consequently, the *tuk* would undesirably apply by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk* (Pāṇini 6.1.71). Anticipating this doubt, he says: *dīrghāccha*. (This indicates that the *uk* in *ūk* is not a mere part of a short vowel, thus the *tuk* is not applied.)

Indeed, the rule *dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.75) is commenced for the sake of establishing the augment *tuk* in examples such as *cecchidyate*. Even there, since the short vowel *i*, which is a constituent part of the long vowel *e*, is included by the term "short" (*hrasva*), the augment *tuk* would be established by the rule *che ca* (6.1.73) alone; thus, the rule *dīrghāt* being rendered superfluous, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that an operation prescribed with reference to a long vowel does not apply when that long vowel is based upon a short vowel.

The point is that, therefore, there is no possibility of the *tuṅ* augment in cases such as *ālūya*. The indicatory letter *k* in the rule *gāpoṣṭak* (Pāṇini 3.2.8) indicates that the elision of the vowel *a* situated within [the long] *ā* does not occur. Now, one might raise the following objection: if the view is held that parts of a phoneme (*varṇaikadeśa*) are included under the term for the whole phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*), then in forms such as *yātā* and *vātā*, the elision of the *a* which is a part of the long *ā* would apply by the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48). Anticipating this doubt, he says: *gāpoṣṭak*.
By the rule *gāpoṣṭak*, the suffix *ṭak* is applied to the roots *gā* (from *gai*, "to sing") and *pā* (from *pā*, "to drink") when they are without a prefix.

The suffix *ṭak* is prescribed when a verbal root meaning "action" (*karman*) is used as an upapada. Examples are *sāmagaḥ* ("one who sings the Sāmans") and *surāpaḥ* ("one who drinks liquor"). The letter *k* is an indicatory phoneme (*anubandha*) attached to *ṭak*; its purpose is to effect the elision of the vowel *ā* in the form *sāmaga-a* by means of the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64). Let that [elision] not take place. Once the elision of the *a* that is a constituent part of the *ā* has been effected by the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), we arrive at the form *sāmaga a a*. At this point, the desired form is established through the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) for the two *a*s. Therefore, what is the use of the indicatory *k* for the purpose of eliding the *ā*?

That [the letter *k*] being employed indicates that there is no elision of the vowel *ā* when it stands as the form *ākāra*. Thus, since there is no elision of the vowel *a*, if there were also no elision of the vowel *ā*, the desired forms would not be established; therefore, the indicatory letter *k* (anubandha) serves its purpose in its own domain (*svāṃśe cāritārthya*) for the sake of preventing the elision of *a*. Its practical utility (*prayojana*), however, is that in forms such as *yātā* and *tā*, there is no elision of the vowel *a* [by Pāṇini 6.4.64].

Although it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ikoguṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3) that the vowel *ā* with the indicatory letter *k* (*āk*) does not undergo *guṇa*, thereby serving as an indicator of this meaning, nevertheless, one must understand that there is no contradiction in a single element serving as an indicator for two things; this is clear from various sources such as the *Pradīpa*. Furthermore, by the evidence of the inclusion of the words *go* and *nau* [in the sūtra *goto ṇit*], it is known that a rule characterized by *vṛddhi* or *yaj* does not apply to a long vowel. This is the Vārttika: *ekavarṇavacca*.

And it must be stated that its long vowel [ā], though consisting of a collection of two short vowels (a+a), is equivalent to a single phoneme (varṇa). Otherwise, in the sense of "crossing by means of speech" (*vācā tarati*), the suffix *ṭhan* would apply after the word *vāc* according to the rule *nau-dvy-acaṣ-ṭhan* (Pāṇini 4.4.7). With the intention that this Vārttika is established otherwise through an indicator (*jñāpaka*), he says: "Because of the mention of *go* and *nau*."

Since the syllable *okāra* consists of the collection of the letters *a* and *u*, the word *go* is *dvyać* (consisting of two vowels). Consequently, since the word *go* would already be included by the rule "dvyać" [Pāṇini 4.1.120] itself, the mention of *go* in the rule "govidaco’saṃkhyāparimāṇāśvāderyat" (Pāṇini 5.1.39) would be redundant. Similarly, the mention of *nau* in the rule "naudvyacaṣṭhan" (Pāṇini 4.4.7) would also be redundant. Therefore, both of these [mentions] indicate that a grammatical operation characterized by the term *dvyać* does not apply when a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is present. Thus, there is no fault; this is the intended meaning.

And thus, the *vārttika* "as if it were a single phoneme" (*ekavarṇavat*) is not necessary; it should be noted that its result is established by the very indicator (*jñāpaka*). [Regarding the rule] *Pāṇini 1.1.3*: "In place of *iK*, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [occur]. By the indicator consisting of the addition of the indicatory letter *k* in the rule *Pāṇini 3.2.8*: "*gā-pōṣṭak*," it is understood that a *guṇa* does not occur for the vowel *ā*. Regarding the rule *Pāṇini 1.1.3*: "In place of *iK*, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*," there is the *vārttika*: "'The mention of *iK* is for the purpose of excluding *ā*, diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*), and consonants.'"

In examples such as *yātā* and *vātā*, the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.84) would require the substitution of *guṇa* for the vowel *ā*; however, because of the inclusion of the term *ig* [in the subsequent sūtra], this does not occur—this is the first purpose [of the *ig* restriction]. But the author of the *Bhāṣya* rejected this purpose. For it is said: the exclusion of the vowel *ā* is not the purpose of the inclusion of *ig*, since it is understood through the power of the *jñāpaka* that *guṇa* does not apply to the vowel *ā*.

In the rule *gāpoṣṭak* (Pāṇini 3.2.8), the inclusion of the *k*-marker (*kit*) in the suffix serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the vowel *ā* does not undergo *guṇa* substitution. For by that very rule, the suffix *ṭak* is prescribed after the roots *gā* and *pā* when they are not preceded by a prefix and when an object is present as a governing word (*upapada*). When the form *sāmagā-aṭak* arises, the vowel *ā* is elided by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*, resulting in *sāmaga*. The *k*-marker of the suffix is applied for the purpose of causing the elision of the vowel *ā*. Let that be unnecessary; let the suffix simply be *ṭa*.

When the vowel *ā* undergoes *guṇa* substitution—becoming *a* by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*—the form *sāmaga* is established. In this state, by applying the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule to the two *a* vowels, the form *sāmaga* is achieved even without the elision of the *ā*. Thus, the *kakāra* suffix (*it*) being redundant indicates that the *guṇa* substitution does not apply to the *ā*. Since the desired form would not be established in the absence of *guṇa* and the absence of the elision of *ā*, the purpose of the *kakāra* suffix is to effect the elision of *ā*; thus, it fulfills its own function.

The intention of the Bhāṣya is as follows: in cases such as *yātā* and *vātā*, where there is another purpose [for the rule], the *guṇa* substitution does not occur for the vowel *ā*. Thus, since the absence of *guṇa* for *ā* is already established by this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), it is not correct to say that the mention of *iK* (in Pāṇini 1.1.3) is for that purpose. This is what he says: "gā-po-ṣṭak" (Pāṇini 3.2.8). The phrase "having no other purpose" means being devoid of any purpose other than the elision of the vowel *ā*.

The purpose for the inclusion of the indicatory letter *k* in the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3) must be its application in the rule *tundaśokayoḥ parimṛjāpanudoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.5). There is no other such purpose for the indicatory *k* in *ṭak*. It is with this intention that it was stated thus. [Now, regarding the suffix *jñāpaṭ*: *īdūtau ca*...]

(Sūtra 1.1.19) || The inclusion of the word *artha* ("meaning") in this rule is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle does not apply to the designation of *pragṛhya*. [Objection: But surely, in the rule "īdūtau ca saptamyarthe" (Pāṇini 1.1.18), the inclusion of the word *artha* should be unnecessary. For if it were absent, in the example "somo gaurī adhiśritaḥ," since the locative case ending is elided, there would be no *ī*-vowel in the form of the locative; consequently, the *pragṛhya* designation would not apply. Yet, its application is desired. It is for this purpose that the word *artha* has been included.

And it should be stated that once that [rule] has been applied, even though the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) is elided, the designation *pragṛhya* will still apply because its meaning remains present. Even in the absence of the explicit mention of "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇa*), since forms ending in *ī* and *ū* in the seventh case are impossible, the sense is obtained through the force of the statement itself: "that which ends in *ī* or *ū* and is accompanied by a seventh case. Thus, even when the seventh case is elided, there exists the quality of being "accompanied by a seventh case" by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the suffix as if it were not elided); therefore, the *pragṛhya* designation applies.

Anticipating the objection that the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning) would remain useless because the attainment of the desired result [of the technical term] would still be possible otherwise, he says: "Not in the case of the designation *pragṛhya*. If the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations by virtue of a suffix) were to apply in the section dealing with the *pragṛhya* designation, then by the rule "The words ending in *ī* and *ū* when followed by a locative [case-ending]"—which means that a word ending in *ī* or *ū* is designated as *pragṛhya* when accompanied by a locative—the designation would occur even when the locative case-ending is elided, by means of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* according to the method previously stated. In that case, what would be the purpose of including the word *artha*? Since that word is indeed included, it indicates the absence of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* in this context.

This indicates [the following]. Thus, the intention is that in examples such as *vāpy-aśvaḥ*, the absence of the designation *pragṛhya* is the purpose [of the rule]. Regarding *bahugaṇa* (Pāṇini 1.1.23): by means of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) found in rules such as *vator iḍ vā* (5.1.23), it is understood that words beginning with *bahu* and *gaṇa* function in the sense of number (*saṃkhyā*). The sūtra *abahaugaṇavatuḍati saṃkhyā* teaches that *bahu*, *gaṇa*, and so forth, receive the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "number. This sūtra can be dispensed with.

Nor should it be argued: "In that case, how could they be grasped by means of a word denoting number (*saṃkhyāśabda*) in the rules prescribing grammatical operations (*vidhipradeśa*)? For it is understood through an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that words such as *baḍ*, *dhaṭ*, *ṭhaṭ*, and *ḍa* function in the sense of number. To illustrate: by the rule "vator iḍ vā" (Pāṇini 5.2.39), the augment *iṭ* is prescribed for the suffix *kan* following a stem ending in *vat*; the examples given are *tāvatikaḥ* and *tāvatkaḥ*.

Furthermore, the suffix *kan* must be applied by the rule *saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan* (Pāṇini 5.1.22). If the word ending in *vat* were not included under the term "number" (*saṃkhyā*), then since *kan* would not apply after it, the prescription of the augment *iṭ* for the subsequent *kan* would be untenable. From the very fact of that prescription, it is understood that the purpose of the term "number" includes words ending in *vat*.

Thus, by the rule *bahupūgagaṇasaṅghasya tithuk* (Pāṇini 5.2.52), the augment *tithuk* is prescribed for the words *bahu* and *gaṇa* when followed by the suffix *ḍaṭ*. And *ḍaṭ* is to be applied by the rule *tasya pūraṇe ḍaṭ* (Pāṇini 5.2.48). Since *ḍaṭ* would not otherwise apply if *bahu* and *gaṇa* were not included among the words denoting number (*saṃkhyā*), the prescription of the augment *tithuk* before that suffix—being otherwise untenable—indicates that *bahu* and *gaṇa* function as numerals.

Thus, by the rule *ṣaṭ-kati-katipaya-catur-ām thuk* (Pāṇini 5.2.51), which prescribes the augment *thuk* after the word *kati*—which ends in the suffix *ḍati*—when *ḍati* follows, it indicates that even for a word ending in *ḍati*, the *thuk* augment serves the purpose of a number (*saṃkhyā*). Similarly, regarding the suffix *vatu*, the rule *vator-iṣṭha-k* (Pāṇini 5.2.53) is also an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the grammatical operations pertaining to numbers.

Accordingly, it is established in the *Bhāṣya* that the rule *bahu-gaṇa-vatu-ḍa-ḍat-dha-saṃkhyā* should be rejected. Having this in mind, he says: "on account of the *jñāpaka* [indicatory evidence] in the rule *vator iḍ vā*," etc. Regarding the rule *avyayībhāvaś ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.41): because of the prohibition in the rule *nāvyayībhāvāt* (Pāṇini 2.4.83), it is known by implication (*jñāpaka*) that elision (*luk*) occurs after an *avyayībhāva* compound. Furthermore, by the rule *avyayībhāvaś ca*, the designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) is prescribed for the *avyayībhāva* compound.

And its purpose is stated in the *Vārttika*: "The elision (*luk*), the face (*mukha*), vowels (*svara*), and usage (*upacāra*). In examples such as *upāgni* and *pratyagni*, the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) following an *avyayībhāva* compound must be prescribed by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*. Since that elision is not possible without the designation of the *avyayībhāva* as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), this elision is the first purpose [of the designation]. And that [purpose] is accomplished precisely through the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence).

For instance, regarding the prohibition in the rule *nāvyayībhāvādato'm tvapañcamyāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.83)—which states that there is no elision (*luk*) of the case endings (*sup*) following an *avyayībhāva* compound ending in *-at*—it must be stated that this prohibition applies to the elision that would otherwise be required by the rule *avyayādāpsupaḥ*. Since the elision of case endings (*sub-luk*) would not apply if the *avyayībhāva* were not an indeclinable (*avyaya*), that prohibition would be redundant; its very existence thus indicates that there is indeed elision of the case endings following an *avyayībhāva*. Likewise...

It is established in the Bhāṣya that since the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) following an *avyayībhāva* compound is already accomplished by the very indicator (*jñāpaka*), even without the designation of "indeclinable" (*avyaya*), it is not appropriate for the purpose of the *avyayībhāva* to be the designation of "indeclinable. Thus he says: "not after an *avyayībhāva*" (*nāvyayībhāvāt*). The prohibition [of the rule] *na lumatā* (Pāṇini 1.1.63) is the indicator that the prohibition does not apply to those [suffixes] which, by virtue of being among *svādiṣu*, would otherwise cause the designation of "word" (*pada*) to apply to them.

In the rule *jhrvi.ṭa ṭhana lumatāṅgasya*, there is the Vārttika: *uttarapadatve cāpadādividhau*. Its meaning is that when the designation of a word (*padavyapadeśa*) is to be applied to the second member of a compound (*uttarapada*), the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of rules conditioned by suffixes) does not take effect, with the exception of operations concerning the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*). In examples such as *paramavācā*: in the analytical derivation (*vigraha*) "that which is both supreme (*paramā*) and speech (*vāk*)," we have the sequence *paramā sū vāc su*. When the compound is formed, there is elision (*luk*) of the case-endings (*sup*) belonging to its members; subsequently, when the case-suffix is added to the whole, the form *paramavācā* results.

In that regard, regarding the word *vāk*, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) applied for the sake of the compound is relied upon by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule; consequently, because it ends in a *sup* suffix, it receives the designation *pada*. Thus, the substitution of *k* for *c* (as prescribed by *coḥ kuḥ*, Pāṇini 8.2.30) would apply. Therefore, it must be stated that when the status of being a *pada* is to be designated for the subsequent member of a compound, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule does not operate.

If, in the case of *dadhisecau*, where the analysis (*vigraha*) is *dadhnaḥ sec-au*, one intends to apply the prohibition of the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.111)—relying on the status of being a *pada* by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle after the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending that is a part of the compound—that prohibition would not occur. Therefore, it is stated [in the Vārttika]: "In the case of a rule concerning what is not the beginning of a word" (*apadādividhau*). The intention of the Vārttika is that since the prohibition of *ṣ* is a rule concerning the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*), the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle certainly applies, and thus there is no fault.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, having provided the explanation that "in the presence of a suffix beginning with *ya* or *ca*, the preceding element receives the designation *bha*," demonstrated that the Vārttika could be rejected on the grounds that in examples such as *paramavācā*, the status of being a *pada* is absent due to the status of being a *bha*, and thus the application of the *kutva* rule does not arise.

If the *vārttika* regarding this were rejected, then since the meaning—"the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* does not apply in the case of a rule concerning what follows a non-word-initial (*apadādi*)"—would not be obtained, one might ask: how could the prohibition of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) based on being a word-initial (*padāditva*) be established in examples such as *dadhiseṣau*? Anticipating this doubt, the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated: in the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*, the analysis is not *padasyādiḥ* ("the beginning of a word"), but rather *padādādiḥ* ("the beginning after a word").

And thus, in the word *dadhi*, there is no substitution of *ṣ* for the initial *s* of the following [suffix]. Regarding this, one might raise the objection: "In cases such as *ṛkṣu* and *vākṣu*, there would also be a prohibition of *ṣ*-substitution; for since the word *ṛc* is designated as a *pada* by the rule *svādiṣu* (Pāṇini 1.4.17), the prohibition of *ṣ*-substitution would consequently apply to the initial *s* of the suffixes following it. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states: the prohibition of *ṣ*-substitution does not apply to those [suffixes] following words that receive the designation of *pada* by the rule *svādiṣu*; therefore, there is no fault in examples such as *vākṣu*.

In the case of *dadhisecāvat*, however, by relying on the intervening case-ending (*vibhakti*), the word *dadhi* receives the designation of *pada* according to the rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam* (Pāṇini 1.4.14), and not [the designation of *pada*] by the rule *svādiṣu*. Therefore, the prohibition of the change to *ṣ* for the following *s* indeed takes effect. The indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this point is the inclusion of the term *sāt* in the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*. For that [term] is intended to prohibit the change to *ṣ* in cases such as *agnisāt*.

Regarding the word *agni*, since it possesses the status of a *pada* by the rule *svādiṣu*, the prohibition of the change to *ṣ* for the initial *s* following it would already be established by the rule *padādādeḥ* alone; thus, the inclusion of the term *sāt* would be redundant. However, since that term is indeed employed, the *Bhāṣya* offers the resolution that this very fact serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the following rule. He recites that very point: "The prohibition of *sāt* is an indicator. [The indicator is: *sthānivadādeśo* (Pāṇini 1.1.56).

Because of the prohibition [of *ātva*] regarding the substitute by the rule *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe* (Pāṇini 7.2.86), there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a substitute is like the original (*sthānivat*). He states *yuṣmadasmadoriti* in order to reject the *sthānivadbhāva* rule. By the rule *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe*, after a case-ending beginning with a consonant (*hal*), the *ā* is prescribed for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*; then, when a substitute follows, that *ātva* is prohibited.

In that regard, since a substitute for a case-ending (*vibhaktyādeśa*) lacks the status of being a case-ending itself, there would be no possibility of *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) occurring after such a substitute; therefore, what is the purpose of the prohibition "provided it is not a substitute" (*anādeśe*)? The fact that this [prohibition] is stated serves to indicate the principle that "a substitute is like the original" (*sthānivad ādeśaḥ*). Consequently, by virtue of the status of being a case-ending being attributed to the substitute for a case-ending through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, *ātva* would apply after it; thus, the term "not a substitute" (*anādeśa*) is stated in order to prohibit that. This is how its own portion [of the rule] finds its utility. And so, the intention is that the entire sūtra may be rejected.

Regarding *jhrjñā.paṭa* (Pāṇini 6.1.8), because of the mention of *lyap* in the rule *ṭhaado jagghirlyaptikiti* (Pāṇini 2.4.36), there is a *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) that in the case of an operation concerning an *al* (vowel or consonant), the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitution of the original element) does not occur. Now, an objection (*nanu*) is raised: To state the prohibition "not in the case of an operation concerning an *al*" (*analvidhau*), it must first be stated that "a substitute (*ādeśa*) is like the original (*sthānivat*). For a prohibition cannot be established without first specifying that which is to be prohibited. Therefore, how can the statement "a substitute is like the original" be rejected? To this [the author replies]:

He says: "The form *jagdhi* [is derived thus]. In forms such as *prajagdhya*, the substitution of *jagdhi* for the root *ad* is prescribed when the suffix *lyap* follows. Since the *lyap*—which is the substitute for *ktvā*—possesses both *kit*-status and the property of beginning with *t* by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, the substitution is established even after *lyap* by the rule *ti kiti* itself; so what is the purpose of including *lyap* in the rule? Its inclusion serves to indicate that the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply in an operation (*alvidhi*) concerning an *al* (phoneme)."

Furthermore, since the substitution of *jagdhi* is prescribed by relying on the phoneme *ti*, the portion [of the rule] stating "because *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply there" and the portion stating "in the case of a non-vowel operation (*analvidhau*)" are established by that very [instance] as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Thus, the sense is that the entire *sthānivatsūtra* would be rendered purposeless. However, in the *Kaustubha*, the necessity of the *sthānivatsūtra* has been established. [Now begins] *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57).

While it should have been stated as *oḥ hrasvāt*, the use of the pratyāhāra *eṅ hrasvāt* indicates that the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply in the case of the elision of the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhilopa*). In the rule *Pāṇini 1.1.57* (*jhrvi.ṭa ṭhaacaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau*), the purpose of the phrase *pūrvavidhau* was stated to be [avoiding the substitution of *guṇa*] in the example *he gauḥ*; however, that [purpose] was refuted in the *Mahābhāṣya*.

For instance, when the word *go* is followed by the vocative suffix *su*, resulting in *go-asu*, the suffix *su* undergoes the treatment of being marked with *Ṇ* by the rule "goto ṇit" (Pāṇini 7.1.90). Consequently, by the rule "aco ñṇiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.115), the vowel *o* undergoes *vṛddhi*, resulting in *gau-as*. At this stage, because the *au* (the result of *vṛddhi*) is caused by a subsequent element, it is treated as if it were the original *o* by the rule "acaḥ parasmin" (Pāṇini 1.1.57). Since it thus retains the status of an *eṅ* (being *au*), the subsequent vocative suffix *su* would have to be elided by the rule "eṅhrasvāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.69). Thus, [the objection] arises that the elision of the vocative suffix would be required.

If, however, it were stated as "in a preceding operation" (*pūrvavidhau*), then because the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) would not apply here—since the elision (*lopa*) would concern only what follows the original vowel (*sthānin*) and not what precedes it—it must be explained that the elision of the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhilopa*) would not occur. But that is not the case. For instance, the mention of *eṅ* in the rule *eṅhrasvāt* would be redundant. Nor should it be argued that in the absence of that [mention of *eṅ*], the elision of the vocative suffix would not occur in forms such as *agno*, *vāyo*, *khaṭve*, and *māle*.

In the case of *agnau* and *vāyo*, the elision of the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhi-lopa*) is established simply by the rule "after a short vowel" (*hrasvāt*), because the quality (*guṇa*) [of *o*] is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). Furthermore, in cases such as *khaṭve* and *māle*, since the single *e* sound—which occurs in place of the long *ā* (*āp*) by the application of the rule "and in the vocative" (*saṃbuddhau ca*, Pāṇini 7.3.106)—is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) and thus possesses the property of being *āp*, the elision of the vocative suffix is established by the very rule "after *hal*, *ī*, and *āp*" (*halṅyābbhyaḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.68). Nor should it be argued that the mention of *eṅ* [in the rule *eṅhrasvāt*] is intended to justify the elision of the vocative suffix even for the word *go*, which would otherwise not be desired.

In that case, one should have simply said *o-hrasvāt*. By not saying that and instead employing the pratyāhāra *eṅ-hrasvāt*, [the author] indicates that in the context of the elision of the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhi-lopa*), the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*)—according to the rule *acaḥ parasmin*—"does not apply. Consequently, since there is no status of being a substitute, the elision would not occur in examples such as *agne* and *vāyo*; thus, the inclusion of *eṅ* is purposeful.

The intention of the Bhāṣya is that even in the case of *gauḥ*, since there is an absence of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original), and because the condition of being followed by *eṅ* is absent, the elision (*lopa*) does not apply; therefore, the purpose of the rule *pūrvavidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.56) is not required there. Thus he says: *ohrasvāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.69). Regarding the rule *pratyayalope* (Pāṇini 1.1.62): due to the prohibition in *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63), it is understood through an *jñāpaka* (indicative mark) that the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the operation based on the presence of a suffix) takes effect even when there is *luk* elision.

Objection: Since the rule *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* states that when a suffix is elided (*lopa*), an operation conditioned by that suffix occurs, it would not apply when there is a suffixal *luk*-elision; for it is said that the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* applies to *lopa*, not to *luk*. Consequently, in forms such as *pañca* and *sapta*, where *jaś* and *śas* are elided by the rule *ṣaḍbhyo luk* (Pāṇini 7.1.22), the designation *pada* would not occur due to the absence of *pratyayalakṣaṇa*. Anticipating this objection, he says: *na lumatā*.

If the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix) were not to apply when a suffix is elided (*luk*), then, since there would be no occurrence [of such an operation], the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* stated in the rule "na lumatāṅgasya" would be inconsistent. Furthermore, this [prohibition] has been formulated to indicate that the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* applies not only where there is the non-appearance of a suffix through the term "elision" (*lopa*), but also wherever it occurs through the various terms for elision (*luc*, *luK*, etc.). Therefore, the intended meaning is that there is no fault.

This is included by the statement in the *Jñāpaka-saṃgraha* that "even elisions (*luk*) and the like are [treated as] deletions (*lopa*). There is a difference in the sequence of the statements, but not a difference in their scope. Because of the prohibition in the rule *na ṅi-saṃbuddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.8), it is understood from this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) that the designation *bha* does not apply by virtue of the characteristic of an affix (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the example *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* [becoming] *rājapuruṣaḥ*, one might raise the objection: even though the genitive suffix *ṅas* is elided by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71), the designation *pada* would be sublated by the designation *bha*—according to the rule *yaci bham* (Pāṇini 1.4.18)—due to the application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle. Consequently, the elision of the *n* by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.7) would not apply. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because of the prohibition [of that]. For if the designation *bha* were to occur here by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa*, then the prohibition of *n*-elision in the locative case (*ṅi*) by the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.8) would be rendered purposeless.

In examples such as *parame vyoman*, even though the case-ending *ṅi* is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), the designation *pada* is superseded by the designation *bha*—which applies because the elided suffix still exerts its influence (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*) according to the rule *yaci bham* (Pāṇini 1.4.18). Consequently, the elision of the *n* by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.7) does not apply; so what is the purpose of that prohibition? The point is that the prohibition being stated serves to indicate that the designation *bha* does not occur by virtue of the influence of an elided suffix; thus, in cases such as *rājapuruṣa*, the absence of the *bha*-designation is established.

The term *upadhā* refers to that which precedes the final vowel (Pāṇini 1.1.65). When the author [of the Aṣṭādhyāyī] states, "In the case of a reduplicated word (*āmreḍita*), [the substitution of] the final [vowel] with the preceding one is optional" (Pāṇini 6.1.99), this indicates that the substitution of a single substitute for both [the final and its predecessor] does not apply to the final [vowel].

In the sūtra *jhrvi.ṭa ṭhaalo'ntyātpūrvaṃ*, after citing the paribhāṣā "nānarthake'lontyavidhiranabhyāsavikāre," the occasion for enumerating its purposes mentions "prayojanamavyaktānukaraṇasyāta itau" as one such purpose. Regarding this, the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) prescribed when the sound *it* follows a vowel belonging to an indistinct imitation (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) would, by the paribhāṣā "alo'ntyaparibhāṣā," apply to the final letter, which is the *t*.

Consequently, one would expect the form *paṭata-iti* or *paṭeti*, whereas *paṭati* is desired. Therefore, the paribhāṣā "nānarthake 'lontyavidhiḥ" (the rule regarding the final letter does not apply when [an affix] is meaningless) must be resorted to. The intention is that since the syllable *ac* in *paṭat* is meaningless, the rule for the final letter does not apply there; thus, by the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) for *at* alone, the desired result is achieved. However, in reality, this purpose is not appropriate, because it is understood from the very same indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the subsequent form does not apply to the final letter. Thus he says: "yadayam... (since this...).

If the intention had been for the final *t* of the word *ac* to undergo the *pararūpa* substitution by virtue of the maxim regarding the final letter (*antyaparibhāṣā*), then the rule would have been formulated simply as *vāmreḍitasya*. This is because, since the *pararūpa* substitution for the final letter is already established as obligatory by the preceding rule (Pāṇini 6.1.98), only an optional provision (*vikalpa*) would need to be enjoined. Since he did not formulate the rule in that way, but instead stated, "*nāmreḍitasyāntyasya tu vā*" ("but optionally for the final of a non-amreḍita [word]"), this indicates that the *pararūpa* substitution does not apply to the final letter.

Furthermore, when *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the form of the subsequent vowel) would have applied to the reduplicated *at*, that was prohibited; thus, the rule prescribing an optional alternative for the final letter finds its utility in its own domain. And so, since by this very [rule] the absence of *pararūpa* for the final letter is established even in the case of *paṭat iti*, the intention is that this is not the purpose of the *paribhāṣā*: "In a meaningless [element], there is no application of the rule for the final letter. [From the *Jñāpakapāda*: "The word itself is the form of the word" (Pāṇini 1.1.68). The mention of the word *rūpa* (form) indicates that there exists for a word a "self" (*svam*) distinct from its form.

Because of the rule *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ* (Pāṇini 1.1.24), which indicates that a numeral ending in *ṣ* or *n* receives the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *ṣaṭ*, it follows that when a word is being designated as a technical term (*śabda-saṃjñā*), there is no application of its own form (*svarūpa-vidhi*). Now, one might object: In the sūtra *svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya*, since the word *sva* denotes "one's own" (*ātmīya*) and thus does not depend on the apprehension of a relationship [as in a genitive], and since it is presented first to the sense of hearing, the word *sva* will naturally grasp the word's own form; so what is the purpose of including the word *rūpa*? To this, he says: "The inclusion of the word *rūpa*... [is for the following reason].

And thus, because of the mention of "form" (*rūpa*), it is understood that the word possesses its own specific form (*svarūpa*) which is distinct from its form [as a mere sequence of sounds] and is qualified by its meaning. Furthermore, because of the mention of "form," it is understood that the word has its own specific form, distinct from its form [as such], and qualified by its meaning. Thus, the mention of "form" is for the purpose of making known that the word's specific form is indeed qualified by its meaning; by this, it is established that in this treatise, only the specific form of the word as qualified by its meaning is taken into account, and not that which is devoid of meaning.

Consequently, since the requirement for "the mention of meaningful items" (*arthavadgrahaṇa*) is obtained from the Sūtra itself, it is established that the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding "the mention of meaningful items" need not be formulated. Furthermore, it should be understood that arguments such as "being the first to present itself" are set aside by the explicit mention of "form" (*rūpa*). Now, one might object: let there be no such restriction as "not when a grammatical designation (*saṃjñā*) is involved. Nor should it be argued that in the absence of that restriction, even in this science of grammar, there would be a grasping of the actual form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*) in cases where designations such as *ṭi* and *ghu* occur.

In the rule *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ*, the term *ṣaṭ* refers to the actual word-form *ṣaṣ*; thus, by the authority of that statement, the designation *ṣaṭ* is established for the form ending in *n*. Consequently, the inclusion of the letter *ṣ* would otherwise be redundant, and this redundancy serves to indicate that in technical grammatical designations (*śabda-saṃjñā*), there is no application of the rule regarding the identity of the word-form itself (*svarūpa-vidhi*). This ensures that in rules such as *ṭi ghu*, there is no grasping of the word-form itself. Thus, he says: *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ*. The implication is that the condition "not being a technical designation" (*aśabda-saṃjñā*) is indeed unnecessary.

Pāṇini 1.2.18: *na ktvā seṭ*. The mention of *jhal* in the rule *iko jhal* (1.2.9) indicates that the prohibition of *kit*-status applies only to that which is original (*aupadeśika*), and not to that which is transferred by extension (*ātideśika*). Objection: In the rule *na ktvā seṭ*, the mention of *ktvā* should be omitted. It cannot be argued that if it were absent, there would be a prohibition of *kit*-status even for the *niṣṭhā* suffixes in forms such as *gudhitaḥ* and *gudhitavān*, which would consequently result in *upadhā-guṇa* (vocalization of the penultimate vowel).

The rule *niṣṭhā śīṅ-svadimi-dikṣvidi-dhṛṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.19) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) since the prohibition [of *kittva*] is already established by the preceding rule *na seṭ* (1.2.18). The restriction is that the *niṣṭhā* suffixes following only the roots beginning with *śīṅ* are not *kit*. Consequently, in forms such as *gudhitaḥ*, there is no fault because there is no prohibition of *kittva* for the *niṣṭhā* suffix.

Nor should it be argued that even in such cases as *papiva* and *papima*, when the forms *papā-iva* and *papā-ima* arise, the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "there is elision of the vowel before a *kṅit* suffix" (*kṅiti*) would not occur, because the prohibition of *kit*-status applies to a suffix marked with *iṭ*. This is not so, because the elision is established precisely by taking *iṭ* as its cause. Nor should it be argued that even in such cases as *jagmiva* and *jaghṇiva*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) by the rule "there is elision for *gam*, *han*, *jan*, *khan*, and *ghas* before a *kṅit* suffix, except for *aṅ*" (*gamahanajanakhanaghasāṃ lopaḥ kṅityanaṅi*) would not occur. This is not so, because by the very same indicator (*jñāpaka*), there is no prohibition of *kit*-status for the *liṭ* suffix when it is marked with *iṭ*.

He states the very indicator [of this]: "the mention of *jhal*. By the rule *iko jhal*, the *kit*-status of a *san* beginning with a *jhal* sound following a stem ending in an *ik* vowel is prescribed; examples include *bumūṣati* and so forth. In that context, it must be stated that by the mention of *jhal*, the *kit*-status of a *san* beginning with *a* and followed by an *iṭ* augment—such as in *śiśayiṣate* and the like—is thereby excluded.

However, in the rule *na ktvā seṭ*, if the mention of *ktvā* were absent, there would be a prohibition of *kittva* for any suffix whatsoever that has a *seṭ* augment; consequently, since this would also result in the prohibition of *kittva* for the *seṭ* suffix *san* in forms such as *śiśayiṣate*, the mention of *jhal* in the rule *iko jhal* would be purposeless. That very mention serves to indicate that the prohibition in the rule *na seṭ* applies only to an original (*aupadeśika*) *kittva*, and not to one that is transferred (*ātideśika*).

The *kit* status of *san* when followed by a *seṭ* suffix is not original (*aupadeśika*), but rather derived through extension (*ātideśika*) by the rule "iko jhala" (Pāṇini 1.2.9). Since this [extended *kit* status] would not be prohibited by the rule "na seṭ" (Pāṇini 1.2.18), the mention of *jhal* was made so that the rule finds its application in its own domain. As for its purpose elsewhere, in forms such as *jagmiva*, the prohibition "na seṭ" does not apply to the extended *kit* status [of the *liṭ*] by the rule "asaṃyogālliṭ kit" (Pāṇini 1.2.5); thus, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) is established by the condition *kṅiti*. This is the intended meaning.

JHRAJÑĀ.PAṬA: *ŪKĀLO’C* (Sūtra 1.2.27). The rule *VIBHĀṢĀ PṚṢṬAPRATIVACANE HEḤ* (Sūtra 8.2.93), which prescribes a protracted (*pluta*) vowel of one measure (*mātrika*), indicates that a [vowel] of one measure does not occur at the end [of a word]. The prescription of lengthening in *ATO DĪR̥GHO YAÑI, SUPI CA* (Sūtras 7.3.101–102) indicates that a [vowel] of one measure does not occur in the middle [of a word]. The prescription of a protracted vowel of two measures in *OM ABHYĀDĀNE* (Sūtra 8.2.87) indicates that a [vowel] of two measures does not occur at the end [of a word].

Objection: In the rule *ūkālaḥ*, the term *ū* is a conjunctive mention (*praśliṣṭanirdeśa*) of vowels having one, two, and three morae (*mātrā*). In that context, it is intended that by following the respective order (*yathāsaṃkhya*), the designation *hrasva* (short) applies to the one-mora vowel, the designation *dīrgha* (long) to the two-mora vowel, and the designation *pluta* (protracted) to the three-mora vowel. How, then, is it understood that this conjunctive mention refers specifically to those arranged in sequence as one-mora, two-mora, and three-mora?

Fearing that if a *mātrika* (one-mora) sound were to occur either in the middle or at the end, or if a *dvimātra* (two-mora) sound were to occur at the beginning or the end, or if a *trimātra* (three-mora) sound were to occur at the beginning or the middle, then the established rule—that shortness belongs exclusively to the one-mora sound and so forth—would not be maintained, he says: "This is the statement regarding the *pluta* [protracted] form of the *mātrika*. For if the *mātrika* were designated as occurring at the end, then according to the rule "that which is at the end is termed *pluta*," it would have to be stated that the one-mora sound possesses the designation *pluta*.

Furthermore, because the single-mora *ik* in the word *hi* would already be a protracted (*pluta*) vowel, the prescription of its protraction in the rule *vibhāṣā pṛṣṭaprativacane heḥ* would be purposeless. Therefore, that prescription indicates that a single-mora vowel does not occur as a final [element]. Likewise, if a single-mora vowel were to occur in the middle, then according to the rule *yo madhye sa dīrghasaṃjñaḥ*, that which is in the middle is termed "long" (*dīrgha*); since a single-mora vowel would thus be long, the prescription of a two-mora protracted vowel in the rule *ato dīrgho yañi* would be purposeless.

Therefore, this indicates that it does not occur at the end of a two-mora (*dvimātra*) vowel. And thus, since its occurrence at the end of a one-mora (*mātrika*) vowel is impossible—whether at the beginning or in the middle—and its occurrence at the end of a two-mora vowel is impossible—whether in the middle or at the beginning—it follows by implication that it occurs at the end of a three-mora (*trimātra*) vowel. Consequently, the designations *hrasva* (short), *dīrgha* (long), and *pluta* (protracted) for one-mora, two-mora, and three-mora vowels are established according to their respective order; this is the intended meaning. [Pāṇini 1.3.1] *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*.

In the rule *aci snuḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), the mention of *snu* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitution of *uvaṅ* does not apply to a suffix. Furthermore, the prescription of the substitution of *au* for the final vowel of *div* before the nominative singular ending (*su*) indicates that the case-endings beginning with *su* (*svādayaḥ*) are produced after the word *div*.

Thus [it is said]. [Objection: But surely, by the rule *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*, the designation *dhātu* (verbal root) is prescribed for those such as *bhū* and others that are recited in the *dhātupāṭha*. Consequently, in the case of *trasnu*, there would be the substitution of *uvaṅ* [for *nu*]. Since *nu* is recited in the *dhātupāṭha*, in the form *trasnu-au*, because *nu* is a verbal root, the substitution of *uvaṅ* by the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvāṃ yvoḥ* would be possible. [Response: It is not the case that *ṇu* is recited among the roots, but rather *nu*; nor does this [form *nu*] possess similarity (*sārūpya*) with that [root *ṇu*].

And thus, one must explain how this doubt could arise: since the *nu* suffix itself is a verbal root (*dhātu*) in its application, the similarity of form (*sārūpya*) exists in the *nu* of *trasnu* as well because of its *st*-nature. To this, he says: "The mention of *śnu*. If the substitution of *uvaṅ* were to apply to a suffix as well, then even in the case of the suffix *śnu*, the *uvaṅ* would be established simply by its being a verbal root; consequently, the mention of *śnu* would be purposeless. Yet, that very mention serves to indicate that the substitution of *uvaṅ* does not occur for that which is a verbal root similar in form to a suffix.

And thus, the sense is that there is no fault. Now, one might object: even so, the word *div* which is not [grammatically] derived (*avyutpanna*) would—by virtue of having the same form as the root *div* listed in the Dhātupāṭha—be designated as a verbal root (*dhātu*). Consequently, by the prohibition "that which is not a root," its designation as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would not be established. And if that were the case, the derivation of case endings such as the nominative (*su*) conditioned by being a nominal stem would not occur. Anticipating this objection, he says: "divaḥ sāu" (Pāṇini 7.1.84).

The rule *diva aut* (Pāṇini 7.1.84), which prescribes the substitution of *aut* for *div* when followed by the nominative singular suffix *su*, would otherwise be inconsistent because *div* lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), making the occurrence of *su* impossible. This inconsistency serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the suffixes beginning with *su* are also produced after the word *div* when it functions as a verbal root (*dhātu*). Thus, there is no fault [in the derivation]. However, in reality, these two indicators are presented without relying on the principle that only those words beginning with *bhū* and denoting an action (*kriyā*) receive the designation of *dhātu*.

It should be noted that in the word *trasnu*, the designation of "root" (*dhātu*) does not apply—despite its similarity in form to a root—because the particle *nu* lacks the capacity to denote an action, or because the word *div* is an underived (*avyutpanna*) term. Furthermore, the recitation of certain roots with the marker *it* (indicating the *it-dhatu* class) accompanied by the augment *num*—such as *undir* in the sense of "cleansing," *skandir* in the senses of "motion" and "drying," and so forth—indicates that the rule for the substitution of *iṭ* does not apply to such types of roots.

Regarding the rule *ṭhacuṭū*, there is the Vārttika: "The addition of *hara* [is required]. In forms such as *rudhira*, it must be stated that *ira* is designated as *it*. Otherwise, by the rule *irito vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.57), the augment *aṅ* would not apply. Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because the *repha* (*r*) is designated as *it* by the rule *halantyam* (1.3.3) and the *ikāra* (*i*) is designated as *it* by the rule *upadeśe 'janunāsikaḥ* (1.3.2); for if that were the case, there would also result the undesired application of rules conditioned by being *idit*.

Furthermore, in cases such as *bhettā* and *chettā*, the augment *num* would apply by the rule *idito num* (Pāṇini 7.1.58). Therefore, since it is impossible to justify this through the designation *it* applied to the individual components, the intention of the Vārttika is that the designation *it* must be stated for the entire cluster *ir*. However, the author of the Bhāṣya maintains that since the desired result is established by the designation *it* applied to each component individually, the designation *it* for the cluster need not be stated. Nor should it be argued that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *num* being applied due to the *it*-designation [of the cluster].

Because certain roots such as *undir* (in the sense of "cleansing") and *skandir* (in the sense of "motion" and "drying up") are recited with the *num* augment attached (*irita*), it is indicated that the purpose of being *irita* does not apply here. Consequently, he explained that there is no occurrence of the *num* augment in forms such as *bhettā*. He states this with the words beginning "undir niśāmane," and so forth. Regarding the rule *ṇeraṇau* (Pāṇini 1.3.67), the prohibition [contained in the rule] *anādhyāne* indicates that the *ātmanepada* indeed occurs for verbs of this class.

Objection: Regarding the rule *ṇeraṇau yatkarma ṇau cetsa kartānādhyāne*, its meaning is that the ātmanepada suffix occurs after a causative (*ṇic*) verb if the very action that was expressed by the non-causative (*aṇ*) is expressed by the causative, and if the factor that was the object (*karman*) in the non-causative becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the causative, provided it is not a case of reflecting (*adhyāna*). In this context, the phrase "provided it is not a case of reflecting" (*anādhyāne*) is redundant.

Since only those actions whose state (bhāva) resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvakriyā*) are the domain of the *karmavadbhāva* rule, and since actions whose purpose is meditation (*ādhyāna*) have their action residing in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyā*), they are not subject to the *karmavadbhāva* rule. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states "anādhyāne" to show its purpose: it indicates that for verbs of this class, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs. The meaning here is that for those roots which are in the non-causative (*aṇyanta*) state whatever is the object, when they are in the causative (*ṇyanta*) state that same thing becomes the agent; even though the action then resides in the agent, the middle voice still occurs.

Kaiyaṭa states that because of this [rule], the ātmanepada is established in such cases as "the servants see the king" (*tena paśyanti bhṛtyā rājānam*) and "the king shows himself to the servants" (*darśayate bhṛtyān rājā*). Those who wish to understand this truth clearly should consult the *Kaumudī*, which is a commentary on this very sūtra, as well as its commentary, the *Bālamanoramā*. [The rule] *jñā-paṭa-anu-parābhyāṃ kṛñaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.79) [is stated]; [the optionality] regarding the *dyutādi* group is due to the statement of the alternative (*vāvacana*).

[The objection: Because of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), it is understood that the *ātmanepada* does not occur where the *parasmaipada* is applicable. [The questioner asks: But even though the *parasmaipada* is prescribed by the rule "anuparābhyāṃ kṛñaḥ," since there is no restrictive rule stating that only the *parasmaipada* must occur, the *ātmanepada* might also occur in that context; therefore, he says: "because of the optional statement (*vāvacana*) regarding the *dyutādi* group."

If the ātmanepada were to occur even in the domain of the parasmaipada, then the optional prescription of the parasmaipada by means of the word *vā* ("optionally") in the rule *dyudbhyo luṅi* (Pāṇini 1.3.91)—following the word *vā* from the preceding rule *vā kyaṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.90)—would be purposeless; for the two [sets of] verbal endings would be established even without the recurrence of the word *vā*. Therefore, the recurrence of the word *vā* serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) that the ātmanepada does not occur in the domain of the parasmaipada. This is the intended meaning: thus there is no fault.

In the *Jñāpaṭala*, up to the rule *kaḍaḍḍatdh;ārādekā saṃjñā* (Pāṇini 1.4.1), there is a single designation. The inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* in the rule *hṛkroranyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 1.4.53) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that when the designation of object (*karma-saṃjñā*) is not applied, the designation of agent (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) does indeed apply. [Objection: But surely, according to the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇāmaṇikartā sa ṇau* (Pāṇini 1.4.52), in examples such as *gamayati devadattaṃ grāmaṃ yajñadattaḥ*, it is stated that Devadatta—who is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the non-causative (*aṇi*) state—receives the designation of object (*karma-saṃjñā*) in the causative (*ṇi*) state.

Just as Devadatta possesses the status of an object (*karman*) because he is the locus of the result produced by the operation [denoted] by the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇij*), so too does he possess the status of an agent (*kartṛ*) because he is the locus of the operation denoted by the verbal root that is the base of the causative (*ṇic*). Consequently, since Devadatta is the convergence of two designations, one might suspect that two case-endings (accusative and instrumental) would apply due to those two designations; anticipating this objection, the author says: "In the case of *hṛ* and *kṛ*" (*hṛkroḥ*).

If the instigating agent (*prayojyakartṛ*) were to possess two designations simultaneously, then [the author] would have included even the roots *hṛ* and *kṛ* along with the group beginning with *gam* (gatyādi) and would not have employed the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally"). By this, it is indicated that when the instigating agent has the designation "object" (*karman*), it does not simultaneously bear the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*). Therefore, there is no fault; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the rule *vipratiṣedhe param* (Pāṇini 1.4.2): the inclusion of the word *śvan* in the *gaura*-group of nominal stems indicates that the accent known as *anudāttanivṛtti-svara* does not apply to the word *śvan*.

In the rule *vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam* ("when there is a conflict, the subsequent operation prevails"), there is the Vārttika *antaraṅgaṃ ca*. Its meaning is that the *antaraṅga* (inner) operation is stronger. Its purpose is demonstrated by the immediately following Vārttika: *yaṇ-okādeśetvotvāni guṇavṛddhidvirvacanāllopasvarebhyaḥ* ("the *yaṇ*, the substitution of *o*, the substitutions of *i* and *u*, prevail over *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, reduplication, elision of *a*, and accent"). In this context, regarding the fact that the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) occurs before the elision of *a* (*al-lopa*) due to its being *antaraṅga*, the example given is *śunā*.

When *śvan* + *a* is present, by the rule *śvayuvamaghonām* (Pāṇini 6.4.133), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), resulting in *śu* + *a* + *an* + *a*. At this stage, both the elision of *an* by *allopo'naḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.134) and the substitution of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) by *saṃprasāraṇācca* (Pāṇini 6.1.108) would apply. However, because the latter is internal (*antaraṅga*), the single preceding form alone takes effect. Now, one might object that there is no difference in the final form whether *an* is elided or the single preceding form is substituted.

If it is argued that the description of the internal factor (*antaraṅga*) as being stronger is irrelevant to the present case, we say no. For when there is elision (*alopa*) of the suffix, since the vowel *a* is udātta, when that [vowel] is elided, the following unaccented (*anudātta*) case-ending becomes udātta by the rule "anudāttasya ca yatro-dāttalopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.161). Thus, the word *śunā* becomes oxytone (*antodātta*).

However, when there is the prior form (*pūrvarūpa*), then by the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.5), the single-substitute form of the vowel *u* becomes udātta, while the case-ending remains anudātta; thus, the word *śunā* becomes mid-toned (*madhyodātta*). Since a difference in accent (*svara*) exists [in this view], the Bhāṣyakāras—having accepted such a difference in accent as the basis for the purpose [of the rule]—refuted that difference in accent in order to reject that [proposed] purpose.

For instance, in the case of *śunī*, even though the elision of the *al* suffix occurs, the accent of the disappearance of the acute (*udāttanivṛttisvara*) applies by virtue of the word *śvan*. Since the word *śvan* ends in *n* within the *gaurādi* group, its form is established simply by the suffix *ṅīp* according to Pāṇini 4.1.5 (*ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*), so what is the purpose of including it there [in the *gaurādi* list]? Furthermore, if the suffix were *ṅīp*, because it is marked with *p* (indicating it is *pit*), it would be unaccented; consequently, the vowel *ī* in the word *śunī* would become unaccented.

However, since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would be acute by the accent of the affix (*pratyayasvara*), the vowel *ī* in *śunī* would be acute; thus, because there is a difference in accent, the word is listed in the *gaurādi* group to ensure that the final syllable is acute. Therefore, one must state how this [listing] can serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Even when the suffix *ṅīp* is present, in the case of *śvan + ī*, after the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) has occurred, we have the form *śu-an-ī*. At this stage, by the rule *allopo'naḥ*, the acute (*udātta*) vowel *a* is elided. Consequently, by the rule *anudāttasya ca yatro dāttalopaḥ*, the grave (*anudātta*) vowel *ī* becomes acute, thereby establishing that the word is oxytone (*antodātta*). Thus, the inclusion of the word *śvan* in the *gaurādi* list is redundant; its very redundancy indicates that the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accentual rule for the disappearance of the acute) does not apply to the word *śvan*. Furthermore, in the case of *śūnā* as well, because the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktyudāttatva*) does not apply due to the elision of the *a* (*allope*), [the same principle holds].

The intention of the Bhāṣya is that because there is no difference between the prior form (pūrvarūpa) and either the accent (svara) or the phonetic form (rūpa), the rule "that which is internal is stronger" does not serve as a justification for the single-substitute (ekādeśa) over the elision of *a* (al-lopa). Having taken all this into account, he says: "the word *śvan* is listed among the *gaura*-group. Regarding the term "accent resulting from the removal of an acute" (*udāttanivṛttisvara*): the meaning is that when an acute accent is lost, the accent consisting of the acute nature of the grave vowel is prescribed by the rule "and where there is the loss of an acute, [there is the acute] of the grave" (*anudāttasya ca yatro-dāttalopaḥ*).

"Jhrjñā. Paṭa: *sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam* (Sūtra 1.4.42). The inclusion of the word *tama* (most effective) indicates that in the application of technical designations (*saṃjñā*) for *kārakas*, there is no comparative degree (*taratama-yoga*). Objection (*vi.ṭa*): Since all *kārakas* are "effectors" (*sādhaka*) insofar as they bring about some action, even if the word *sādhaka* were not used [in the sūtra], the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) would simply not apply to what is not an effector. Therefore, the inclusion of the word *sādhaka* will itself imply the meaning "the most effective effector" (*sādhakatama*); so what is the purpose of including the word *tama*? [Response: [The word *tama* is necessary to exclude other *kārakas* from being designated as the instrument when they are equally or more effective than the actual instrument.]

Just as when it is said, "A maiden should be given to one who is handsome," since there is no inclination to give her to one who is not handsome, the phrase "to the most handsome" is understood even without explicitly mentioning the word "most" (*tama*), so too [one might object]. Anticipating this, he says: "The mention of *tama*. And thus, by the mention of *tama*, it is indicated that in other sections concerning grammatical relations (*kāraka-prakaraṇa*), apart from this specific sūtra, the comparative and superlative degrees (*taratama-bhāva*) are not resorted to.

Otherwise, in the rule *ādhāro’dhikaraṇam* (Pāṇini 1.4.45), since the status of being a substratum (*ādhāra*) would already be obtained through the force of the great technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*) which is significant according to its etymology (*anvartha*), the explicit mention of that [substratum] again would serve a specific purpose: namely, that the substratum called "predominant" (*prakṛṣṭa*)—that is, one which pervades all parts—is what constitutes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). If that were the case, the designation would apply only to instances such as "oil in sesame seeds" (*tileṣu tailam*) or "clarified butter in curds" (*dadhi sarpiḥ*), but it would not apply to cases such as "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*). This is the intended meaning. Thus ends the first chapter.
Now begins the second chapter.

In the rule *yuvā khalati* (Pāṇini 2.1.66), although the condition "with a word in grammatical apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇena*) is understood from the previous context, the mention here as being in a different grammatical relation (*vyadhikaraṇa*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This indicates that a compound occurs between a preceding member and a succeeding member only when they are of the same kind. Thus, by the rule *yuvā khalati-palita-valina-jaratībhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.67), the formation of a compound between the word *yuvan* and words such as *khalati* is prescribed; and in that rule, the term "with a word in grammatical apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇena*) continues to apply.

Since it is impossible for the masculine noun *yuvan* to stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with feminine words such as *khalatī*, this Vedic-style (*sautra*) reference is inconsistent; being so, it indicates that here, by the word *yuvan*, a term of the same gender-class as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is understood. Because the subsequent member *jaratī* is feminine, when a compound with it is intended, the feminine word *yuvati* alone is compounded with it—this is the meaning.

Although grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is observed even between two words of different genders, as in *mukhaṃ candraḥ* ("the face is the moon"), this is not the case everywhere; rather, it occurs only in instances where there is common consensus, and even then, only when one of the two has a fixed gender—this is the intention of the Bhāṣya, according to the Udyota. The purpose of making this statement known is that, as clarified in the Bhāṣya, the desired grammatical operation is accomplished even without the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating: "When a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included."

Pāṇini 2.2.19: *upapadaṃ tiṅ* (an affix other than a verbal suffix is a *karmadhāraya* compound with its *upapada*). The prohibition of *atiṅ* (the mention of "not being a verbal suffix") in this rule makes it known that the rule *sup supā* (2.1.4) does not apply here. Objection: In the rule *upapadaṃ tiṅ*, the inclusion of the term *atiṅ* should be unnecessary.

Furthermore, one cannot argue that in the absence of *atiṅ*, in the example *kārako vrajati*, the word *vrajati* would still form a compound with the word *kāraka* because *vrajati* is designated as an *upapada* by the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* (3.3.10), since that rule uses the locative ending *kriyāyām*. [This objection is raised to show that the mention of *atiṅ* is indeed necessary.]

Anticipating the objection that since the word *sup* from the rule *sup supā* also recurs here, the meaning of the sūtra would be that a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is compounded with another capable word (*samartha*) ending in a case-suffix—and thus, because *vrajati* does not end in a case-suffix, the possibility of compounding does not arise—he says: "The prohibition [is indicated] by the term *atiṅ*. Consequently, being otherwise redundant according to the previously mentioned reasoning, the inclusion of the term *atiṅ* in this sūtra indicates that the rule *sup supā* does not recur in this sūtra nor in the preceding sūtra *kugatiprādayaḥ*.

Furthermore, if that [restriction] were not followed, a compound would occur even with a form ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*); therefore, the mention of *atiṅ* (not ending in a verbal suffix) is for the purpose of preventing that, and thus it serves its purpose within its own scope. Now, one might object: "Since the mention of *atiṅ* occurs in this very rule (*sūtra*), let it be understood that it excludes *su*-suffixes; however, how can its exclusion from the preceding rule be known? To this they reply: In the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ," the connection is divided into two parts: "kuprādayaḥ" and "gatiḥ."

In that regard, the meaning of the first sūtra is that words beginning with *ku* and so forth are compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Likewise, the two rules—*"upapadam"* and *"atiṅ"*—are divided as separate applications (*yoga-vibhāga*). This term *atiṅ* serves as a supplement (*śeṣabhūta*) to both "gati" and "upapada. The term *supā* (with a word ending in a case-suffix) is excluded from both [rules] due to the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*). This term *atiṅ*, being in the nominative case, functions as an adjective qualifying the compound established by the two rules.

And thus, the meaning is that the compound prescribed by the two rules does not consist of a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). Consequently, because the term *ātiṅ* (excluding verbal suffixes) is connected to both rules, the implication is that those two rules also indicate the cessation of the application of the term *supā* (with a nominal suffix).

Thus, since the word *sup* is omitted in both of these two sūtras, the compound of *gatis*, *kārakas*, and *upapadas* with a *kṛt*-derived form is established prior to the addition of the case-endings (*sup*). Consequently, it is stated in the Bhāṣya that the result [of this teaching] is the establishment of the *paribhāṣā*: "The statement regarding the compounding of *gatis*, *kārakas*, and *upapadas* with a *kṛt*-derived form occurs prior to the addition of the case-endings. One should not object: "How can the compounding of *kārakas* be obtained prior to the addition of the case-endings? Some maintain that this is established through the principle of "acceptance by way of a partial admission" (*ekadeśānumati*).

Kaiyaṭa, however, maintains that the compound of *kārakas* is formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32). In this case, because of the mention of *kṛt*, the compound is established prior to the generation of the nominal suffix (*sup*). For, since a compound with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) would not even be possible—due to the continued application of the word *sup* [from the previous rule]—and since the compound is already established with a *kṛdanta* [word], Kaiyaṭa says that the mention of *kṛt* is for the purpose of forming the compound while the word is still in its *kṛdanta* state, before the *sup* has been produced. [Then follows: *anekam anyapadārthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.24).

The prescription of a *dvigu* compound for the final member indicates that a compound may consist of even many words. [Objection: But surely, since the rule *anekam anyapadārthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.24) follows from the rule *sup supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4), the meaning obtained is that a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) denoting a different referent is compounded with another word ending in a case-suffix; thus, by implication, a compound of many words ending in case-suffixes [is established].

The mention of the word *aneka* (more than one) would be redundant because [the formation of] a compound is already obtained. Nor should it be argued that the mention of *aneka* is for the sake of obtaining a compound of many [words], because the formation of a compound of many words is obtained through an *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) itself. He states this very *jñāpaka*: "in the case of the *uttarapada*. By the rule *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.51), a compound of a word denoting a number with a *sub*-ending word in grammatical apposition is prescribed when an *uttarapada* follows.

In the analysis (*vigraha*) "one whose wealth consists of five cows" (*pañca gāvo dhanaṃ yasya*), when the three words form a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there occurs a *dvigu* compound of the two constituent parts "five" (*pañca*) and "cow" (*go*) within the word "wealth" (*dhana*). In that case, if the three words were not first combined into a single compound, the word "wealth" would not possess the status of being the final member (*uttarapada*) of the compound; for the term "final member" (*uttarapada*) is conventionally restricted to the last constituent element of a compound.

And thus, by virtue of the rule prescribing *dvigu* compounds when a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows, it is indicated that a compound may occur even of many inflected words (*subanta*). The sense is that, since the formation of a compound of many words is thereby obtained, the requirement of the term "multiple-word" (*anekapada*) is not tenable. Regarding the phrase "the prescription of *dvigu*": this is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). It should be understood that the prescription of a compound for a word denoting direction (*digvācaka*) with an inflected word (*subanta*) when a subsequent member follows—by means of the rule concerning the meaning of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*)—is also an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned purpose.

The compound *dvandva* is used in the sense of *ca* (Pāṇini 2.2.29). Because of the inclusion of the word *artha*, it is understood that *ca-artha* means "that which has been made by *ca*" (*ca-kṛta-artha*). [Objection: But surely, by the rule "the *dvandva* [compound] is used in the sense of *ca*," it is understood that a *dvandva* occurs wherever the meaning of *ca* is perceived. And thus— "Day after day, leading away a horse, a man, and a beast..."

Regarding the verse, "Vaivasvata is not satiated, like a drunkard with liquor," since the cows and the others are construed with the action of leading in their mutual association, one might fear that even in the sentence "cow, horse, man, beast" (*gāmaśvaṃ puruṣaṃ paśum*), the technical designation *dvandva* would apply because the words function there in the sense of *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction), which consists of mutual association. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because of the mention of 'artha' (meaning). Since the mere statement "or [it is] *dvandva*" would make the grammatical operation impossible for the word *ca*, it will be understood that the operation applies to the *artha* (meaning).

Since this is already established in this way, the fact that [the sūtra] employs the term *artha* ("meaning") indicates that a *dvandva* compound occurs where a meaning is expressed by the particle *ca*. By the inclusion of the word *artha*, a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is understood: a *dvandva* occurs only where a meaning is expressed—that is, manifested—by the particle *ca* itself. However, in the case of "gām aśvam" (cow and horse), the sense of conjunction is understood solely through the repetition of the words "day after day" (*aharahaḥ*), and not by the particle *ca*; therefore, it is not a *dvandva*. This is the intended meaning. [Pāṇini 2.2.36: *niṣṭhā*].

Because of the rule prescribing that the *niṣṭhā* suffix following words denoting genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), or things that are naturally hard (*lūkha*), etc., is udātta at the end [of the compound], there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in this case the *niṣṭhā* occurs as the final member. [Objection: But surely, by the rule "niṣṭhā," the prior placement of a word ending in *niṣṭhā* in a *bahuvrīhi* is taught; examples such as *kṛtakṛtyaḥ* are given. Therefore, in the form *auddālakāyana*, there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix *phak*. In this context, although not included in the Bhāṣya, the statements read there in the Kaimudī are collected and explained. [From *glau*: *glāvam*, *glāvaḥ*. Anticipating the objection that words such as *gaurava* (heaviness) and *māndya* (slowness), being denoters of qualities (*guṇavācaka*), do not form a compound with a word ending in the genitive case—since this is established by the rule *pūraṇaguṇa-sūtra* and others—the author says: "This [rule] is non-eternal. This prohibition of a genitive compound with a quality-word is not universal; for it is indicated by the use of the compound *saṃjñāpramāṇatvāt*, where a name-word (*saṃjñāśabda*) ending in the genitive is compounded with the quality-word *pramāṇatva*.

The meaning is that by this [rule], the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) in certain instances is indicated; thus, the correctness of expressions such as *arthagaurava* (the weightiness of the meaning) is established. Regarding the rule *saptamīviśeṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 2.2.35): precisely because of this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), a *bahuvrīhi* compound may consist of words in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇapada*). Indeed, a *bahuvrīhi* with words in different cases is observed in usage, such as in the phrase *sacchāstrajanmā hi vivekalābhaḥ* ("for the attainment of discrimination arises from the true scriptures"), where the analysis (*vigraha*) is *sacchāstrāt janma yasya* ("that which has its birth from the true scriptures").

How is its correctness established? Since it has been settled as a doctrinal position (*siddhāntita*) in the rule *anekamanyapadārthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.24) that a *bahuvrīhi* compound consists of words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), he says: "Precisely because of this indicator (*jñāpaka*). The prescription of prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) for a word ending in the locative case in *bahuvrīhi* compounds—such as in *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("one whose throat is black")—indicates that a *bahuvrīhi* compound can occur even between words with different case endings. Therefore, the sense is that the correctness of the previously mentioned usage is thereby established.

Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.7: *saptamī-pañcamyau* (The locative and ablative case endings [are used] when joined with the word *adhika*). The locative and ablative cases are prescribed when in conjunction with the word *adhika*, based on the indications of the sūtras "tadasminnadhikam" (5.2.45) and "yasmādadhikam" (2.3.9). Objection: But in examples such as "loke lokādvā adhiko hariḥ" (Hari is superior to the world), since there is no rule prescribing the ablative and locative cases when joined with the word *adhika*, how can those two cases be considered grammatically correct?
