Anticipating the objection that the genitive case alone would be appropriate when the relation is that of being a limit (*avadhitva*), he says: "by the word *adhika*. The sense is that the correctness of the forms *tasi* and *tasil* follows precisely from the authority of the author of the Sūtras’ own usage. Regarding the rule *karmapravacanīyayukte* (Pāṇini 2.3.8): even though the instrumental case for a cause (*hetu*) is prescribed later [in Pāṇini 2.3.23], it is superseded by this [rule]. This is because, although the desired result could have been established by the rule *lakṣaṇetthaṃbhūtākhyāna-* (Pāṇini 1.4.90) and others, the force of enjoining this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) again [in 2.3.8] serves to set aside those other rules.

Objection: In the sentence *anu japaṃ prāvarṣat* ("It rained after the recitation"), the word *anu* receives the designation of *karmapravacanīya* by the rule *anurlakṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 1.4.84). Consequently, by the rule *karmapravacanīyayukte dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.8), the second case ending is desired after the word *japa*. However, in that context, the recitation (*japa*) possesses not only the character of a *lakṣaṇa* (indicator) but also the character of a *hetu* (cause). Thus, one might suspect that the third case ending prescribed by the subsequent rule *hetau* (Pāṇini 2.3.23) would supersede the second case ending; anticipating this, he says: *parāpi*.

Since the designation *karmapravacanīya* is already established by the rule *lakṣaṇetthambhūtākhyāna...* (Pāṇini 1.4.90) when a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that is not a cause (*ahetu*) is to be expressed, it must be stated that the rule *anurlakṣaṇe* prescribes the *karmapravacanīya* designation specifically for a characteristic that is a cause (*hetubhūta*). And in that case, since the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would otherwise have applied to express the cause...

The meaning is that there is no fault because the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is superseded by the second case (*dvitīyā*) through the maxim of "that which was not previously applicable" (*yenāprāptinyāya*), due to the prescription of the designation *karmapravacanīya* for the second case [in the rule *namaḥ-svasti-svāhā-svadhā-alam-vaṣaṭ-yogācca*]. Furthermore, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is also correct when used in connection with words such as *prabhu* ("lord"), based on the grammatical indications in the rules *tasmai prabhavati* (Pāṇini 5.1.101) and *sa eṣāṃ grāmaṇīḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.78).

Now, one might raise the following objection: since the *vārttika* on the rule *namaḥ-svasti-svāhā-svadhā-alaṃ-vaṣaṭ-ḍat-dhya-yogācca* states that "the word *alam* is taken here in the sense of sufficiency (*paryāpti*)," and since the use of the dative case alone is prescribed as correct when joined with a word having the meaning of sufficiency, how can the use of the genitive case—as in the phrase *prabhububhūṣurbhuvanatrayasya*—be considered grammatically valid? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "in connection with *prabhu* and so forth."

Since the correctness of the genitive case is established by the designation "he is their leader" (*sa eṣāṃ grāmaṇīḥ*), the word *alam* itself—by the force of that very [designation]—is understood to have a meaning other than mere sufficiency (*paryāpti*). Furthermore, regarding the use of the dative case in connection with it, the particle *api* (in the phrase *ṣaṣṭhy api*) is intended to ward off the misconception that might arise, namely: "In connection with a word whose meaning is sufficiency, the dative is not used, but rather only the genitive. Thus, the sense is that the dative is correct in connection with a word signifying sufficiency, because of the designation of the dative in the rule "it prevails over that" (*tasmai prabhavati*).

Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.29: *anyārāt* || However, this [rule for the fifth case] does not apply when used in conjunction with a word denoting a part (*avayava*). This is because of the technical usage in the rule: *tasya paramāmreḍitam* (Sūtra 8.1.2). Objection: In the rule *anyārāditarartedikchabdāñcūttarapadājāhiyukte*, the term *dikśabda* ("direction-word") refers to any word observed to denote a direction. Consequently, even when joined with words like *pūrva* and so on—which are well-known as denoting directions but are currently being used to denote time—the fifth case ending occurs.

Therefore, the explanation was made that [the rule] establishes such cases as "Phālguna is prior to Caitra. If this were so, however, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) would also apply when joined with a word denoting a part (*avayava*). Consequently, one might object: "In the expression *pūrvaṃ kāyasya* ('the front part of the body'), even though the word *pūrva* denotes a bodily part, since it elsewhere denotes a direction (*dik*), the ablative would be required by its connection with that [directional sense]; thus, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would not be grammatically correct. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "denoting a part" (*avayavavācin*).

In the sūtra *tasya paramāmreḍitam*, the word *tasya* refers back to the previously mentioned *dviruktam* (the reduplicated form). By the word *para*, the subsequent member (*parāvayava*) is denoted. If the ablative case were to occur even when joined with the word *para*—which denotes a member—then the use of the genitive case in *tasya* would be inconsistent. Consequently, this indicates that when a word seen in the sense of direction is currently used in the sense of a member, the ablative case does not occur in its conjunction.

Therefore, the intention is that there is no occurrence of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in such instances as "prior to the body" (*pūrvaṃ kāyasya*). According to the rule *apādāne pañcamī* (Pāṇini 2.3.28), the fifth case is used when joined with words having the sense of "starting from" (*prabhṛti*), as evidenced by the usage in the *Bhāṣya*: "from the full moon of Kārtika" (*kārtikyāḥ prabhṛti*). [Objection: Even so, how is the fifth case justified in examples such as "Hari is to be served starting from or beginning from existence" (*bhavāt prabhṛti ārabhya vā sevyo hariḥ*), given the absence of connection with words like *ādi*? [Response: To this he says: "because of the usage in the *Bhāṣya*."

For instance, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *apādāne pañcamī*, after citing the *Vārttika* "yataścādhvakālanirmāṇam" and providing the example "kārtikyā āgrahāyaṇī māse," the author introduces the rejection of that *Vārttika* by stating, "this need not be stated. He then says: "This [usage] which ought to be employed here—namely, 'kārtikyāḥ prabhṛtyāgrahāyaṇī māse'—is not actually used. The meaning is that even in the absence of the word *prabhṛti*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is established through the presence of its sense.

By stating this, the author of the Bhāṣya indicates the rule that the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in connection with words having the sense of *prabhṛti* ("starting from"). Otherwise, in the absence of the word *prabhṛti*, the necessity of a Vārttika for the sake of the ablative would be evident, and thus [the Bhāṣya] would be inconsistent. Consequently, the ablative is used even in connection with words synonymous with *prabhṛti*. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa says in his commentary on the Bhāṣya passage "from the Kārttikī full moon": "The meaning is 'beginning from that'."

Regarding this, the authors of the *Bālamanoramā* state that the suffix *tasi* is used here from the ablative case (*pañcamī*) as in the word *tataḥ*. According to the rule *apa-pari-bahis* (Pāṇini 2.1.12), which prescribes compound formation, the ablative case is employed in connection with *bahiḥ*; this serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence). Thus, even in the absence of a specific sūtra prescribing the ablative for connection with *bahiḥ*, the ablative is established by means of this *jñāpaka*.

The rule *apaparibahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā* prescribes a compound with the word *bahiḥ* when it ends in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). Since this prescription would be impossible without a fifth-case ending in connection with *bahiḥ*, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the fifth case occurs in such a construction. Thus, the point is that the grammatical correctness of usages such as *grāmādbahiḥ* ("outside the village") is established. [Pāṇini 2.2.52] *adhīgartha*: The explicit mention of the word *adhi* is for the purpose of indicating the rule: "The verbal roots *iṅ* and *ik* do not deviate from being preceded by the prefix *adhi*."

JHRVIṬA: Now, one might object: "In the rule *adhīgartha* (Pāṇini 2.3.52), the utterance of the word *adhi* need not be included; for by the phrase *igartha* alone, the verbal roots having the sense of 'remembering' (*smaraṇa*) are obtained. To this, he replies with the word *adhīti*. The point is that the utterance of *adhi* is intended to indicate that the root *ig*—meaning 'to remember'—must be used only in conjunction with the prefix *adhi*. Although the utterance of the word *adhi* here might serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the root *ig* is never separated from the prefix *adhi*, it would not necessarily indicate that the root *iṅ* (the root for 'studying') is likewise inseparable from it.

Nevertheless, just as the root *iṅ* in the sense of "studying" (*adhyayane*) does not deviate from its prefix *adhi*, so too does the root *ik* in the sense of "remembering" (*smaraṇe*); thus, the inclusion of the root *iṅ* within the body of the rule is for the purpose of providing an illustration. It should be understood that the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the fact that *iṅ* is never separated from the prefix *adhi* is the explicit mention of the word *adhi* in the sūtra *ṇeradhyayane vṛttam* (Pāṇini 7.2.26). [The roots] beginning with *nandi* and *grahi* (Pāṇini 3.1.134) constitute the *pacādi* group, which is an open-ended class (*gaṇa*).

This is because the suffix *ac* is applied to the roots *kṛ* and *ghaṭ* in the two rules: *śivaśamariṣṭasya kare* (Pāṇini 4.4.143) and *karmaṇi ghaṭo’ṭhac* (Pāṇini 5.2.35). Furthermore, the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅluk*) is prescribed when the suffix *ac* follows. [Objection: But surely, in the rule *nandigrahipacādibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ*, three groups of roots are specified: the *nandyādi* group, the *grahyādi* group, and the *pacādi* group. Among these, the *nandyādi* and *grahyādi* groups are not *ākṛtigaṇas* (open-ended classes).

Fearing that because *pac* and others are mentioned together with those two [suffixes], the class beginning with *pac* (*pacādi*) might also not be an *ākṛtigaṇa*, he establishes its status as an *ākṛtigaṇa* by means of an indicator: "The *pacādi* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*."

In the sūtra *śivaśamariṣṭasya kare*, the word *kara* is derived from the root *kṛ* by adding the suffix *ac*, since it is not listed in the *pacādi* group; likewise, in the sūtra *ghaṭo'ṭhac*, the word *ghaṭa* is derived from the root *ghaṭ* by adding the suffix *ac*, as it is not listed there. From these usages, it is understood that the *pacādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). Similarly, by the sūtra *yaṅo'ci ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.74), the elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ* affix is prescribed when the suffix *ac* follows a stem ending in *yaṅ*.

The point is this: since there is no mention of a form ending in *yaṅ* in the *pacādi-gaṇa*, the suffix *ac* is difficult to obtain from it; therefore, the prescription of the elision (*luk*) of *yaṅ* when *ac* follows would be inconsistent unless it serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) that the *pacādi-gaṇa* is an open-ended class (*kṛtigaṇa*). Regarding the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.188): it does not supersede the *kta* suffix used in the sense of the past (*bhūte*), because of the evidence (*liṅga*) provided by the rule *upajñāte* (Pāṇini 4.3.115), which occurs under the governing heading *tena* (Pāṇini 4.3.112).

Objection: By the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca*, the suffix *kta* is specifically prescribed after verbal roots meaning desire (*icchā*) and so forth in the sense of the present tense. This would constitute an exception (*apavāda*) to the general suffix *kta*—known as *niṣṭhā*—which is prescribed for the past tense (*bhūta*) after roots having those same meanings. Consequently, it would follow that usages such as *pūjito yaḥ surāsuraiḥ* ("he who was honored by gods and demons") would be grammatically incorrect. Nor can it be argued that even in those cases, the suffix *kta* retains its sense of the present tense.

If that were the case, then by its connection with that [word], the sixth case (genitive) would apply according to the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne* (Pāṇini 2.2.67), resulting in the undesirable consequence that the third case (instrumental) would be grammatically incorrect. To this, he says: "This is not so. By that, in the sense of "discovered by" (*upajñātam*), the suffix *cha* is prescribed by the rule *upajñāte* (Pāṇini 4.3.115); for example, *pāṇinīyam*, meaning "discovered by Pāṇini. In that instance, by the power of its co-occurrence with the third case, it is determined that the word *upajñāta* ends in the past passive participle suffix *kta*.

Furthermore, if the *kta* suffix prescribed by the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.188), which denotes the present tense, were to supersede the *kta* suffix denoting the past tense, then the grammatical instruction *tenopajñātam* would be inconsistent; for the term *upajñā* also carries the sense of "intellection" (*buddhi*).

And thus, since Pāṇini has prescribed the *kta* suffix for roots meaning "cognition" (*buddhi*) when referring to the past tense, it is established that the *kta* suffix ordained by the rule "matibuddhi... is not an exception to the *kta* suffix used in the past tense; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, regarding the rule *yaj-yāca...* (Pāṇini 3.3.90), there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) because of the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule *praśne cāsanne* (Pāṇini 3.2.117).

Objection: From the root *praccha*, by the rule "yajayācayatavicchapraccharakṣo naṅ," the suffix *naṅ* is applied; then, by the rule "cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.19), the *ch* is replaced by *ś*, resulting in the desired form *praśnaḥ*. In that case, since the suffix is marked with *ṅ*, when it follows, the *r* of the root would undergo *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) according to the rule "grahijyāvayi... (Pāṇini 6.1.16). Anticipating this objection, he says: "And [the *r* is] not changed in *praśna*."

The meaning is this: the fact that the author of the Sūtras provides an instruction [for this root] without employing *saṃprasāraṇa* indicates that there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* in this verbal root. [Regarding the rule] *sthā-gā-pā-pacaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.95): the forms *avasthā* and *saṃsthā* are established by the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule *vyavasthāyām* (1.1.34). Now, an objection: by the rule *striyāṃ ktin* (3.3.94), and specifically by the rule *sthā-gā-pā-paco bhāve*, the suffix *ktin* is prescribed for the root *sthā* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). Furthermore, by the rule *ātaścopasarge*...

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṅ* prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.3.97] (*sū.3-3-106*). Forms such as *prasthitiḥ* and *upasthitiḥ* [are derived from this rule]. If this is so, one might raise the objection: "How can forms ending in *aṅ*, such as *avasthā* and *saṃsthā*, be grammatically correct? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "*avasthā saṃsthā*. The meaning is that, by the force of the sūtra reference "*vyavasthāyām*" [in Pāṇini 3.3.43], it is understood that the suffix *aṅ* also occurs after the root *sthā* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) in the feminine.

*Khanaḥ gha ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.125). The inclusion of the marker *ghit* is for the purpose of indicating that this [suffix] occurs even from other roots. By means of that, from the root *bhaj*, we have *bhagaḥ* meaning "foot," where the suffix *gha* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe ghaḥ*). [Objection: But surely, by the rule *khano gha ca*, the suffix *gha* is prescribed. The example is *ākhanaḥ*. In that case, the letter *gh* in the suffix is marked with the *it*-designation. And yet, in the present context, there is no purpose for that [designation].

Anticipating the objection that, since there is no *ca* or *ja* in the verbal root [bhaj], the substitution of *ku* (the guttural *g*) by Pāṇini’s rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.52) would not apply, he states: "The designation *ghi* [is used] as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the suffix *gha* occurs after other roots as well, even those not suitable for the *ku*-substitution. By this, when the suffix *gha* is added to the root *bhaj* and the *ja* is replaced by *ga*, the word *bhaga* is established. [Then follows: *anupasarjanāt* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.14).

This very [rule] indicates that the *tadantavidhi* (the rule of application to that which ends with a specified element) applies even in the case of feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*). Objection: In examples such as *bahukurucarā* ("that [city] in which there are many inhabitants of Kuru"), the feminine suffixes such as *ṅīp*—which are prescribed by rules like *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15)—would otherwise apply to words like *kurucara* when they are used as *upasarjana*s (subordinate members of a compound). To prevent this, the governing rule (*adhikāra*) *anupasarjanāt* ("provided it is not a subordinate member") is required.

And that [objection] is futile; for since the word *bahukurucara* does not end in a *ṭi*-suffix, the suffix *ṅīp* is not applicable in the first place. Nor should it be argued that because the *ṭi*-suffix qualifies the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is an application of *ṅīp* even after a form ending in something that ends in a *ṭi*-suffix, by means of the rule of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*). This is because the prohibition of the rule of extension to what ends in a suffix applies specifically to the formation of compounds and secondary derivatives (*samāsa-pratyaya-vidhi*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "This very [point]... (referring to the following).

Since the rule regarding non-subordinate elements (*anupasarjanādhikāra*) would otherwise be redundant according to the aforementioned reasoning, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, in the case of feminine suffixes, there is an application of the rule regarding "that which ends with" (*tadantavidhi*). Therefore, in examples such as *bahukurucarā*, the *anupasarjanādhikāra* is necessary to prevent the addition of the suffix *ṅīp* and others; thus, it achieves its purpose within its own domain. Its utility elsewhere, however, is seen in rules such as *vano ra ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.7), where it ensures the inclusion of forms ending in a stem that itself ends in *van*. Regarding the rule *strīpuṃsābhyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.87): the sense of "like" (*vatyartha*) is not included here. This is indicated by the subsequent rule *strī puṃvacca* (Pāṇini 6.3.34). Thus, we have *strīvat*.

Regarding the term *puṃvat*: by the rule *jhrvi.ṭa ṭhastrīpuṃsābhyāṃ nañsnañau bhavanāt* ("after *strī* and *puṃs*, the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* [are applied] before the scope of *bhavana*"), it is stated that for meanings prior to those covered by the rule *dhānyānāṃ bhavane* (Pāṇini 5.2.1), the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* are respectively applied after *strī* and *puṃs*. However, these two suffixes are not desired in the sense of *vati*. The sense of *vati* refers to meanings prior to *bhavana* (Pāṇini 5.1.115). Thus, having raised the objection that *nañ* and *snañ* might consequently apply even in the sense of *vati*, he says: "not in the sense of *vati*."

If the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* were to apply after the words *strī* and *puṃs* even in the sense of *vat*, then the mention of *puṃvat* would not be appropriate; for *snañ*, being prescribed as a specific rule, would supersede *vat*. Although the mention of *puṃvat* might serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that [the rule] applies only to the word *puṃs*, nevertheless, since an indicator depends on the context of this very sūtra, the intended meaning is that *nañ* and *snañ* do not apply after *strī* and *puṃs* in the sense of *vat*. [Pāṇini 4.2.4: *lubaviśeṣe*].

By the rule *vibhāṣā phālgunīśravaṇākārtikīcaitrībhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.23), it is indicated that the elision (*lup*) of the suffix occurs specifically on the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*). Consequently, the form *pauṣī*—meaning the full moon joined with the constellation Puṣya—is established. Now, an objection is raised: according to the rule *lubaviśeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.4), the elision (*lup*) is prescribed for the suffix *aṇ* ordained by the rule *nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.3) when no specific sub-division of time is understood—that is, when the sixty-ḍaṇḍa period of time is not perceived as having an internal distinction. [How then is this form justified?]

"Today is Puṣya" is the example. For here, although specific [times] such as "yesterday" or "tomorrow" are understood, the *lup* elision occurs because there is no comprehension of a sub-division of time consisting of a day and night (*ahorātra*). Likewise, in the case of *pauṣī*—meaning the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) conjoined with Puṣya—the *lup* of the suffix *aṇ* would also occur due to the lack of comprehension of a sub-division of time consisting of a day and night; therefore, he says: "In the case of the full moon day, however, the *lup* does not take place."

The meaning is that because the term *phālgunī* is used without elision (*lup*) in the sense of "the full moon day joined with the constellation Phalgunī," the intention is that the elision (*lup*) does not apply when the full moon day is joined with a [different] constellation. Although an objection might arise—namely, that since the term *śravaṇā* is used with elision (*lup*) in that very same context, how can it be possible to establish such a rule?—nevertheless, the intention is that by using that specific designation, one merely indicates the absence of elision (*lubabhāva*) in that particular case. [From the *Jñāpakapradīpa*: By the rule *na vyo liṭi* (Pāṇini 6.1.46), which prevents the substitution of *samprasāraṇa* for the root *vyo* in the *liṭ* tense, this [rule] sets aside even the subsequent *halādiśeṣa* (the rule concerning the retention of the first consonant). For that which...

There is *saṃprasāraṇa* [of the semivowel], due to the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of including both [classes of roots]. [Objection: But surely, when the root *vyeñ* (in the sense of "covering") is in the *liṭ* [perfect] tense with the suffix *ṇal*, the form *vye-a* arises; then, by the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115), *vṛddhi* occurs, resulting in *vyai*. When the root undergoes reduplication, we have *vyai-vyai-a*. Then, by the rule *liṭyabhyāsasyobhayepām* (Pāṇini 6.1.17), *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs for the *yakāra* of the reduplicated syllable, and after the formation of the single substitute (*pūrvarūpa*), we have *vivyai-a*. Finally, with the substitution of *āy* (*āyādeśa*), the desired form *vivyāya* is obtained. [Response: This is true. However, the inclusion of both classes of roots is for the sake of the subsequent rule. Otherwise, if there were no *saṃprasāraṇa* of the *yakāra* of the reduplicated syllable, the form would be *vivyāya*, which is not desired. Therefore, the inclusion of both is indeed purposeful. Thus, in this case, *saṃprasāraṇa* applies to the *yakāra* of the reduplicated syllable. Consequently, the form *vivyāya* is established.

That is not established; for, prior to the *saṃprasāraṇa*, because it is subsequent, the *yakāra* would be eliminated by the *hal-ādi-śeṣa* rule, and once the *vakāra* undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa* to become *ukāra*, the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of *uvyāya* would follow. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even though [it is] subsequent."

In the rule *liṭy abhyāsasya* ("in the reduplicated syllable of the perfect tense"), because both *vacisvapiyajādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.1.15) and *grahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicativṛścatipṛcchatibhṛjjatīnām* (Pāṇini 6.1.16) are understood through *anuvṛtti* (carrying over), the term *ubhayeṣām* ("of both") is already present; therefore, the mention of *ubhayeṣām* again is for the purpose of re-enactment (*punarvidhāna*). Consequently, this results in a double prescription: that the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) of the reduplicated syllable of both the *vac*-class verbs and the *grah*-class verbs occurs in the perfect tense.

In this context, the second rule is for the purpose of restriction: that for both [types of reduplication], there shall be *saṃprasāraṇa* alone and nothing else. Thus, by setting aside the *halādiśeṣa* rule, the form *vivyāya* is established through the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the reduplicated *y* (*abyāsa-yakāra*). This is the intended meaning. [From the *Jñānapradīpa*: Regarding the sūtra *dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.75): this *tuk* augment applies to a long vowel, but not to the *ch* [of the *chvi* suffix]. This is known from the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the sūtra *senāsurācchāyā* (Pāṇini 2.4.25).

Objection: In the rule *dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.75), the word *che* is carried over from the rule *che ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.73). Since both the ablative (*pañcamī*) and the locative (*saptamī*) are mentioned in this context, the ablative mention is more powerful; thus, the ablative *dīrghāt* would effect a change of the locative *che* into a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Consequently, the meaning of the rule would be that *tuk* is inserted after a long vowel before a *ch*.

Anticipating the objection that if the rule is applied as "when *ch* follows," the *tuk* augment would occur immediately after the letter *ch* and not after a long vowel, he says: "This *tuk* belongs to the long vowel. Although, when both [the fifth and seventh case endings] are used for reference, the reference by the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is stronger, nevertheless, in this sūtra, it is accepted that the reference by the seventh case (*saptamī*) is more powerful, and thus that reference is interpreted as implying a sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). The evidence for this is Pāṇini’s own usage in the rule "senāsurācchāyā" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.25).

For if *tuk* were to belong to *cha*, then the letter *ca* would have been indicated after the letter *cha*. However, by the power of indicating *ca* after a long vowel (*dīrgha*), the intention is to convey that this *tuk* belongs to the long vowel. The ultimate point is that through the rule "senāsurācchāyā" (Pāṇini 2.4.25), which indicates a genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) for what was previously a locative case ending (*pañcamyanta*)—namely, "after a long vowel"—it is made known that this *tuk* belongs to the long vowel. In the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77), the status of the *ik* as the cause (*nimitta*) is not sublated by its status as the substitute (*sthānin*).

"Therefore [the doubling does not occur], because of the subsequent [rule]," according to the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *vāṭvṛtupitruṣasaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.31). [Objection: Now, in the case of *dhātraṃśaḥ*, regarding the letter *r*, the doubling that would result from the option under the Vārttika *yaṇo mayo dve vācye*—wherein *mayaḥ* is a fifth-case [ablative] and *yaṇaḥ* is a sixth-case [genitive]—is prevented by the rule *aco rahābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.46), since the status of being the effect (*kāryitva*) is overridden by the status of being the cause (*nimittatva*) as directly heard in the text. If it is prevented in that manner, then the same should apply here in *sudhyupāsyaḥ*.

Since the status of being a cause (*nimittatva*) is sublated by the status of being a substitute (*sthānitva*) as heard in the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, the substitution of *yaṇ* for the vowel *ī* would not occur when that [vowel *u*] follows; therefore, he says: "by virtue of being a substitute. The sense is that it is made known—by the evidence (*jñāpaka*) consisting in the prescription of the *yaṇ* substitute for the vowel *i* when the vowel *u* follows in the rule *ityuttarasya*, and by the prescription of the *yaṇ* substitute for the vowel *ṛ* when the vowel *u* follows in the example *pitruṣasaḥ*—that the status of being a cause is not sublated by the status of being a substitute for the vowel *i*.

Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.137: *saṃparibhyāṃ karotau* (after *saṃ* and *pari*, the augment *suṭ* is added before the root *kṛ*). The augment *suṭ* is applied to the root *kṛ* preceded by *saṃ* even in some cases where it does not mean "adornment," as indicated by the rule *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.16). The augment *suṭ* is prescribed for the root *kṛ* preceded by both *saṃ* and *pari* when the meanings are "adornment" (*bhūṣaṇa*) and "collection" (*saṃghāta*), respectively, according to the two rules: *saṃparibhyāṃ karotau bhūṣaṇe* and *samavāye ca*.

The augment *suṭ* is not applied only to the two meanings already mentioned; it is observed even in other senses, as in the example *aṣṭasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ puroḍāśaḥ* ("the sacrificial cake prepared on eight potsherds"), where *suṭ* is seen. To justify this, he says: "of that preceded by *sam*" (*saṃpūrvasya*). In the rule *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ*, the word *saṃskṛtam* means "made the object of an action whose result is its use for eating and so forth. This is evident from the example *bhrāṣṭre saṃskṛtā bhrāṣṭrā yavāḥ* ("barley grains prepared in a frying pan"). Likewise...

The sense is that the correctness of that [word] is known from the specific mention of *suṭ* even in the case of non-decorative [ornaments]. Regarding the rule *vīravīryau* (Pāṇini 6.2.120): the word *vīrya* ends in the suffix *yat*; in that case, the mention of *vīrya* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the acute accent on the first syllable—prescribed by the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.213)—does not apply. For if that were the case, the desired form would already be established by the preceding rule alone.

Objection: But surely, in the case of *suvīraḥ* and *suvīryaḥ*—formed by the addition of the prefix *su-* to the words *vīra* and *vīrya* within a *bahuvrīhi* compound—the rule "vīravīryau" prescribes that they have the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). In that context, the prescription of the initial acute accent for the word *vīrya* is redundant.

Anticipating the objection that the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) of the word *vīrya* is already established by the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.213), since the rule *ādyudāttaṃ hyac chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.2.119)—which means that in the Vedic language, a *bahu-vrīhi* compound ending in *su* that begins with an acute-accented *hyac* [i.e., a stem consisting of two vowels] also has its first syllable acute—would apply here, [the author] states "In that case... and so forth, explaining that it is precisely for this reason that it is indicated (*jñāpyate*) that the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ* does not apply to the word *vīrya*. For in that case, [the condition] "provided that... applies.

The meaning is: "provided that [the word] *anāḍhya-* has an acute accent on its first syllable. "By the preceding rule alone" means: by the rule *ādyudāttaṃ dvyac chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.2.119) alone. Regarding the rule *kṛtyokeṣṇuccārvādayaśca* (Pāṇini 6.2.160): when *iṣṇuc* is mentioned, there is also the inclusion of *khiṣṇuc*, because the suffix is introduced with an initial *ikāra* (the letter *i*) for the sake of its specific application. Example: *anāḍhyaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*.

Objection: In the case of *anāḍhya āḍhyo bhavati* and *āḍhyaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*, when a word meaning "becoming" (*bhavyārtha*) is the upapada, the suffix *khiṣṇuc* is applied to the root *bhū* by the rule *kartari bhuvaḥ khiṣṇuckhukañau* (Pāṇini 3.2.57). In that context, for the negative compound *na āḍhyaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ* = *anāḍhyaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*, the rule *kṛtyokeṣṇuccārvādayaśca* prescribes an acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable; however, that would not occur [if the analysis were as proposed].

Raising the objection that since only the suffix *iṣṇuc* with a single indicatory letter (*ekānubandhaka*) is mentioned there, the suffix *khiṣṇuc* with two indicatory letters (*dvyanubandhaka*) would not be included, [the author] replies: because one can establish the initial *ikāra* by simply applying the augment *iṭ* to the suffix *khaṣṇuc* after the root *bhū*, the prescription of *iṣṇuc* beginning with *ikāra* indicates that the term *iṣṇuc* is intended to include *khiṣṇuc* as well. Therefore, he states "in the mention of *iṣṇuc*" to show that there is no fault. [Sūtra 6.4.11: *aptṛntṛc*.

Since the desired result would be achieved by simply using *tṛ*, the separate mention of both *tṛn* and *tṛc* is for the purpose of indicating that even when a general term is used, sometimes only a specific form is intended to be included. [Objection]: But surely, in the rule *aptṛntṛc* (Pāṇini 6.4.11), one could have read *tṛ* instead of *tṛn-tṛcau*. By the general term *tṛ*, both *tṛn* and *tṛc* will be understood, just as in the rule *turiṣṭhemeyassu* (Pāṇini 6.4.154), where *tṛ* is used to denote both *tṛn* and *tṛc* in a general sense. To this, he replies: *tṛ ityeva...* ("since [the result] would be achieved by *tṛ* alone...").

And likewise, in order to indicate that even when there is a general mention (*sāmānya-nirdeśa*) in some instances, only a specific [term] is intended to be understood, the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc* are mentioned separately. The purpose of this indication is as follows: although in the rule *na kopadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.37) there is a general mention of *ka*, only the *ka* belonging to a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is understood, and not the *ka* belonging to a primary derivative (*kṛt*). Consequently, in the case of *pākabhāryaḥ*—meaning "one whose wife is a cook" (*pākā bhāryā yasya*)—the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not apply.

For the word *pāka* ends in the suffix *kap*, being prescribed as such among the *uṇādi* formations; by this, the rule "in the prohibition regarding [words] having *k* as an upadhā, there is the inclusion of *taddhita* and *vuñ*" becomes justified. Others, however, say: "Although one could simply have said 'aptṛ', the separate mention of *tṛn* and *tṛc* is for the purpose of excluding *arvaṇas-tṛ*. Even though that exclusion is established by the *arthavat-paribhāṣā* (the maxim that a meaningful element is significant), nevertheless, the separate mention of those two [suffixes] is intended to indicate that the *paribhāṣā* is not universally applicable (*anitya*)."

Therefore, they say that the rule is established by the principle: "The mention of *ani*, *nas*, and *man* causes the application of the *tadanta-vidhi* (the rule that an operation applies to a word ending in what is specified) whether [the suffix] has meaning or is meaningless. This alternative view is also set forth in the *Tattvabodhinī*. Regarding *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.112): In the rule *āta au ṇalaḥ*, since the form *au* would have been sufficient, the specific prescription of *au* is for the purpose of its being heard (*śravaṇārtha*) after the elision of the *ś* of the root *daridrāti*. Some maintain that because of this very *jñāpaka* (indicative mark), the augment *ām* does not occur.

Regarding the root *daridrā* in the *liṭ* (perfect tense), the form *daridrāñcakāra* is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *kāspratyayādām amantre liṭi* (Pāṇini 3.1.35) by means of the *vārttika*: "The suffix *ām* [is applied] after *kāsi* and after roots with more than one vowel, for the sake of forms such as *lulumpa*. However, Kaiyaṭa, not accepting the suffix *ām*, maintains that the forms are simply *dadaridrau* and so forth. For instance, regarding the rule *āta au ṇalaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.34), since there is no reason for the first *a* to undergo change, it would be more appropriate to prescribe the substitution of the *o* sound alone.

Since forms such as *yayau* can be correctly derived solely by means of the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by the rule *vṛddhireci* (Pāṇini 6.1.88) for the vowels *ā* and *o*, the specific prescription of the vowel *au* [in the root *daridrā*] must therefore apply to the root *daridrā* when followed by the suffix *ṇal*.

The elision of *ā* in the root *daridrā* before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix must be stated; this results in the hearing of the vowel *au* in forms such as *dadaridrau*. However, if the rule for the substitution of *o* were applied instead, then once the elision of *ā* had occurred, a *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) would be impossible, and thus only the vowel *o* would be heard in *dadaridro*. He states that view [of others] with the words: "in the rule *āta au ṇalaḥ*. For this very reason—that is, because the substitution of *au* is prescribed for the sake of hearing the vowel *au* from this root *daridrā*—it is understood that there is no *ām* augment for *daridrā* in the *liṭ* (perfect tense).

The sense is that if [the form] *āmi* were present, *ṇal* would not even be applicable. Regarding the rule *aṣṭābhya auś* (Pāṇini 7.1.21): the mention of the form with the vowel change (*ātva*) indicates that the substitution of *ā* occurs in the domain of the case-endings *jaś* and *śas*. In the rule *aṣṭābhya auś*, the word *aṣṭā* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the word *aṣṭan* after the vowel change has been applied. Consequently, the meaning of the rule is established as follows: *auś* is substituted for the case-endings *jaś* and *śas* when they follow the word *aṣṭan* after the vowel *ā* has been substituted.

Regarding this, since the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.1.21) draws down the condition *halī* from the preceding rule, the substitution of *ā* for *aṣṭan* is prescribed only when followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*) beginning with a consonant (*hal*); thus, the substitution of *ā* does not occur when *jaś* and *śas* follow. How then can it be inferred that *jaś* and *śas* also undergo the substitution of *ā* after the word *aṣṭan* which has already had *ā* substituted? To this he says: *kṛtātva-*. Nor should it be argued that this is not an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a form where *ā* has been substituted, but rather that this form is produced by the force of the grammatical rule itself.

This being the case, since the substitution of *āt* for *aṣṭan-* is optional, the intention is that one would simply say "aṣṭabhya auś" for the sake of brevity. Regarding the rule *trestrayaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.53): Since the substitution of *traya-* is already established by the very mention of "of the three *ṇij*s" in the rule *ṇijāṃ trayaṇām* (7.4.75), this present sūtra is intended to provide a technical indication (*jñāpana*) that "even nipātanas [irregular forms] do not constitute exceptions [to other rules]. By means of this, the form *purātana-* is established.

Now, one might object: regarding the doubt as to whether the word *trayaḥ* in the rule *trestrayaḥ* ends in *a* or in *s*, its determination as ending in *a* must be made on the basis of the usage in *ṇijāṃ trayāṇām*. If that were so, then by the very power of that usage—which, through the sublation of the augment *nuṭ* and the lengthening of the vowel, establishes the substitution of *traya*—the rule *trestrayaḥ* would be redundant. Anticipating this objection, he states [the purpose of the rule] as follows: "By that very usage," meaning that the rule possesses significance for the sake of making known a specific grammatical statement.

And thus, since the substitution of *traya-* for *tri-* is not an exception (*abādhaka*) [to the general rule], the form *trīṇām* would also result as an alternative possibility; therefore, the rule *trestrayaḥ* is formulated to prevent that. The purpose of this indication (*jñāpanaphala*), however, is the derivation of the word *purātana*. Otherwise, from the word *purā*, by the rule "From *sāyam*, *ciram*, *prāh*, *hṛd*, *haṭ*, *prage*, and indeclinables, the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* are added, along with the augment *tuṭ*" (Pāṇini 4.3.23), [the form *purātanam* would be derived].

The sense is that, although the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* along with the augment *tuṭ* would be applicable by the rule *purāṇaprokteṣu* (Pāṇini 4.3.105), this specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*) would subvert [the application of] the rule *purāṇaprokteṣu* (4.3.105). And regarding the rule *dvārādīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.4): *śauvastikam*. Among the suffixes beginning with *vuñ* and *chaṇ*, since the *ṭhaC* suffix is marked with *c*, it is indicated that the substitution of *iK* is stronger than the *antaraṅga* operations.

Objection: From the word *śvas*, by the rule *śvasastuṭ ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.15), when the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied, since the augment *tuṭ* is taught as being dependent on the presence of that suffix (*pratyayasanniyogaśiṣṭa*), it is internal (*antaraṅga*). Consequently, the substitution of *ik* would occur before the addition of *tuṭ*. Since the letter *ṭha* would then not be at the beginning of the suffix, the substitution of *ik* would not take place—as in the case of the letter *ṭha* in *karmaṭha*. This is because the rule *ṭhasyekaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.50) prescribes the substitution of *ik* only for a *ṭha* that follows an *aṅga*. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the case of *vuñ*, *chaṇ*, and so forth..."

In the sūtra beginning with *vuñchaṇ* (Pāṇini 4.2.80), the addition of the marker *c* (*cit*) to the suffix *ṭhak* is for the purpose of making it *antodātta* (having its final syllable accented). One might ask: even in the absence of that *cit* marker, since the substitution of *i* (for *ṭha*) is *antaraṅga*, the rule *ādyudāttaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.3) would first cause the vowel *a* of *ṭha* to become udātta; subsequently, when the substitution of *i* occurs, the desired *antodātta* status would be established anyway. So what is the use of the *cit* marker? Its inclusion serves to indicate the maxim: "The substitution of *i* is stronger than *antaraṅga* operations."

And likewise, since the accentuation rule "the first syllable is acute" (*ādyudāttaśca*) would apply immediately after the substitution of *i* for the first time, the vowel *i* itself would become acute and not the final syllable; thus, the inclusion of the marker *c* (in the suffix *thak*) serves its own purpose in this regard. However, the actual utility [of the marker *c*] is that in forms such as *śauvastikam*, the substitution of *i* occurs prior to the internal *tuṭ* augment, thereby ensuring the attainment of the desired form.

In this context, the fact that *ṭhak* is a *cit* suffix is merely an illustration; the *cit*-status of *ṭhak* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) based on general principles, such as the rule: "Substitutes related to a suffix are stronger than internal operations. This and other points are clear in the *Śabdaratna*. Regarding the rule *yajayāca* (Pāṇini 7.3.66): [the form] *arcyam* is derived from the root *arc*. Even though the root has a vowel (*ṛ*) as its penultimate letter (*upadhā*), the suffix *ṇyat* is applied precisely because of this very indicator. Now, an objection: one might argue that from the root *ṛc*, by the rule *ṛhalorṇyat* (3.1.124), the suffix *ṇyat* is added, and the substitution of *k* for *c* (as prescribed by *cajoḥ ku* [7.3.52]) would apply. However, this is prevented by the rule *yajayācarucapravacarcaśca*... [and so forth].

Thus, when the prohibition by the aforementioned sūtra is applied and the augment *ṇuṭ* is added to the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), the form *arcyam* is desired; however, that is not established. Raising the objection that by the sūtra "ṛdupadhāccāklṛpiciteḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.110), only the suffix *kyap*—which is an exception to *ṇyat* and is characterized by having an *ṛt* vowel as its penultimate—would apply, he says: "even though it has an *ṛt* vowel as its penultimate."

The meaning is as follows: since the prohibition of *kutva* for the word *ṛc* when followed by the suffix *ṇyat* would otherwise be inconsistent in the absence of that suffix, it is understood through the prohibition of *kutva* that *ṛc* takes only the suffix *ṇyat* and not *kyap*. Regarding the rule *atrānunāsikaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.2), the mention of the option (*vā*) is for the sake of clarity; for the desired result is already established by the very indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *anunāsikātparaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.4). Now, one might object: let the option (*vā*) not be mentioned in the rule *atrānunāsikaḥ pūrvasya tu vā*.

Even in the absence of that [the *anunāsika*], regarding the rule "anusvāra follows after an *anunāsika*" (*anunāsikātparo'nusvāraḥ*), one may resort to an ablative case (*pañcamī*) based on the elision of the suffix *-lyap* (i.e., interpreting it as "after leaving aside the *anunāsika*"), explaining it as "in the case of the absence of the *anunāsika*"; and since this is its meaning, the optional nature of the *anunāsika* is established simply because the case of its absence would otherwise be impossible if the *anunāsika* were not optional. To this he says: "The mention of *vā* (or) is for the sake of clarity."

To indicate this very point, the *Vṛtti* does not mention the words *tu* or *vā*, but simply states: "there shall be an anusvāra for the vowel preceding the *r*. Regarding the rule *kharavasānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.15), the *repha* (*r*) at the end of a word does not undergo *visarga* by virtue of being treated as if it were the final element of a word (*antavadbhāva*). This is established by such indications as *ubhayatharkṣu* (8.3.8) and *kartari carṣidevatayoḥ* (3.2.186).

Regarding the objection that in forms such as *prārcchati*, after the substitution of *vṛddhi* by the rule "upasargād ṛti dhātau" (Pāṇini 6.1.91), the single-substitute *ār* would—by virtue of its being treated as the end of the preceding element (*pūrvāntavadbhāva*)—be considered a word-final *r*. Consequently, the rule "kharavasānayor visarjanīyaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.15) would require the substitution of *visarga*, he says [in response]: "by virtue of being treated as the end. There is no *visarga* for the *r* which has been rendered word-final through this treatment as the end of the preceding element.

Regarding the form *ubhayatharkṣu*, because of the grammatical instruction (*nirdeśa*) in the rule *carṣidevatayoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.2.130], the form *ubhayathārkṣu* is established. Once this is established, by applying the *guṇa* substitution according to the rule *ād grahaṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.87], the form *ubhayatharkṣu* results. In this case as well, since the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) *ar* would, by virtue of being treated as the end of the preceding member (*pūrvāntavat*), cause the *repha* (the letter *r*) to be considered a word-final (*padānta*), it would follow that a *visarga* should occur, and thus the form should have been taught as *ubhayathaḥ kṣu*.

The sense is that because it has not been taught in that manner, it is indicated (*jñāpyate*) that there is no *visarga* for the letter *r* at the end of a word by virtue of its being a member of a finite verbal form (*antavadbhāva*). Regarding the rule *dvistriścatur* (Pāṇini 8.3.43), the inclusion of the term "having the sense of -kṛtvaḥ" (*kṛtve'rtha-grahaṇam*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that association (*sāhacarya*) is not a regulator in all cases. By this, in the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām* (Pāṇini 1.1.6), although there is association with verbal roots (*dhātu-sāhacarya*), the augment *iṭ* is nevertheless included.

[Objection: But surely, because of the association (*sāhacarya*) with *dvi* and *tri*, which end in the suffix *suc*, the word *catur* must also be understood as ending in *suc*; thus, since it is established that all three occur in the sense of the *kṛtvas* suffix, the mention of "in the sense of *kṛtvas*" in the rule *dvistriścaturiti kṛtvo'rthe* is redundant. To this, he says: "But the mention of 'in the sense of *kṛtvas*'... [etc.]

And thus, since concomitance (*sāhacarya*) does not serve as a determinative factor in all cases, the inclusion of the term "kṛtvo'rtha" was made so that the word *catur* might not include forms ending in *asun*; this constitutes its utility within its own scope. He states the purpose elsewhere with the words "by that" (*tena*).

The intention is that in the rule *dīdhīvevīṭam*, because of the association (*sāhacaryāt*) with the two roots *dīdhī* and *vevī*, there arises the possibility of taking the root *iṭ* belonging to the Bhūvādigaṇa in the sense of motion; however, since it is accepted that association is not a universal regulator, only the augment *iṭ* is taken. Regarding the root *cit* (Pāṇini 1.2.7) in the sense of remembering: although one might have expected it to be read as *cint*, the inclusion of the marker *it* is a sign (*liṅga*) that the suffix *ṇic* is optional. Consequently, in forms such as *cintyāt* and *cintyate*, there is no elision of the nasal (*nalopa*).

Some maintain that this indicator (*jñāpaka*) refers to the general rule, while others hold that it refers to a specific case. Now, one might object: in the *curādigaṇa*, the root *cit* meaning "to remember" is listed with the marker *it*. Let there be no such *it*-marker for it; for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation, one should simply list it as "cinta smṛtyām. Nor can it be argued that the *it*-marker is necessary to prevent the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*), since the elision of the nasal does not apply here anyway.

Nor should one suspect that the *it*-marker [in the root *cit*] is for the purpose of preventing the elision of *n* in the case of the desiderative (*ṇic*) in the form *cintyāt* (where the *āśīr-liṅ* suffix is used), or in the passive (*karmalakāra*) with the *yak* suffix in the form *cintyate*. This is because, since the addition of *ṇic* is obligatory, the usage of *cintyāt* or *cintyate* from the simple root alone would be as impossible as a hare's horn. Therefore, he says "cinta," etc. By the word "tena" (by that), the meaning is "by way of being optional. Thus, since the usage *cintyāt* or *cintyate* does occasionally occur, the intention is that the *it*-marker is employed there to prevent the elision of *n*. This serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

It is not the case that [the rule] applies only to those instances where the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is applicable within the *cint*-dhātu; rather, it has as its scope the *cint*-dhātu in general. For this very reason, forms such as *cintati* and *cintet*, which lack the causative suffix *ṇic*, are grammatically correct. Alternatively, it refers to the general status of belonging to the *curādi* class. It is for this reason that the author of the *Vṛtti* cited *jagāṇa* and *jagaṇatuḥ* under the rule *ata ekahalmadhye 'nādeśāder liṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.120). With this intention, he says: "And this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*)."

They maintain that the indication of the optionality of *ṇic* pertains only to the verbal root *cit*, and not to the class of roots beginning with *cur* in general. Otherwise, if every root in the *cur*-class were subject to the optionality of *ṇic*, the rule prescribing the optional application of *ṇic* for those few roots listed within the sub-group (*gaṇa*) starting with *ā-ḍṛṣ*—namely, *ga.sū.* "āḍṛṣādvā"—would be rendered useless. He states their view: "Others say it depends on specific [roots]. This is the interpretation favored by the *Bālamanoramā*.

Between these two views, the position that there is an indicator (jñāpaka) dependent on a specific distinction is indeed the correct one. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, how could the usage of the word *jagaṇa* and *jagaṇatuḥ* in the *Vṛtti* be consistent; for since the root *bhū* belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class, its formation is established from a root included therein.

The authors of the *Nattvabodhinī* point out that there is considerable difficulty in the view that [the substitution of *ṣ*] depends upon a general indicator (*sāmānyāpekṣajñāpakatvapakṣe*). For the sake of making the rule "ādhṛṣādvā" meaningful, one must resort to the principle that what is established by an indicator is not universally applicable; thus, one would have to assume that for roots beginning with *ā-dhṛṣ*, the option is optional at will, whereas for others, it is restricted by the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭaprayoga*), and so forth. In the form *eṣiṣati* (from *iṣ*), even though doubling (*dvitva*) is compulsory here, it is superseded by the *guṇa* [substitution]. For the operation concerning the penultimate vowel (*upadhākārya*) is indeed more powerful than doubling.

This is because the inclusion of the augment *ṛ* in the root *oṇ* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) based on a general principle. [Objection: But surely, when the suffix *san* is added to the root *iṣ*, since it does not begin with a consonant (*hal*), the *kit* designation is absent; thus, in the stage *eṣ-iṣa*, by the rule "the second syllable of a non-initial vowel begins twice," *ṣis* is doubled, and after *hal-ādi-śeṣa* and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* of the suffix, the form *eṣiṣiṣati* is desired. That, however, is not established.

An objection is raised: "Since the substitution of *guṇa* applies whether doubling (*dvitva*) has been performed or not, it is *nitya* (obligatory); therefore, let it supersede doubling. Once doubling is performed first, the vowel *i*, being a part of the root, lacks the status of an *upadhā* (penultimate vowel), and thus *guṇa* does not apply. In response to this doubt, he says: "In this case, even though [the rule for] *guṇa* is *nitya*... Because the operation concerning the *upadhā* is stronger than doubling, the *guṇa* of the *upadhā* occurs first, and doubling follows immediately after. Therefore, there is no fault. That the operation concerning the *upadhā* is stronger than doubling is indicated by the fact that the root *oṇ* is marked with the *ṛt* indicatory letter (*ṛdit*).

To explain: from the root *oṇ* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense with the *caṅ* reduplication, when the prohibition "the penultimate vowel becomes short before *caṅ*" (*ṇo caṅyupadhāyā hrasvaḥ*) applies, we have the form *oṇi-at*. If the *ṇi* were to undergo reduplication, the form would be *oṇiṇat*. In this context, the designation of *oṇ* as *ṛdit* (having an *ṛ* as its indicatory letter) is for the purpose of prohibiting the shortening of the penultimate vowel. If the penultimate vowel were shortened, we would have *uṇ-i-at*; then, upon reduplication of *ṇi*, the form would be *anuṇiṇat*. In that case, the long *o*-vowel would not be heard [in the final result]. Such is the established position.

If, however, because of its permanence (*nityatva*), doubling were to occur even before the shortening of the penultimate vowel—that is, while the rule *oṇir ati* is still in effect—then, since the vowel *o* would no longer be a penultimate vowel, the shortening would not apply anyway; consequently, the designation *ṛdit* (which is applied to prevent such shortening) would be rendered useless. Therefore, it is understood that a modification of the penultimate vowel consisting of shortening is stronger than doubling.

[Objection: Granted that, by the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*), the shortening of the *upadhā* is established as more powerful than reduplication, how is it established that the *guṇa* substitution for the *upadhā* is more powerful than reduplication? To this, he says: "With reference to the general rule" (*sāmānyāpekṣā*). Those statements which were not compiled in the *Jñāpakasaṃgraha*, but are supported by the *Bhāṣya*, have been collected here in the first appendix (*pariśiṣṭaka*). Following the sequence of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* and according to the path adopted by Nāgeśa, I have compiled them to the best of my ability along with my own commentary.

Certain statements not seen in the *Bhāṣya* and other works have also been established by the most excellent Dīkṣita [Nāgeśa] in the *Kaumudī* through the use of *jñāpaka*s (indicative evidence). Observing their utility regarding the correctness of words (*śabdasādhutva*), I have included them in this second supplement (*pariśiṣṭa*). Thus ends the second supplement, the *Jñāpakasaṃgraha*.
Now begins the third chapter.

The suffix *kyap* [is introduced after the roots] *eti*, *stu*, *śās*, *ṛ*, *dṛ*, and *juṣ* (Pāṇini 3.1.109). This enumeration indicates that *kyap* is not applied after every verbal root (*dhātu*). In the Bhāṣya on the rule for the suffix *thap* (3.1.113), there is a concern that the application of *kyap* would be untenable in the rule *hanasta ca* (6.4.38). This is because the genitive case in *hanaḥ* is construed with the modification into the letter *t*, and since the *kyap* being drawn forward from the preceding rule lacks an explicitly stated relatum (*pratisambandhin*), its prescription would be impossible. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) in that context.

The word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*) is understood [from the previous rule]; therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that *takāra* is substituted for *han*, and *kyap* is added to the verbal root (*dhātu*). Having thus resolved this, one might again raise the objection: "In that case, since *kyap* would apply to any root in general, it would follow [undesirably] for all roots. To prevent this application of *kyap* to roots in general by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), he says: "The enumeration beginning with *eti-stu*. If *kyap* were to occur after every root whatsoever, then the specific enumeration of *eti*, *stu*, and so forth in the rule *hanasta ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.109) would be purposeless.

The meaning is that this enumeration [of suffixes] indicates that the *kyap* suffix does not occur after every verbal root (*dhātu*). Regarding the rule *paraśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.2): the attachment of indicatory letters (*anubandha*) such as *k* and others indicates that those which are never seen otherwise than as subsequent elements are elided. The author of the *Vārttika* stated the purpose of the rule *ṭhaparaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.79) as follows: "Or rather, it is for the sake of the elision of those [suffixes] which are never seen otherwise than as subsequent elements."

The rule *paraśca* exists for the purpose that there may be elision (*lopa*) of suffixes such as *kvip* and others which are not seen anywhere by means of a subsequent primary suffix (*pratyaya*). This is because, if that were the case, then the grammatical operations (*kārya*) prescribed by rules such as *kiti* would apply when *kvip* follows, and not otherwise; such is the meaning [of the rule]. The author of the *Bhāṣya*, having established through an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that suffixes such as *kvip* are elided when they follow [the base], has refuted this very *vārttika*. He states this as: "the attachment of indicatory letters (*anubandha*) such as *ka*."

If the preceding elements were to be elided, then the attachment of indicatory letters (*anubandha*) such as *k* in *kvip* and other suffixes would be purposeless; for every purpose served by an indicatory letter is caused by a suffix that follows [the base]. Thus, it indicates that all suffixes which cause total elision (*sarvalopin*) are elided only when they follow [the base]. Regarding the rule *jhrjñā.paṭa ijādeśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.36): the mention of the *guṇa* substitution for the root *ṛcch* in the *liṭ* (perfect tense) by the rule *ṛcchatyṝtām* (Pāṇini 7.4.11) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *liṭ* occurs after the root *ṛcch*.

JHRVIṬA: Now, one might object: in the sūtra *ijādeśca gurumato 'nṛcchaḥ*, let the term *anṛcchaḥ* not be included. Nor should it be argued that in its absence, the suffix *ām* would apply even to the root *ṛcch*. For it is understood through a *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) that *ām* does not occur after *ṛcch*. He states that very *jñāpaka*: "*ṛccher liṭi*" [Pāṇini 7.4.11]. Indeed, by the rule "*ṛcchatyṝtām*" [Pāṇini 7.4.11], *guṇa* is prescribed for *ṛcch* in the *liṭ* (perfect tense).

If the *ām* suffix were to apply to the root *ṛcch* in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, then because of the intervention of *ām*, the condition of being followed by *liṭ* would be absent, and thus the *guṇa* substitution would not take effect; consequently, the prescription of *guṇa* would be purposeless. Therefore, by the very prescription of *guṇa*, it is indicated that there is no *ām* after *ṛcch*. Thus, since the prohibition of *ām* is already established by that [indication], the prohibition "not after *ṛcch*" (*anṛcchaḥ*) would be redundant—this is the intended meaning. [Now, the rule: *yak* is added to a *sārvadhātuka* affix after roots ending in *jha*, *ñ*, *ṣ*, or *ṭ*. (Pāṇini 3.1.67)

Because of the prohibition [stated] in the rule *na duhasnunamāṃ yakciṇau* (Pāṇini 3.1.89), it is known that the suffix *yak* occurs when the agent is simultaneously the object (*karmakartṛ*). [Objection: But surely, since *yak* is prescribed only after a verbal suffix (*sārvadhātuka*) expressing either a state (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*), it would not apply when a *lakāra* expressing a *karmakartṛ* follows; for [if it did apply], it would supersede the *śap* suffix [prescribed] for the agent. To this, he says: *na duha...*.

By the rule *na duhasnunamāṃ yakciṇau*, the affixes *yak* and *ciṇ* are prohibited for the roots *duh*, *snū*, and *nam* when a lakāra (tense/aspect marker) expressing the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*) follows. Now, this prohibition would be inconsistent because there is no possibility of the application of *yak* or *ciṇ* in the first place when the root is in the *karmakartṛ* state without *yak*. Therefore, the sense is that this very prohibition serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the fact that *yak* does indeed occur in the *karmakartṛ* state. [Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.93: *kṛdatiṅ*]

In certain instances regarding the rules for secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), the mention of *tiṅ* in the rule "tiṅaśca" (Pāṇini 5.3.56) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that suffixes such as *aṇ* and others do not occur after a finite verb (*tiṅ*). Now, one might object: "In the rule 'kṛdatiṅ', the mention of *atiṅ* should be omitted. It cannot be argued that in its absence, finite verbs (*tiṅ*) would also receive the designation of *kṛt*, and consequently, because they would end in a *kṛt* suffix, forms such as *paṭhati* would acquire the designation of nominal stem (*prātipadika*). This objection is invalid, because even if the designation of nominal stem were applied, there would be no fault.

Because [grammatical] numbers such as singularity and so forth are already expressed by the *tiṅ* suffixes, it is impossible to apply *sub* suffixes and the like; furthermore, since a word ending in a *tiṅ* suffix cannot be connected with femininity, it is impossible to derive feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp*. Nor should it be said that primary (*aṇ*) and secondary (*taddhita*) suffixes could arise from words ending in *tiṅ*, because secondary suffixes are prescribed for meanings such as "offspring," and a word ending in *tiṅ* cannot be connected with such meanings as "offspring."

Therefore, because it is impossible to bring about the production of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) from that [verbal form], or rather, because it is possible to prevent the production of suffixes such as *aṇ* from a verbal ending (*tiṅanta*) by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). He states that very indicator: "In some cases, in the rule for secondary derivatives. If the production of a secondary derivative were to occur from a verbal ending as well—on the grounds that it possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—then the rule "also after a verbal ending" (*tiṅaśca*, Pāṇini 5.3.56) would be rendered useless in the section on secondary derivatives, since its purpose would already be accomplished by the rule "the suffixes *tamap* and *iṣṭhan* are used in the sense of excellence" (*atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau*, Pāṇini 5.3.55).

Consequently, since there would be no fault if *tiṅ* were included in the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *kṛt*, and likewise if that which ends in *taṅ* were included in the designation of a nominal stem (*pratipadika*), the intention is that the mention of *atiṅ* in the rule *kṛdatiṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.93) should be rejected. Regarding the rule *kṛtyāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.95): the inclusion of the terms *kṛtya* and *tṛc* in the sense of "fitness" (*arha*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the designation *kṛtya* applies prior to the suffix *ṇvul*. Objection: In the rule *kṛtyāḥ*, it should have been stated as "prior to *ṇvul*" (*prāṅ ṇvulaḥ*).

Otherwise, one might suspect that the suffix *ṇvul* would also incur the designation *kṛtya*; anticipating this objection, he says: "In the sense of 'fitness,' the *kṛtya*-suffixes [are used]. For if the designation *kṛtya* did not apply prior to the rule "ṇvultṛcau" (Pāṇini 3.1.133), then since *tṛc* would also possess the *kṛtya* designation, it would have been possible to formulate the rule simply as "arhe kṛtyāḥ," and the mention of *tṛc* would be redundant. Since the rule "arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca" (Pāṇini 3.3.169) mentions *tṛc* separately, it is inferred from that that the *kṛtya* designation applies prior to *ṇvul*.

It should not be argued that, although the meaning is obtained through the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the designation *kṛtya* applies prior to the suffix *tṛc*, it does not follow that it applies prior to the suffix *ṇvul*. This is because an indicator depends upon a specific rule; thus, it indicates that the governing heading for the *kṛtya* designation applies prior to the rule "ṇvultṛcau" (Pāṇini 3.1.133), which contains the term *tṛc*. Consequently, since this is established by the indicator, the statement "prior to *ṇvul*" need not be explicitly stated. It is therefore established that the reading of the rule as "kṛtyāḥ prāṅṇvulaḥ" found in the *Kāśikā* is to be disregarded.

Regarding *Pāṇini-sūtra* 3.2.158, *spṛhigṛhi-*: The prescription of *āluc* when *luś* would have already sufficed is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this suffix also occurs after other roots. Objection: In the rule *spṛhigṛhipatidayinidrātandrāśraddhābhya āluc*, why not prescribe the heavy suffix *āluc* instead? Let only the suffix *luś* be prescribed.

Having raised the objection that once the suffix *śap* is applied, the form *spṛhayāluḥ* is established by the lengthening rule "ato dīrgho yañi" (Pāṇini 7.3.101), he says: "luśeti. Thus, the prescription of the suffix *āluc* indicates that *āluc* occurs even after verbal roots not explicitly mentioned in the sūtras. Consequently, forms such as *śayaluḥ* are established.

In that context, the meaning is that because the suffix *śap* is elided by the rule "adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.72), a long vowel for the *at* [of the root] is impossible; therefore, the resolution [of the grammatical operation] cannot be achieved through *lu*. The rule "anadyatane luṭ" (Pāṇini 3.3.15) [indicates]: the mention of the technical designation *sat* for *lṛṭ* in the future tense indicates that *lṛṭ* occurs in the sense of "not today" (*anadyatana*). The rule "ṭhalṛṭaḥ sadvā" (Pāṇini 3.3.14) follows the sequence of rules beginning with "anadyatane luṭ."

In this regard, a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) must be made for the rule *anadyatane luṭ*. In the sūtra *anadyatane*, the phrase *lṛṭaḥ sat* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). The meaning of that is: when [the time] is not of the current day (*anadyatana*), the substitutes *śatṛ* and *śānac*—which bear the technical designation *sat*—are applied in place of *lṛṭ*. By means of this, forms such as *śvo 'gnīn ādāsyamānena* ("by one who will take up the sacred fires tomorrow") and *śvaḥ somena yakṣyamāṇena* ("by one who will sacrifice with Soma tomorrow") are established. Nor should it be asked how this is possible, given the absence of an explicit grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) prescribing *lṛṭ* for the future not of the current day.

It is established in the *Bhāṣya* that by means of the *yogavibhāga* (division of rules), through the prescription of substitutes designated as *sat* for *lṛṭ* in the sense of non-today (*anadyatana*), it is indicated that *lṛṭ* exists in the sense of non-today. Thus he says: "Regarding *anadyatane lṛṭ*" (*Jñāpakapāṭha*: "In the sense of hope, as if past" [Pāṇini 3.3.132]). By the indicator (*jñāpaka*) "If 'alam' is used in the sense of possibility" (*sambhāvane'lamiti cet* [Pāṇini 3.3.154]), it is understood that even in the sense of possibility, the word 'alam' is not intended to be mandatory.

Objection: Since there is no distinction between *āśaṃsā* (expectation) and *saṃbhāvanā* (possibility), those suffixes prescribed for *āśaṃsā* would also apply to *saṃbhāvanā*, and those prescribed for *saṃbhāvanā* would also apply to *āśaṃsā*. Furthermore, while the sense of "capability" (*alam-artha*) is invariably understood in *saṃbhāvanā*, it is not understood in *āśaṃsā*. Thus, even though there is no difference in their meanings, a distinction exists based on the presence or absence of the sense of "capability. Taking this as the basis, the rule will be settled; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not arise. This should not be said.

If that were the case, then in the sūtra "saṃbhāvane 'lamiti cet" (Pāṇini 3.3.154), the qualification "alamiti cet" would be purposeless. For if the sense of "alam" were necessarily understood in the context of "saṃbhāvana" (possibility), then, due to the absence of any deviation, the qualification "alam" would not have been adopted. Indeed, a qualification is meaningful only when there is both possibility and deviation [from the rule]. Thus...

It is established that it is impossible to state a distinction between *saṃbhāvanā* (possibility) and *āśaṃsā* (expectation) based on whether they are produced by the presence or absence of alarm (*ālarka*). Thus he says: "In the case of *saṃbhāvanā*. If it is asked, "In that case, since there is no distinction between the two, what is the resolution for the previously mentioned lack of systematic order? Kaiyaṭa states: "The resolution is consistent because of the difference between them: *āśaṃsā* is a specific kind of desire in the form 'May this happen to me,' whereas *saṃbhāvanā* is a specific kind of uncertain knowledge restricted to one alternative. [Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.157: *tum-arthe sesan-kasunah*].

The inclusion of the term *tum-artha* (meaning "having the sense of *tumun*") indicates that there exists another [grammatical] agent distinct from the agent of the *tumun* suffix. By means of the rule beginning with *vidiṣṭaṭhatumarthe seseṇase*, suffixes such as *se* and *sen* are prescribed in the Vedic section for the sense of *tumun*. In this regard, the doubt arises: what is the meaning of *tumun*? It cannot be the agent; for if that were the case, the meaning of the rule would be that *se*, *sen*, and so forth occur when the agent is expressed.

In that case, the phrase *tum-arthe* would be redundant, because the fact that those [kṛt suffixes] have the agent (*kartṛ*) as their meaning is already established by the rule *kartari kṛt*. Therefore, he says: "The mention of *tum-artha*... Thus, since the mention of *tum-artha* is redundant according to the previously stated reasoning, it indicates that there is another meaning for the suffix *tumun* besides the agent. And that [other meaning] is the action (*bhāva*); furthermore, suffixes such as *se-sen-ādi* are desired in the sense of action (*bhāve*). This is the intention behind making the mention of *tum-artha* for that purpose.

The purpose of making this known is that the *vārttika* "avyayakṛto bhāve" need not be stated; for it is clear in the *Bhāṣya* that by the continued application of the mention of "tum-artha," the fact that indeclinable *kṛt*-suffixes such as *ktvā* and others denote the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) is established. Regarding the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), the particle *eva* in the subsequent rule *tayoreva* (3.4.70) indicates that from this point onward there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) [of both the agent and the action].

The particle *ca* in the rule *ādikarmaṇi ktaḥ kartari ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.71) indicates that there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) prior to the mention of the suffix *kta*. [Objection: But then, what is the purpose of the particle *eva* in the rule *tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ*? It cannot be argued that it is for the sake of indicating that the *kṛtya* suffixes and so forth should apply only to the meanings of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), and not to the agent (*kartṛ*).

Having raised the objection that the intended meaning is already established because the rule *tayoh* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the general rule *kartari kṛt*, [the author] states that the particle *eva* is for the purpose of indicating that even when *kṛtya* suffixes are used, there is also the inclusion of the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, since the sense of the agent would also be included [by the general rule], the particle *eva* serves its purpose by excluding that [agentive sense] in this specific instance. However, its utility elsewhere is that in words such as *bhavya* and so on, the agent is indeed understood.

For this very reason, both the usage *goyo māṇavakaḥ sāmnām* ("the boy is the singer of the Sāmans") in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), and the usage *geyāni māṇavakena sāmāni* ("the Sāmans are to be sung by the boy") in the sense of the object (*karman*), are justified. Thus he says: "The word *eva* [in the rule] is for the sake of restricting [the application] to those two alone. Consequently, the intention is that the mention of the option (*vā*) in the rule *bhavyageya...* (Pāṇini 3.4.68) need not be made. [Objection: But if this is what is being indicated, then in the rules *dāśagohnau saṃpradāne* (3.4.73) and *bhīmādayo 'pādāne* (3.4.74), a co-application (*samāveśa*) would also result.

And thus, their usage would also occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*); therefore, he says "in the sense of the inception of an action" (*ādikarmaṇi*) and so forth. The meaning is this: let it simply be that the suffix *kta* [is used] in the sense of the agent in the case of the inception of an action; there is no purpose for the word "and" (*ca*). For the inclusion of the meaning of the word "and"—namely, the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*)—is established by the previously mentioned statement itself, which is indicated by the particle "only" (*eva*). However, the presence of the letter *c* (in *ca*) indicates that in the subsequent sūtras following "in the inception of an action," there is no co-occurrence with the agent. And thus, in cases such as *dāśa* ("butcher") and *goghna* ("cow-slayer"), there is no co-occurrence with the meaning of the agent. Thus ends the third chapter. Now begins the fourth chapter.

Because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.48), which prescribes the suffix *ṅīṣ*, no *taddhita* suffix arises from the word *praṣṭha*. In the *Bhāṣya* on that very rule, *praṣṭhī* and *pracarī* are cited as examples; thus, in the sense of "the woman of the *praṣṭha*," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied to the word *praṣṭha*.

One might object: since the sense of "the wife of the *praṣṭha*" is present in the meaning "belonging to him" (*tasyedaṃ*), would not a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) ending in *aṇ* be required? Anticipating this, he says: "because of the prescription of *ṅīṣ*. For if the production of a secondary derivative from the word *praṣṭha* were mandatory, then—since it would end in *aṇ*—the form *prāṣṭhī* could be established by the suffix *ṅīp* alone according to the rule *ṭiḍḍhaṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15). In that case, the prescription of *ṅīṣ* by the rule *puṃyogādākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.48) would become redundant.

Furthermore, there is no difference in form between the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ*; nor is there any difference in accent, for just as *ṅīṣ* is acute, so too *ṅīp* is acute by the rule "anudāttasya ca yatro-dāttalopaḥ" [Pāṇini 6.1.161]. Therefore, the purpose of prescribing *ṅīṣ* being otherwise redundant, it serves to indicate that a taddhita suffix does not arise from the word *praṣṭha*. Nor can it be argued that in the sense of "this belongs to Bhānu," the suffix *cha* would be applied to the word *bhānu* by the rule "vṛddhācchaḥ" [Pāṇini 4.2.114], resulting in the feminine form *bhānavīyā* with the addition of *ṭāp*.

In that case, let the rule *puṃyogāt* exist for the purpose of prescribing the suffix *ṅīṣ* while setting aside *ṭāp*. If so, it must be explained how that [rule] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). [The answer is: because the mention of the word *ākhyā* would otherwise be redundant. Since that [mention] is purposeless, it indicates that the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after any word denoting a male that applies to a female, even without the production of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

In the case of *bhānavīyā*, the word *bhānu* which denotes a male does not apply to a female, and that which applies to a female—the form ending in the suffix *cha*—does not denote a male; therefore, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is not applied there. However, since the word *praṣṭha* denotes a female even without a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after it. Thus, the intended meaning is that the suffix *ṅīṣ* is not applied to the word *praṣṭha* when a secondary derivative follows. [Pāṇini 4.1.68] *svāṅgāccopasarjanāt* (Sūtra 4.2.54).

Because of the prohibition in the rule *sahanavidyamānapūrvācca* (Pāṇini 4.1.57), which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), it follows that [the suffix] occurs even after a word that is oxytone (*ānantodātta*). [Objection: But in the rule *svāṅgāccopasarjanādasaṃyogopadhāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.54), the term *upasarjanāt* ("after a secondary member") is redundant. This is because the term *upasarjanāt* is already obtained by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *bahuvrīheḥ* from the preceding rule *bahuvrīheścāntodāttāt* (4.1.52).

Furthermore, by the principle of simultaneous prescription (*saṃniyogaśiṣṭanyāya*), the term *antodāttāt* (from a word having an acute accent on the final syllable) would also be understood as continuing [into this rule]. To prevent that, the word *upasarjanāt* (from a secondary member) is employed. Once that is included, by its force, the suffix *ṅīṣ* will occur after any secondary member ending in a word denoting a body part, whether it has an acute accent on the final syllable or not. It should be stated that, precisely through the power of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), it is understood that *antodāttāt* does not continue into the rule *svāṅgācca*. He states the indicator: "with *saha*, *nañ*, and *vidyamāna*."

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is prohibited after a *bahuvrīhi* compound beginning with *saha-* and so forth, when the member preceding it is a *svāṅga* (body part). Examples are *sakeśā* ("having hair") and *akeśā* ("hairless"), as well as *vidyamānanāsikā* ("possessing a nose"). In these cases, because the *bahuvrīhi* begins with *saha-* etc., the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member applies; consequently, by the rule of "remaining unaccented" (*śeṣanighāta*), the *svāṅga* does not possess an acute accent on its final syllable. Thus, since there is no possibility for the application of *ṅīṣ* by the rule "*svāṅgāccopasarjanāt*" [Pāṇini 4.1.54], the prohibition is redundant.
