Being redundant, it serves to indicate that the word *antodāttāt* ("from that which has an acute accent on the final syllable") is not to be carried over [into this context].

And likewise, since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply even after an anudātta-final stem such as *saha-* when preceded by [words like] *sa-* etc., the rule *sahanaj...* (Pāṇini 5.2.28) is meaningful as a prohibition of that [suffix]. Thus, since the word *upasarjanāt* can be obtained simply by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase *bahuvrīheḥ*, the intention is that the mention of *upasarjana* need not be made. [The rule] *ḍhaki lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.133) indicates this very point: that the suffix *ḍhak* occurs after *pitṛṣvasṛ*.

[Objection: Now, it might be argued that from the word *pitṛṣvasṛ*, by the rule "ḍhaki lopaḥ," the final vowel *ṛ* is elided, and thus the form *paitṛṣvaseya* is intended. That [form] is not established, because there is no grammatical injunction (*anuśāsana*) prescribing the suffix *ḍhak* after the word *pitṛṣvasṛ*. To this, he says: "This very... [and so forth].

The meaning is this: since the rule prescribing the elision of *t* when the suffix *ḍhak* follows the word *pitṛṣvasṛ* would be inconsistent if *ḍhak* were absent, the very prescription of the elision of *t* when *ḍhak* follows serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that *ḍhak* indeed occurs after the word *pitṛṣvasṛ*. By means of this indicator, one should assume the inclusion of the word *pitṛṣvasṛ* within the *śubhrādi* group [of words that take the suffix *aṇ*]. Alternatively, it should be understood that in the rule *strībhyo ḍhañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.120), the term *strībhyaḥ* refers to the general sense of "feminine" rather than just the specific word-form.
Thus, the formation of *pitṛṣvasrīya* by means of *ḍhak* is established; so the author of the Uddyota has demonstrated. (Jñāpakasamuccaya, p. 6).

Regarding *brāhmaṇamāṇava-* (Pāṇini 4.2.42): The prescription of the suffix *yañ* when [the general rule for] *yañ* is already in effect indicates that this [suffix] applies to other words as well. [Objection]: But surely, by the rule *brāhmaṇamāṇavavāḍavād yan* (4.2.42), the suffix *yan* is prescribed after words such as *brāhmaṇa* in the sense of a collection (*samūha*). Examples include *brāhmaṇyam* ("a collection of Brāhmaṇas") and so forth. In that case, the mention of *yan* in the rule need not exist; for the desired forms would be established by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of *yañ* from the preceding rule *kedārād yañ ca* (4.2.40).

For there is indeed no distinction between the suffix *yañ* and *yan* with respect to form or sound; nor can it be argued that when *yañ* is present, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would apply by the rule "yañaśca" (Pāṇini 4.1.16), whereas it would not when *yan* is present—this being the distinction. This is because it is stated in the *Kaumudī* that the suffix *ṅīp* applies only after a word ending in *yañ* belonging to the section on offspring (*apatya*). Furthermore, since words such as *brāhmaṇa* are inherently "vṛddha" (possessing a heavy first vowel), the initial *vṛddhi* substitution occurs even when *yañ* is present; thus, even this specific distinction is impossible. Anticipating this objection, he says: "When *yañ* is the subject under discussion."

And thus, the inclusion of *yañ* is purposeful, as it indicates that [the suffix] occurs after words other than *brāhmaṇa* and so forth. By this, the form *pṛṣṭhyam*—meaning "a collection of *pṛṣṭhas*"—is established. Furthermore, since there would be initial *vṛddhi* (*ādi-vṛddhi*) when *yañ* is present, the inclusion of *yañ* is made for that reason; thus, its purpose is fulfilled. Consequently, the Vārttika stating "an addition regarding *pṛṣṭha*" need not be composed, because the desired result is achieved through this very indicator (*jñāpaka*). [Sūtra 4.2.45: *khaṇḍikādibhyaś-ca*. (And [the suffix *cha* is added] after *khaṇḍika* and others.)

The inclusion of the word *kṣudrakamālava* in the *khaṇḍikādi* group indicates two things: first, that the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) applies here; and second, that the suffix *vuñ* (which precedes) is superseded by the suffix *añ* (which follows). Since this cannot be accounted for otherwise, there is no contradiction in the fact that a single reading serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for both points. [Objection]: But surely, by the rule *khaṇḍikādibhyaśca*, the suffix *añ* is prescribed in the sense of a collection (*samūha*). And since the word *kṣudrakamālava* is recited in the *khaṇḍikādi* list, what is the purpose of its inclusion?

Since the suffix *añ* is already established there by the rule *anudāttāder añ* (Pāṇini 4.2.44), [the formation of the word] is accomplished; the fact that the compound *kṣudrakamālava* begins with an anudātta vowel is as follows: in the sense of "the descendants of the Kṣudrakas," there is elision (*luk*) of the *tadrāja* suffix prescribed by the rule *janapadaśabdāt* (4.1.168); however, from *mālava*, there is the suffix *ñyaṅ* characterized by *vṛddhi*. Then follows the *dvandva* compound. Kaiyaṭa states that because of the udātta accent at the end of the compound, it begins with an anudātta vowel. From that, the suffix *añ* is applied in the sense of a collection (*samūha*).

Nor should it be argued that the recitation of that [word *kṣaudrakamālava*] is for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *vuñ* prescribed by the rule "gotrokṣoṣṭra" (Pāṇini 4.2.39). For, since the rule "anudāttāder añ" (Pāṇini 4.1.45) is subsequent, the suffix *vuñ* of the former [rule] cannot apply in its domain; furthermore, there is no possibility of the application of *vuñ*—which is prescribed after a *gotra* name—to the word *kṣaudrakamālava*, as it does not end in a *gotra* suffix. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states two statements: "For this very reason, the recitation [of that word] makes known that even the preceding *vuñ* sets aside the subsequent *añ*, and that here there is the rule of 'application to what ends with that' (*tadantavidhi*)."

And thus, the *Bhāṣya* establishes as its final conclusion that the word *kṣudrakamālava* is included in the list [of *khaṇḍika*-type words] for the purpose of forming a collective (*samūha*), thereby setting aside the suffix *vuñ*. He states this with the words "in the *khaṇḍika*-type group," and so forth. Now, one might object: how can two distinct meanings be indicated by a single [rule]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "by the impossibility of otherwise" (*anyathānupapattyā*). For indication (*jñāpakatva*) occurs precisely through such impossibility. The sense is that since the prescription of the suffix *añ* after *kṣudrakamālava* would otherwise be untenable without both [conditions], it is possible to indicate both of them.

The authors of the Vārttikas state that this reading is not merely for the sake of providing information; rather, it serves to distinguish between cases: when there is a desire to express a collective group (*samūha*) in the form of an army (*senā*), as in *kṣaudrakamālavī senā*, the suffix *añ* is applied; however, when there is a desire to express another type of collective group, the suffix *vuñ* is applied, as in *kṣaudrakamālavakam*. Regarding the rule *śeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.92): the prescription of the suffix *cha* after a word ending in *phiñ*—as in the rule *pheścha ca* (4.1.149)—is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that suffixes such as *gha* and others do apply even in cases where *aṇ* would otherwise be expected.

The rule *jhrvi.ṭa ṭhaśeṣe* is an *adhikāra-sūtra* (governing rule) signifying that the suffixes *gha* and others, which will be described hereafter, occur in meanings other than "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth. In the absence of this governing rule, the suffixes *gha* and others would apply even in the senses of "offspring" and so on, just like the suffix *aṇ* and others; furthermore, because the *gha*-suffixes are exceptions (*apavāda*) [to the general rules], they would otherwise take precedence. Therefore, the governing rule for the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) has been established. However, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, even though the governing rule for the remainder was not present, rejected the necessity of the *śeṣa-adhikāra* by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), having excluded the application of the *gha*-suffixes to the senses of "offspring" and so forth.

He says that with the words *pheś cha ca*. By the rule *pheś cha ca*, the suffix *cha* is prescribed after a word ending in *phiñ* belonging to the Sauvíra gotra in the sense of "descendant," and by the word *ca*, the suffix *ṭhak* is also prescribed. For example: the descendant of Yamunda is *Yāmundāyaniḥ*; because [Yamunda] belongs to the *Tika*-class, the suffix *phiñ* is applied. His descendant is *Yāmundāyanīyaḥ* or *Yāmundāyanikaḥ*. In that case, let the rule simply be *phervā*. From the preceding rule, *vṛddhāṭ ṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.1.148), the term *ṭhak* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).

In that regard, since the suffix *cha* will apply to the word *mukta* by the rule "vṛddhācchaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.2.114), there is no need for the prescription of *cha*. However, that [prescription] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) to show that in cases where *aṇ* would otherwise apply—such as in the sense of offspring (*apatya*) and so forth—the suffixes *gha* and others do not occur. Thus, since the suffix *cha* would not otherwise be applicable, its prescription is made in order to ensure its application; this constitutes its utility within its own scope (*svāṃśe cāritārthyam*). Consequently, since the desired result is established by this very [indicator], the governing heading "the remainder" (*śeṣādhikāra*) may be rejected; such is the intended meaning.

Although there may be a doubt that the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*) concerns only the domain of [patronymics] formed for the sake of offspring, nevertheless, regarding other meanings as well, the indicators stated in the Bhāṣya—namely, "the mention of *gotra* serves as an indicator for collective derivatives (*sāmūhika*), the mention of *daivayātavagrahaṇa* for those relating to specific objects (*vaiṣayika*), and the mention of *bhastrāyaṇagrahaṇa* for those relating to inhabitants (*naivāsika*)"—should be kept in mind here. [The rule: *kalāpivaiśampāyanāntevāsibhyaśchaṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.104).

Because of the inclusion of *kalāpin* and *vaiśampāyana* [in the rule], it is known that the suffix does not apply to the pupils (*antevāsin*) of those pupils. [Objection: But surely, by the rule "from the pupils of Kalāpin and Vaiśampāyana" (*kalāpivaiśampāyanāntevāsibhyaśca*), the suffix *ṇini* is prescribed after words ending in the third case—meaning "taught by him"—to denote those who study what was taught by them. For example, Haridru was a pupil of Kalāpin.

Then, from *haridru* with the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of "studied [from]," the form *hāridravaṇi* arises. *Ālambi* was a disciple of Vaiśampāyana; from that, with the suffix *ṇini*, the form *ālambina* arises. Among those, Kalāpin was one of the nine disciples of Vaiśampāyana.

Since the term "pupil" (*śiṣya*) is seen to be used in common parlance even for the pupil of a pupil in the world, and since Haridru—the pupil of Kalāpin, who was himself the pupil of Vaiśampāyana—is already included by the very mention of "the pupils of Vaiśampāyana," the mention of "Kalāpin" need not have been in the Sūtra. Similarly, the Sūtra *śaunakādibhyaś chandasi* (Pāṇini 4.3.106), which prescribes the suffix *ṇini* in the sense stated above, also includes the word *khāṇḍāyana* in the list of *śaunaka*-type names.

Khāṇḍāyana was a disciple of Kaṭha, who himself was a disciple of Vaiśampāyana. Thus, one might raise the objection that since Khāṇḍāyana is already included by the mention of "disciple of Vaiśampāyana" according to the logic previously stated, his separate mention in the list beginning with Śaunaka is redundant. Anticipating this, [the author] states its purpose as a *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence): "because of the mention of Kalāpin and Khāṇḍāyana. Accordingly, in the rule (*sūtra*), the term *antevāsin* refers specifically to direct disciples only.

However, the separate mention of *antevāsī* and *antevāsinaḥ* is for the purpose of establishing the suffix *ṇini* in the case of Kalāpin and Khāṇḍāyana, who were the pupils of the pupils of Vaiśampāyana; thus, it serves its purpose within its own scope. As for its purpose elsewhere, it is that the suffix *ṇini* does not apply after the pupils of the pupils of Vaiśampāyana, nor after the pupils of the pupils of Kalāpin. These [names] are to be sought in the Purāṇas and other such texts.

Harīdru, Chagalī, Tumburu, and Ulapa—these four were the disciples of Kalāpin. Ālambi, Kaliṅga, Kamala, Ṛcābha, Āruṇi, Tāṇḍya, Śyāmāyana, Kaṭha, and Kalāpin—these nine were the disciples of Vaiśampāyana; thus says the *Bālamanoramā*. Thus ends the fourth chapter.
The fifth chapter begins.

In the *Jhr-jñā-pa-ṭa* [section], under the rule *upasargāc chandasi* (Pāṇini 5.1.118), it is noted that the mention of *striyāḥ pumvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.34) indicates that the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* do not occur in the sense of *vati*. [Objection: But surely, when the suffix *vati* is added to the words *strī* and *pum*, the forms *strīvat* and *pumvat* are desired; yet these cannot be derived.

By the rule *strīpuṃsābhyāṃ nañstañau bhavanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.87), the suffixes *nañ* and *stañ* are prescribed for all meanings prior to *bhavana* (i.e., from 4.1.83 onwards) based on specific bases. Since these two suffixes are thus prescribed, one might suspect that they would even supersede the suffix *vati* in the rule *tena tulyaṃ kriyā ced vatiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.115). Anticipating this objection, he says: "The mention [in Pāṇini’s grammar] is *striyāḥ puṃvat*."

The rule *strīpuṃsābhyāṃ nañsnañau* does not apply in the sense of *vat*. The point is that if it were to apply, then the designation *puṃvat* would be incorrect. [From the Jñāpakapāda: "Not from a Tatpuruṣa compound preceded by *nañ*" (Pāṇini 5.1.121). By the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *naño guṇapratiṣedhe saṃpādyārhahitālamarthāstaddhitāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.155), it is understood that all these secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) occur after a word that requires another word for its completion (*sāpekṣa*).

By the rule *jhrvi.ṭa ṭhana nañpūrvāttatpuruṣādacaturasaṃgatalavamavaṭayudhakatarasalasebhyaḥ*, it is established that the abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) prescribed by the rules immediately following this one shall not occur after a negative (*nañ*) *tatpuruṣa* compound. Examples include *apatitvam* (the state of not falling) and *apaṭutvam* (the state of not being clever). Regarding this, the author of the *Bhāṣya* provides a *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in order to justify the rejection of the rule; he demonstrates that the abstract suffixes prescribed by the subsequent rules do not apply in cases such as *apatitvam*. Thus he says: "on account of this *jñāpaka*."

The intended meaning is as follows: in cases such as *vatsabhyo na hitam*, because there is a dependence on the negative particle (*nañ*) and thus a lack of semantic independence—the defining characteristic of which is required for the application of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) under the heading of "samartha" (semantically connected)—the production of such a suffix would not occur. Consequently, the rule prescribing that the final syllable of a word ending in a secondary suffix denoting meanings such as "beneficial" (*saṃpādya*) and so forth should be udātta-accented would be untenable. However, since that rule is indeed formulated, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that all secondary suffixes arise even when they depend on the meaning of the negative particle.

The meaning is that in the case of *apatitvam* (the state of being one whose husband is not [alive]), since a negative (*nañ*) tatpuruṣa compound lacks dependence on another word, subsequent secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) are impossible; thus, the desired result is achieved through the suffixes *tv* and *tal*. Therefore, the rule "not after a negative-prefixed tatpuruṣa" (*na nañpūrvāttatpuruṣāt*) is worthy of being rejected. Regarding the rule *samāṃ samāṃ vijāyate* (Pāṇini 5.2.12), the mention of the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) indicates that elision (*luk*) does not occur here.

Objection: In the rule *samāṃ samāṃ vijāyate*, the suffix *kha* is prescribed after the aggregate expression *samāyāṃ samāyām* in the sense of "giving birth every year. The example is *samāṃsamīnā gauḥ* ("a cow that calves every year"). That which gives birth every year is so described. Since this form ends in a *taddhita* suffix, it receives the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); consequently, by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71), the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) belonging to its component would seem to apply. However, by the fact that *samām* is taught with the elision of the *yaK* suffix (*yalopa*), it is indicated (*jñāpaka*) that there is no elision of the case-ending in the preceding member here.

For if there were elision of the *sup* suffix (*supo luk*), then because the augment *yāṭ* would be part of a *sup*-inflected form, the elision of the *ya* [of *yāṭ*] would already be established by that very elision of the *sup*. Consequently, the specific mention of the elision of *ya* (*yalopa*) in the rule would serve as a restrictive injunction (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the elision applies only to the letter *ya*, and not to the entire suffix. Nor should it be argued that, this being the case, there would likewise be no elision of the *sup* suffix in the second member (*uttarapada*) of a compound. This is because we rely on the principle that the specific mention of the elision of *ya* (*yalopa*) applies only to the first member (*pūrvapada*), and thus the audible presence of the vowel *āḥ* occurs in the first member but not in the second.

Nor should it be argued that the mention of the word *samā* with its case-ending (*savibhaktika*) in the rule for the elision of *ya* when a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows in a compound is inconsistent; for the elision of *ya* is stated as an option between the two members in a sentence (*vākya*), and the mention in the Sūtra takes the form of a sentence. Thus he says: "The statement regarding the elision of *ya*. In the rule *yattadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe* (Pāṇini 5.2.39), the inclusion of the term *parimāṇa* (measure) indicates that *pramāṇa* (extent/proof) is one thing and *parimāṇa* (measure/capacity) is another.

Regarding the rule *yattadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatup*: one might object that the inclusion of the term *parimāṇa* is redundant, since the meaning "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is already obtained through the continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *pramāṇe* from the preceding rule *pramāṇe dvayasac* (Pāṇini 5.2.37). Anticipating this objection, he states—*parimāṇagrahaṇam*—that the term is included in order to indicate that *parimāṇa* is distinct from *pramāṇa*.

That by which grain and the like are measured according to their height and circumference—being made of wood or other materials—is *parimāṇa*, and it is called a *prastha* and so forth. Kaiyaṭa states that the width of wood, cloth, and the like, by which they are measured, is *pramāṇa*, such as a *hasta* (cubit) and so on. "Indeed, *unmāna* is measurement from above; *parimāṇa* is measurement from all sides; while *pramāṇa* is length."

"Number, however, is external in every respect. Here, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *arhādagopucchasaṃkhyāparimāṇāṭ ṭhak* (Pāṇini 5.1.19) should be consulted. Regarding the rule *etado 'n* (Pāṇini 5.3.5): because the substitution [of *an*] is prescribed when a suffix beginning with *tha* follows, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the suffix *thamu* occurs here. In the *bhāṣya*, a formal split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *etadaḥ* and *an* was made in order to derive the form *ittham* in the sense of "in this manner."

In this context, the meaning of the rule *etadaḥ* is as follows: the rule *etetau rathoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.4) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. This means that the substitutes *eta* and *it* are applied to the word *etad* when followed by a suffix beginning with *r* or *th*. The suffix *rhil*, prescribed by the rule *anadyatanerhilanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.3.21), begins with *r*; an example for this is *etarhi*. A suffix beginning with *th* is *thamu*.

In this regard, others raise the following objection: since the rule *idamasthamuḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.23) prescribes the suffix *thamu* after the word *idam* alone in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*), the prescription of the substitution of *id* for *etad* before a suffix beginning with *tha* is not logically consistent, as *thamu* is not prescribed after the word *etad*. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that by virtue of this very indication (*jñāpaka*), even after the word *etad*, when a suffix beginning with *tha* occurs in the sense of "manner," there is a prescription of the substitution of *id* for it.

It should not be asked how [the suffix] can have the status of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) since its meaningfulness is possible; for the meaning of the rule is that when a suffix beginning with *th*—prescribed after pronouncing the word *idam* by means of the qualification "beginning with *th*"—is present, there is the substitution of *id* for *etad*. Indeed, *thāl* is not prescribed by restating the word *idam*; rather, only *thamu* is to be understood here.

Nor is the prescription of the substitution of *id* for *etad* logical in the absence of *thamu* when it follows; therefore, the sense is that by the force of that [prescription], it is understood that *thamu* occurs after *etad*. Thus ends the fifth chapter. Now begins the sixth chapter.

Pāṇini 6.1.2 (*ajāder dvitīyasya*) states: "Of [a root] beginning with a vowel, the second [monosyllabic portion] is reduplicated. Pāṇini 6.1.3 (*na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*) provides a prohibition [of this rule], which indicates that when the preceding [portion] is removed, the consonant [following it] is not removed. Objection: It must be stated that by the rule *ajāder dvitīyasya*, which prescribes the doubling of the second monosyllable following the initial vowel, the doubling of the first monosyllable—which would otherwise be obtained by the rule *ekāco dve prathamasya*—is superseded.

In that case, since reduplication (dvirvacana) would apply to the first monosyllable along with its consonant, such a reduplication would be sublated by the second reduplication; consequently, the consonant contained within the first monosyllable would not undergo reduplication. Thus, in the form *aṭiṭiṣati*, this [root] *aṭ* constitutes the first monosyllable.

Furthermore, by the rule *dvitīyaikāc*, one might intend for the doubling of the word *ṭi* by taking the vowel *i* as qualified by the letter *ṭ*; however, that would not be established. Anticipating this objection, he says: *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*. For by the rule *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*, the doubling of the letters *n*, *d*, and *r*—provided they are the first members of a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) following a vowel—is prohibited.

For example, in the case of *ūrṇunāva*, when the doubling of the entire word *rṇu*—characterized by the letter *r*—would otherwise apply according to the rule for the second singular *ekāc* [stem], the doubling occurs of the word *nu* alone, with the *r* being excluded. In that context, since the absence of doubling is already established by the very fact that the doubling of the first *ekāc* (*ūr*)—which contains the *r*—is barred, the explicit prohibition of its doubling is redundant; this redundancy serves to indicate the principle: "when the preceding element is removed, the consonant is not removed."

The meaning is that when the doubling of the first monosyllable is superseded by the doubling of the second monosyllable, the doubling of the consonant contained within that [first monosyllable] is not superseded. Thus, since the doubling of the *repha* (the letter *r*) would also follow as a consequence, the rule "na ndrāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.3) is intended to prohibit that. In this way, the doubling of the word *ṭi* in forms such as *aṭiṭiṣati* is established without obstruction; this is the intended sense. [Now follows: *grahijyā-vayi-* (Sūtra 6.1.16).

Because of the prohibition of *saṃprasāraṇa* for the letter *y* of the root *vay-* in the rule *liṭi vayo yaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.38), there is an *jñāpaka* (indicative mark) that the prohibition of *saṃprasāraṇa* for *vay-* does not apply due to the inclusion of the root *veñ*.

In the *bhāṣya* on the rule *grahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicativṛścatipṛcchatibhṛjjatīnāṃ ṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), the author of the *bhāṣya*, wishing to reject the inclusion of *vayi* [in the rule], argues as follows: Since *veñ* is read among the roots beginning with *yaja-* (the *yajādi* group), the substitution of *vayi* for *veñ* is effected by the rule *veño vayiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.41) in the *liṭ* tense. Consequently, because *vayi* possesses the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for *veñ*, the semivowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) is already established by the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.15). Therefore, the reading of *vayi* in the rule *grahijyāvayī* is redundant for the purpose of effecting vocalization.

Nor should it be argued that its recitation there is for the sake of establishing *saṃprasāraṇa* even before an affix marked with *ṅ*; for *vayi* is restricted solely to the domain of the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, and thus there is no usage of it before an affix marked with *ṅ*. Furthermore, since the *liṭ* affixes possess the *kit* designation, the *saṃprasāraṇa* is established by virtue of [the root] belonging to the *yajādi* class, as he has stated.

Regarding this, one might raise the objection: since the rule *veñaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.40) prohibits *saṃprasāraṇa* for the root *veñ* in the *liṭ* tense, the same prohibition would apply to *vay* as well; therefore, the reading of *vay* [in the *gaṇapāṭha*] should be intended to override that prohibition. Anticipating this doubt, he stated: "Or rather, the prohibition of the *yakāra* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is no prohibition [of *saṃprasāraṇa* for *vay*]. His intention was as follows: by the rule *liṭi vayo yaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.38), the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the *yakāra* of *vay* is prohibited in the *liṭ* tense.

In that regard, concerning the rule *veñaḥ* which is intended to prohibit *saṃprasāraṇa*, if the mention of *veñ* had included *vay* as well, then the prohibition would have been accomplished by that very rule; consequently, the rule *liṭi vayo yaḥ* would not have been formulated. Since that rule was indeed formulated, it indicates that *vay* is not included within the mention of *veñ* in the prohibitory rule.

And thus, although the inclusion of *veñ* in the prohibitive rule [Pāṇini 6.1.45] prevents the inclusion of *vay-i*, there is no obstacle to the inclusion of *vay-i* in the prescriptive rule "vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti" (Pāṇini 6.1.15); therefore, since the samprasāraṇa is established by that very rule, the mention of *vay-i* in the rule "grahijyāvayi... (Pāṇini 6.1.16) may be rejected. Having all this in mind, he says: "Thus, of the *yakāra* of *vay-i*. [This concludes the discussion on] "ādeca upadeśe" (Pāṇini 6.1.45).

In the rule *mīnātiminotidīṅāṃ lyapi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.50), the continued application of the term *ej* indicates that the substitution of *ā* does not occur for a substitute whose cause is subsequent (*paranimittaka*). Furthermore, the prohibition regarding the suffixes beginning with *aś* (i.e., those other than *śit*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the rules for *āy* and other such replacements do not supersede the substitution of *ā*. The author of the Bhāṣya, wishing to demonstrate the purposelessness (*vaiyarthyam*) of the inclusion of the term *upadeśe* (in the original instruction) in the rule *ādeca upadeśe 'śiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), raises the following objection: if the term *upadeśe* were not employed, then even in cases such as *cetā* and *stotā*, where the *guṇa* substitution has already taken place, the substitution of *ā* would still apply because the condition of ending in an *ej* vowel remains present. Anticipating this, he addresses the rule *mīnātiminotidīṅāṃ lyapi ca*.

The rule prescribing *ātva* for roots ending in *ej* (such as *mī*), by virtue of the letter *cakāra*, would otherwise be redundant under the rule *ādeca upadeśe* since the form *mātā* and others would be established by that very rule simply because they end in *ej*. Thus, the rule *mīnāti*—being otherwise purposeless—indicates (*jñāpaka*) that *ātva* does not apply to a root ending in *aij* when that *aij* is conditioned by a subsequent cause (*paranimittaka*). Consequently, a root ending in *ec* that has acquired such a quality through a subsequent cause would not attain *ātva*; therefore, the rule *mīnāti* exists to ensure that *ātva* is indeed attained in such cases.

It is meaningful. Consequently, he explained that even in cases such as *cetā* and so forth, because the single vowel *e* has already been transformed into a guṇa by virtue of the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the substitution of *ā* for the whole [of the root] via the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti* does not occur. He states this: "In this context, there is the continued application (*anuvartana*) of the mention of *ej*. Here, the commentary *Udyota* should be consulted, which states: "The sense is that if the meaning were 'there is the substitution of *ā* for roots ending in *ej*, such as *mī* etc.', then since the substitution of *ā* would be established by this very [present] rule, the aforementioned rule (*ādeca...*) would be redundant; therefore, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this specific point."

In that very same commentary (*bhāṣya*), regarding the word *upadeśa* as having the sense of an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), it is stated that by the word *upadeśa*, the treatise (*śāstra*) is denoted. Since this is a qualification of the treatise, and because there is no application of the rule for [compounds] ending in such a term (*tadantavidhi*), the meaning obtained is: "the substitution of *ā* occurs for that *ec* which is in an *upadeśa*. In that case, however, the word *upadeśa* has the sense of an object (*karmasādhana*), and thus the word *upadeśa* denotes that which is being taught (*upadiśyamāna*).

Since that which is being taught (*upadiśyamāna*) ought to be a qualifier of the vowel *eC* (the first element of the *eC* diphthongs), the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*) results in the meaning: "the substitution of *ā* occurs for that which ends in *eC* when it is being taught. In this context, regarding the alternative view that "the teaching (*upadeśa*) consists of the *eC* vowels," as well as the other view, in the case of the root *glai* with the suffix *anīyar*, in the form *glai-anīya*, the substitution of *ā* would be superseded by the substitution of *āy* because the latter is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Consequently, the form *glānīyam* would not be established.

Likewise, having raised the objection that *āt* would apply in the case of *niśānīyam*, it is stated: "In this case as well, the prohibition of *śit* (the marker for the present stem) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *āy*-substitutes do not subvert the application of *āt*. For the purpose of the prohibition of *āt* when *śit* follows is indeed to ensure the absence of *āt* in forms such as *glāyati* when *śap* follows. Even there, in the stage *glai a ti*, since the desired form is established by the substitution of *āya*—which, being subsequent in order, subverts *āt*—what is the use of the prohibition of *śit*?

And that prohibition [of the augment *iṭ*] serves to indicate that the *āya*-class suffixes do not subvert the substitution of *ā*. Therefore, since the substitution of *ā* would otherwise apply, the term "before a non-*śit*" (*aśiti*) is stated for the purpose of prohibiting it; thus, the absence of *ā* in forms such as *glāyati* is established, while the presence of *ā* in forms such as *glānīyam* is also established. Having this in mind, he says: "The prohibition is by the rule 'before a non-*śit*'. [Now follows the rule: *halṅyābbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.68).

The prohibition [of *nalopa*] in the vocative case by the rule *na ṅisaṃbuddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.8) indicates that the elision of a consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is established as not being subject to the elision of *n*. In the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), regarding the form *rājan-s*, one might object: "Since the elision of the suffix *su* is already accomplished by the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.23), let there be no need for the mention of 'the first consonant' (*prathamahal*) in that rule. Anticipating this objection, [the author of the Bhāṣya] states that if the elision of *n* were to take place, the elision of the final consonant cluster would be treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to it, and thus the elision of *n* would not be achieved.

Desiring to refute the solution stated by the author of the *Vārttika*, the author of the *Bhāṣya* said: "When the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is to be performed, the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is established, since [Pāṇini] teaches the prohibition of the elision of *n* in the vocative case in the rule 'not in the vocative ending in -ṅi' (8.2.8). If, from the word *rājan* in the vocative, the elision of the final consonant cluster were to be considered non-established (*asiddha*) when the elision of *n* was to be performed, then—because the *n* would not be at the end of a word—the elision would not even arise, and thus the prohibition of that [elision] would be purposeless.

Therefore, that prohibition makes it known that when *nalopa* is to be applied, *saṃyogāntalopa* is not *asiddha*. Consequently, in the case of *rājā*, since the desired result is achieved solely through *saṃyogāntalopa* of the suffix *su*, the purpose stated in the *vārttika* for the inclusion of the term "first" (*prathama*)—namely, to effect the elision of *su* in *rājā*—is not tenable; such is the intention of the *Bhāṣya*. Thus he says: "The prohibition [applies] in the case of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) by the rule *na ṅisaṃbuddhyoḥ*. [This concludes the discussion on] *prathamayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102).

The mention of *ij* in the rule *nādici* (Pāṇini 6.1.104) indicates that the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) does not apply to the case-endings *jas* and *śas*. [Objection: But in forms such as *vṛkṣāḥ*, when the stage *vṛkṣa-as* is reached, the long vowel of the same class as the preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is desired; however, that would not occur, because the *pararūpa* substitute, being a universal exception (*sarvāpavāda*), would be applicable. As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The substitutes *guṇa* and *yaṇ* are general rules (*utsarga*); the exceptions (*apavāda*) to them are the *vṛddhi*, the *savarṇadīrgha*, and the *pūrvasavarṇa* substitutes."

Anticipating the objection that "for all of these, the subsequent form [of the vowel] would result in an elision," he establishes the absence of the subsequent form by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), stating: "the mention of *ij*. In the rule *nādici* (Pāṇini 6.1.104), which prohibits the homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*), the purpose of mentioning *ij* is to ensure that there is no prohibition of the homogeneous preceding vowel in cases such as *vṛkṣāḥ*. If, in those instances, the subsequent form were to occur by overriding the long homogeneous preceding vowel, then since the long homogeneous preceding vowel would not even be applicable, [there would be no need for the mention of *ij*].

Since even a prohibition does not occur [in this case], what is the purpose of the mention of *ij* which has the result of preventing that prohibition? The intention is that its inclusion serves to indicate (*jñāpaka*) that the single-substitute *pararūpa* does not take place when *jaś* and *śas* follow. Nor should it be argued that the mention of *ij* is for the sake of carrying over (*anuvṛtti*) into the subsequent rule, "After a long vowel, before *jas* and *ca*" (Pāṇini 6.1.105); for if that were the case, one should have mentioned *ij* right there in that rule as "after a long vowel, before *ij* and *jas*" (*dīrghādijjasoḥ*). Since it is mentioned here, it must be stated that it is for the sake of the present context alone.

Since it has already been stated that even that is not possible, the inclusion of the term *sad* is redundant and serves merely as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). The detailed explanation is found in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the rule *plutapragṛhyā aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.125): because of the injunction for the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) in the rule *plutaḥ prakṛtyā*, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs by means of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) through the application of the principle of mutual exclusion (*vipratiṣedha*). Objection: But why is the preservation of the original form for the protracted vowel (*pluta*) stated in the rule *plutapragṛhyā*?

Nor should it be argued that this [rule] is stated for the purpose of overriding vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*); for since the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.1), only vowel-sandhi in the form of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) and so forth would apply, rendering the prescription of the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) useless. Anticipating this objection, he says: "By the rule *plutaḥ prakṛtyā*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.125). If vowel-sandhi were to occur because the protracted vowel is non-existent, then the prescription of the preservation of the original form would be purposeless.

Precisely because of this prescription, it is made known that the *pluta* vowel is established; by means of this indication, it is taught that the *pluta* arises from the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) operation. Thus, the intention is that the prescription of the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form retention) for the *pluta* is purposeful, as its result is the absence of *saṃdhi*. Regarding the rule *anudāttaṃ padam* (Pāṇini 6.1.158): since the simultaneity [of accents] is already established by the rule *tvaicāntaśca yugapat* (6.2.51), the fact that this [present] rule teaches simultaneity indicates that accentuation does not occur simultaneously.

In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam* (Pāṇini 6.1.158), it is stated in the verse: "The accent of the word as a whole [is prescribed] with the exception of one [element], for the purpose of precluding separate accents for the augment, the substitute, the base, and the suffix. Having thus stated the purpose of the sūtra—that since multiple accents would simultaneously apply to the base, suffix, and so forth within a single word, whereas only one accent is desired, this sūtra is formulated for that reason—it is then argued: "This is not a valid purpose, because this [word] *tavai*..."

Since simultaneity is already established by the rule *cāntaśca yugapat* (Pāṇini 6.1.51), the fact that the teacher teaches simultaneity again serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that "the accent does not occur simultaneously. Its purpose is explained in the *Khaṇḍikāvṛtti*. The intention is as follows: by the rule *tavai cāntaśca*, it is prescribed that for a word ending in the suffix *-tave*, both the final acute accent (*antodātta*) and the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member—which is designated as a *gati*—occur simultaneously; the example is *anvetavai*.

In that regard, since there is no contradiction in the establishment of multiple accents (*aneka-svara*) within a single word at one time even without simultaneous application, the mention of "simultaneous" (*yugapad*) would be redundant; therefore, it indicates that multiple accents do not occur simultaneously. Thus, in forms such as *anvetavai*, the mention of "simultaneous" was made for the purpose of the simultaneous operation of the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*) and the accent of the particle (*gati-svara*); in this way, its utility is established in its own specific scope. By this, it is proven that in other words, accent does not occur simultaneously.

And thus, for one who employs the Sūtra, its establishment is achieved solely through an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This is what he states with the words "that this... (*yadayam*): since the alternative (*paryāya*) is already established by the rule *ṛte vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.2.208), the prescription of that alternative serves as an indicator that elsewhere no alternative occurs. [Objection: But even if the absence of multiple accents simultaneously is established by this indicator, an alternative [application] of multiple accents would still result through the option (*vikalpa*). However, only a single accent is desired.

Anticipating the question of how its establishment occurs, he says: "In the case of *rikta*, there is an option (*vibhāṣā*). By the rule "in the case of *rikta*, there is an option," it is prescribed that the word *rikta* may optionally have an udātta accent on the first syllable. In the alternative case, it has an udātta accent on the final syllable by virtue of the accent of the suffix.

If, moreover, those respective accents were to occur alternately, then—since there would be two alternating accents such that sometimes the initial udātta by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātu-svara*) and sometimes the final udātta by the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*)—the desired result would be achieved simply by the rule for optional application (*vikalpa-vidhāna*). What, then, would be the purpose of the rule "in the case of *rikta*, it is optional" (*rikte vibhāṣā*)? And yet, that rule has been established; it serves to indicate that multiple accents do not occur alternately.

Thus, since both successive application (*paryāya*) and simultaneous application (*yaugapadya*) have been refuted, it is established that there is no need for this rule (*sūtra*), because the accent will be determined by the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*)—"Of rules that are subsequent, permanent, internal, or exceptional, each subsequent one is stronger"—which takes into account factors such as being subsequent or non-permanent. However, a doubt remains: although these two indicators establish that multiple acute accents (*udātta*) cannot coexist within a single word, they do not establish the absence of the coexistence of an acute accent (*udātta*) and a circumflex accent (*svarita*).

Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "Even in a circumflex (svarita) vowel, there is an unraised (anudātta) [pitch]. Since the simultaneous occurrence of the rising (udātta) pitch has been ruled out by the interpretive indicator (jñāpaka), and because the rising pitch exists even within the circumflex, [the rule] applies to both the rising and the circumflex pitches as well.

The intention of the Bhāṣya is that [the rule] is established upon the rejection of both succession (*paryāya*) and simultaneity (*yaugapadya*). However, in this treatise, by the mention of *udātta*, there is no inclusion of an *udātta* that is a constituent part (*avayava*) of a *svarita*. For this very reason, the separate mention [of them] in rules such as "udāttasvaritayoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.4) is consistent. And thus, for the purpose of excluding coexistence with the *svarita*, the sūtra "anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam" is indeed necessary.

For this very reason, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), keeping this in mind, stated immediately after [the words] "even when this rule (*yoga*) is being commenced": "In that regard, the *Codyota* explains: 'By this, it is shown that the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) is inconsistent with having the circumflex (*svarita*) as its object. It should be noted that the Commentator says 'even when it is being commenced' precisely on this basis, thereby clearly demonstrating the necessity of the rule (*sūtra*)."

From the evidence (*jñāpaka*) in *Jhr-jñā-pa-ṭa*—namely, the prescription of the *anudātta* accent for the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following *tāsī*—it is understood that the accent of the *vikaraṇa*, even though it is *satiśiṣṭa* (later-added), does not sublate the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka*. Now, regarding *Vi-ṭa*: by the Vārttika rule "The accent of what is *satiśiṣṭa* is stronger" (*sati śiṣṭasvarabalīyastvaṃ ca*), it is stated that when there is already an accent for one element in a single word, an accent subsequently taught or prescribed for another element is stronger.

If that were so, then in forms such as *sunutaḥ* and *dhinutaḥ*, the accent of the *vikaraṇa* would supersede the accent of the *sārvadhātuka*. This is because, since the *vikaraṇa* is prescribed when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows, the accent of the *vikaraṇa* applies first; thus, once the *sārvadhātuka* accent has occurred, the *vikaraṇa* accent would remain as the "later" (*śiṣṭa*) one. Anticipating this objection, he says: "after *tās*" (*tāseḥ parasya*).

By the rule *tāsyanudāttenṅidadupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudāttam* (Pāṇini 6.1.186), the *anudātta* (low-pitched) nature of the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following *tās* is prescribed. The examples are *kartārau* and *kartāraḥ*.

If the accent of the *sārvadhātuka* were to be sublated by the accent of the *vikaraṇa* according to the principle of "that which remains" (*satiśiṣṭa*), then, since the *vikaraṇa* *tās* would be acute, the remainder of the word would be unaccented by the rule "the word is unaccented" (*anudāttaṃ padam*), and the *lasārvadhātuka* would consequently be established as unaccented. In that case, what would be the purpose of specifically prescribing the unaccented nature of the *lasārvadhātuka* following the *tās*? That very prescription indicates that even an accent of a *vikaraṇa* that is "remaining" (*satiśiṣṭa*) does not sublate the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka*.

And likewise, in accordance with that [principle], when the acute accent (*udātta*) would otherwise apply to the *sārvadhātuka* suffix in forms such as *kartārau*, this rule becomes meaningful by prescribing an *anudātta* (grave) accent to override it. Consequently, the result of this technical indication (*jñāpana*) is that in forms such as *dhinutaḥ*, the final acute accent is established by the accentual rule for *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes; this is the intended meaning. [Now begins] *caturaḥ śasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.167).

The inclusion of the term *halādiḥ* (beginning with a consonant) in the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.179) indicates that a *nipātana-svara* (an accent assigned by specific grammatical derivation) does not supersede a *vibhakti-svara* (the accent of a case ending). Regarding the rule *caturaḥ śasi*, there is a *vārttika* which states: "In the case of *caturaḥ śasi*, there is no prohibition [of the rule] because of the *ādyudātta-nipātana* (the specific assignment of an initial acute accent). This is its meaning: by the rule *caturaḥ śasi*, the word *catur* is prescribed to have an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) when followed by the locative plural suffix *śas*.

And likewise, in the feminine gender, in the case of *catasraḥ paśya*, the word *catasṛ* would also incur an acute accent on the final syllable by virtue of its being treated as the substitute for *catur*; therefore, a prohibition must be stated for that. It need not be stated; for the word *catasṛ* will be prescribed with an acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by nipātana.

In this regard, since the word *catuḥ* ends in the suffix *-uran*, it is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable); consequently, by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute retains the properties of the original), the word *catasṛ* which replaces it would also be established as *ādyudātta*. Nevertheless, the specific *nipātana* (irregular accentuation) of *ādyudātta* is prescribed here to override the final acute (*antodātta*) that would otherwise be required by the rule *caturaḥ śasi*. Thus, this *ādyudātta* nipātana serves as an exception to the final acute accent mandated by the rule *caturaḥ śasi*.

Regarding this, one might raise the following objection: just as the introduction of this initial udātta (acute accent) subverts the natural final udātta prescribed by the rule *caturaḥ śasi*, so too would it subvert the accent of the case-ending (*vibhakti-svara*) prescribed by the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.179). Consequently, in forms such as *catasṛbhiḥ*, the udātta accent of the case-ending would not occur. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Thus [the purpose of] the mention of *halādi*."

The inclusion of the term *halādi* (beginning with a consonant) is indeed intended so that the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the suffix *śas* does not occur in the word *catastraḥ*. However, the point is this: if the specific rule for the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttanipātana*) were to override the general rule for the accent of case-endings (*vibhaktisvara*), then the form *catastraḥ* would indicate that the acute accent on the first syllable of *catasṛ* is stronger [and thus prevails]. Nor should it be argued that the purpose of including *halādi* is to exclude those case-endings beginning with vowels (*ajādī*) that follow words designated as *ṣaṭ* (the numerals six). For the dual and singular endings do not exist for words bearing the designation *ṣaṭ*.

Since *jas* and *śas* are elided by the rule "after [stems ending in] ṣaṭ and dant, there is elision" (*ṣaḍbhyo luk*, Pāṇini 7.1.22), they are excluded [from the scope of the present rule]. Similarly, because the word *tri* also falls within the domain of the plural, the dual and singular endings do not apply to it. As for *jas*, its exclusion follows precisely from the qualification "not being a sarvanāmasthāna. Regarding *śas*, however, in the form *tri-as*, when the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of the same quality as the preceding) occurs, the resulting accentuation is desired to be acute according to the rule "an *ekādeśa* with an acute [vowel] is acute" (*ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*); thus, that too is not to be excluded. The same applies to the word *tisṛ*.

In the example *śasi paraṃ tistraḥ paśya*, the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.174) intends precisely that the word be oxytone; thus, even that [example] is not to be excluded. Only *catastraḥ paśya* is to be excluded. And since it can be resolved there by the very method previously stated, the inclusion of the term *halādi-* is redundant; being so, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned statement—this is clear in the Bhāṣya. [Now follows: *tāsyanudāttet* (Pāṇini 6.1.186).

The mention of *anudātta* and *ṅit* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the property of being *anudātta* does not apply to those [verbal bases] from which the *vikaraṇa* has been elided. [Objection: But surely, according to the view that "the *anubandhas* are non-terminating" (*anekāntā anubandhāḥ*), since the *śap* [suffix] is also taught as having an *a* vowel (*adupadeśa*), the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following it—such as in *juhutaḥ* and so on—would incur the status of being *anudātta* by the rule: "A *lasārvadhātuka* suffix is *anudātta* after a root taught with an *anudātta*, a *ṅit*, or an *at*. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The mention of *anudātta* and *ṅit*..."

In rules such as *āste* and *śete*, the term *anudātta* (unaccented) is included in the sūtra *tāsyanudāttenṅidadupadeśāt* for the purpose of establishing the unaccented nature of the *lasārvadhātuka* affixes. Both of these [provisions] would be redundant; for the unaccented nature is established simply by taking the position of the *śap* affix following an *adupadeśa* (a verbal root taught with an initial vowel). Therefore, this indicates that the *lasārvadhātuka* affix following elided *vikaraṇas* does not become unaccented. Thus, the sense is that there is no fault.

Regarding the rule *samāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.223): after stating "not before a word beginning with an unaccented vowel in a compound-final member" (*nottarapade 'nudāttādau*, 6.2.142), there is a prohibition regarding "earth, Rudra, Pūṣan, and Manthin" (*apṛthivīrudrapūṣamanthiṣu*). By virtue of this [prohibition], it is established as a *jñāpaka* (indicative mark) that the [rule] applies there even in cases where [the first member] begins with a consonant and ends with a consonant. [Objection: But surely, what is prescribed for a word beginning with an unaccented vowel or ending in a circumflex accent would not apply to a word beginning with a consonant or ending in a consonant, because properties such as being acute (*udātta*) or unaccented (*anudātta*) are attributes of vowels (*aj-dharma*), not consonants.

Furthermore, regarding the form *dādhittha* in the phrase *dādhittham*, one might raise the objection that the suffix *añ* [prescribed by] Pāṇini 4.3.140 (*anudāttādeśca*) would not apply, nor would the acute accent prescribed for the third case endings and so forth following an oxytone final member—such as in *paramavāc* and similar forms by Pāṇini 6.1.169 (*antodāttād uttarapadād anyatarasyām anityasamāse*)—be established. Anticipating this, he says: "of the compound," and so forth.

By the rule *notarapade'nudāttādāvapṛthivīrudrapūṣamanthiṣu* (Pāṇini 6.2.142), in a *devatā-dvandva* compound where the second member (*uttarapada*) begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*), the simultaneous preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) for both the first and second members—which was established by the rule *devatādvandve ca* (6.2.141)—is prohibited. Furthermore, within that context, by the phrase *apṛthivīrudra* etc., a prohibition of that very prohibition is stated when the second members are words such as *pṛthivī*.

Since the prohibition does not apply to words such as *pṛthivī* because they lack the status of being *anudātta*-initial and so forth, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not *pṛthivī*" and so on would otherwise be redundant; being thus purposeful, it indicates that what is prescribed for words beginning with *anudātta* and ending with an *udātta* applies also to those beginning with a consonant (*vyañjana*) and ending in a consonant. Therefore, the sense is that the exclusion "not *pṛthivī*" becomes meaningful, and the desired result is achieved in cases such as *dādhityam*. [Jñāpakasamuccaya 6.2.52: *anigante 'ñcatau*]

Because of the prohibition [stated] in the rule *aharaṇe* (Pāṇini 6.2.65), which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), the accent of a *kṛt*-suffix does not override the accent of the word *hārin*. [Objection: But surely, in the case of *bāḍahārya*, the initial acute accent of the word *bāḍa* would be obtained by the rule *saptamīhāriṇau dharmye'haraṇe* (Pāṇini 6.2.65), which means that a word ending in the locative case and a word denoting one who carries (*hārin*) are both acutely accented on their first syllable when followed by a word expressing a duty (*dharmya*). Thus, the initial acute accent of *bāḍa* would apply here.

Likewise, by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the accentuation of the final syllable (*antasvaritatva*) would apply due to the accent of a *kṛt*-suffix (specifically the *ṇyat* suffix). In that case, because it is subsequent in the order of rules, the *kṛt*-accent would prevail, overriding the *hāri*-accent. However, it is desired that the first syllable of the preceding member be acute (*pūrvapadādyudāttatva*) by means of the *hāri*-accent. To explain how this is accomplished, he says: "because of the prohibition regarding non-carrying (*aharaṇe*). The intention is as follows: *bāḍhavaḥ* is one who carries a load (*bhāra*), and *bījāśvaḥ* is a horse for seed.

That which is given after the infusion of the seed for the sake of nourishing the body is called *haraṇa* or *hārya*. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound as *bāḍava-haraṇa*, it becomes *bāḍavaharaṇa*. One who accepts what is to be given is called *hārī*. Thus, since the word *bāḍava* signifies one who takes (*hārī*), by this [rule], the initial syllable of the word would have obtained the udātta accent when followed by the word *haraṇa*, which denotes its object (*dheya*). Furthermore, by the rule "ano bhāvakarmavacanaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.2.150), the final syllable of the second member would also have obtained the udātta accent.

In this context, because [the rule] is subsequent, the accent on the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapadāntodātta*) would subvert the accent of *hāri*, resulting in the non-application of the *hāri*-accent. Therefore, the prohibition contained in the word *aharaṇe* (in the case of non-carrying) serves a specific purpose: it indicates that the *kṛt*-accent does not subvert the *hāri*-accent, but rather the *hāri*-accent itself subverts the *kṛt*-accent. Furthermore, one might object that since the *kṛt*-accent—governed by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt*—is subsequent, it would apply first; however, in the case of a second member meaning "carrying" (*haraṇa*), the rule *ano bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* applies as an exception (*apavāda*).

Immediately after that [application], it is stated: "In the case of a word ending in the seventh case, when it denotes one who takes [something] (hārin), provided there is no taking away (aharaṇe). Now, although it might be possible to understand from the phrase "provided there is no taking away" that the accent of the *hārin* does not sublate the accent of the suffix *anaḥ* (as in *ano bhāve*), one must explain how it can be made known that the accent of the whole (*kṛtsvara*) does not sublate the accent of the *hārin*.

When it is made known that the accent prescribed by *saptamī-hāriṇau* (P. 6.2.151) sublates the accent prescribed by *ano bhāva-karmaṇoḥ* (P. 6.2.150)—which itself sublates the accent prescribed by *kṛt-svara*—then, by the logic of the "how much more so" (*kaimutika-nyāya*), it is established all the more clearly that the latter [the accent of *saptamī-hāriṇau*] necessarily sublates the former. Consequently, it is indicated that, in the general domain of *kṛt*-suffixes, the accent of *hārin* sublates every accent that might otherwise apply by any subsequent rule through the application of *pūrva-vipratiṣedha* (priority of the preceding).

Thus, even though the accent of *hāri* would apply when the word *haraṇa* follows, the term *aharaṇa* was stated in order to preclude that; hence, its purpose is fulfilled within its own scope (*svāṃśe*). However, its purpose elsewhere is as follows: in the case of *bāḍavahāryam*, when the word *hārya*—which is different from the word *haraṇa*—follows, the present rule "the seventh [case-ending] and *hārin*" (*saptamīhāriṇau*) applies, thereby causing the acute accent on the first syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapadādyudāttatva*), which overrides the general accent rule for a compound ending in a primary derivative (*kṛtsvara*). [The sūtra: *antaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.143).

The word *kapi* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) becomes udātta. The rule *antaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.222) is a governing rule (*adhikārasūtra*). Having attained syntactic unity with the subsequent rule, it conveys the meaning: "the final syllable becomes udātta. In this context, when there arises the expectation of what [word's] final syllable becomes udātta, the term *samāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.223), which is also under discussion, applies; thus, the resulting meaning is: "the final syllable of the compound (*samāsa*), or rather, the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), becomes udātta."

In that regard, regarding the position that the final syllable of the *uttarapada* (the second member of a compound) is accented, [it would follow that] in the cases of *anṛcaḥ* and *bahvṛcaḥ*, the suffix *ap*—prescribed by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ pathāmānakṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.74) as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*)—would be intended to be accented. However, that would not be established. For the vowel *a* is a constituent part of the entire compound (*samāsa*), not of the *uttarapada*; thus, one might suspect that its accentuation would not apply. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The mention of *kap* [is for the sake of] the preceding [rule]. When there is an expectation as to whose end [is accented], it connects only with "of the compound" (*samāsasya*) and not with "of the *uttarapada*."

And thus, the meaning of the rule is simply that the end of a compound is acute. The indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this is the rule "kapi pūrvam" (Pāṇini 6.2.173). For the meaning of that rule is: when *kap* follows, the penultimate syllable of the final member of the compound—which itself follows the negative particle (*nañ*) or a word ending in *su*—becomes acute. For example, in *sukumārīka*, the vowel *ī* is acute.

For if it were the case that "the end of the *uttarapada* is acute," then, since the suffix *kap*—being a constituent of the compound—is not a constituent of the *uttarapada*, the vowel *ī* at the end of the *uttarapada* "kumārī" itself would become acute by the rule "nañsubhyām" (Pāṇini 6.2.172); what then would be the purpose of the rule "kapi pūrvam"?

Furthermore, this [fact that the accent is applied] indicates that the acute accent belongs to the end of the compound itself, and not to the final member (*uttarapada*) of the compound. Thus, the purpose of the rule *kapi pūrvam* (Pāṇini 6.2.173) is established, and the end-acute accent of the compound is also successfully achieved in examples such as *anṛcaḥ*. However, according to this view, in the case of *idaṃprathamakāḥ*, the end-acute accent prescribed by the rule *bahuvrīhāvidametattadbhyaḥ prathamapūraṇayoḥ kriyāgaṇane* (Pāṇini 6.2.162) would result in the application of the suffix *kap* because it is a compound-final element.

However, it is desired that [the elision] apply to the form of the word *maṣ*. That would not be established. Therefore, it must be stated that in that sūtra, only the phrase "of the subsequent member" (*uttarapadasya*) is connected, and not "of the compound" (*samāsasya*). This is clear from both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa. [In the rule] *jñāpakāraṇāmni ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.10), this very mention of the non-elision (*aluk*) indicates that a compound occurs here.

By the rule *jhrvi.ṭa ṭhakāranāmni ca prācāṃ halādau*, the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case is prescribed when the name of a place in the eastern region (*prācāṃ deśe*) begins with a consonant (*halādi*) as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) following a word ending in a consonant. Regarding this, the authors of the Vārttikas, having deliberated whether this is an option for what is already established (*prāptavibhāṣā*) or an option for what is not yet established (*aprāptavibhāṣā*), stated: "It is a prescription of compounding where [elision] was not previously established. In examples such as *mukuṭekārṣāpaṇam* ("a kārṣāpaṇa on a crown"), since elision would not have occurred by the rule *haladantāt saptamyāḥ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.9), it is stated that this is an option for what was not previously established; thus, the lack of being a technical name (*asaṃjñātva*) [is implied].

[The compound] *phalati* [is formed]. Since a compound is difficult to obtain there, the compound must also be prescribed. However, according to the view that this is an optional rule (*prāptavibhāṣā*), since the compound would already be established by the rule "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*, Pāṇini 2.1.44) as an option restricted to the domain of names, the intention of the Vārttika is that only the non-elision (*aluk*) is to be prescribed. But the author of the Bhāṣya says: "This is not a fault; this very fact makes it known that a compound occurs here, because he teaches the non-elision of the locative case when the name of a reason is expressed."

Even in the view that this is an *aprāptavibhāṣā* (an optional rule where [the application] was not otherwise established), it is understood that the compound occurs precisely by virtue of the force of prescribing the non-elision (*aluk*) despite the absence of a technical name (*asaṃjñātve*). Otherwise, since the elision (*luk*) would simply not apply, the prescription of non-elision would be purposeless; such is the intent of the *Bhāṣya*. This is what he states: "This very [prescription] of non-elision... [referring to *Pāṇini 2.4.71*]. The rule *cau* (Pāṇini 6.3.138) indicates this very point: that *ca* does not apply to every individual member (*pratyaṅga*).

Objection: In forms such as *prācā* and *dadhīcā*, after the elision of the *n* (nalopa), since the rule for lengthening (*cau*) would not apply due to the absence of a final vowel (*ajanta*) once the single-substitute replacement (*ekādeśa*) and the *yaṇ*-substitution have taken effect by virtue of their being "internal" (*antaraṅga*), how is the lengthening obtained? To this, he says: "This very [fact] indicates... The meaning is that, by the force of the rule prescribing the lengthening, whatever is "internal" (*antaraṅga*) with respect to the rule "cau" does not take effect [prior to its application].

In reality, however, this [interpretation] is questionable: because the instruction *cau* indicates that this sūtra operates after the elision of the vowel *a*, and because the single-substitute *yaṇ* and other such operations lack the suitability to operate after the elision of the vowel *a*. The word *pratyaṅ* contains the term *antaraṅga*. [Pāṇini 6.4.46] *ārdhadhātuke*: the fact that the elision of *śap* is prescribed for roots beginning with *ad-* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the elision of the vowel *a* of *śap* does not occur by this [rule].

Alternatively, the prescription of *luk* (elision) after verbal roots ending in long vowels (*ākāra*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Having raised the doubt as to what the purposes of the governing rule for *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes might be, the *Bhāṣya* states: "The elision of the final vowel after *at*, the elision of *y*, the elision of *ṇi*, the elision of the vowel after *ā* [in the case of *ātaḥ*], the substitution of *ī* [for *ai*], the substitution of *e* [for *ay*], and the treatment like *ciṇ* (*ciṇvadbhāva*) before the *sīyuṭ* augment are the purposes."

Having thus enumerated the purposes [of the rule], he then objects: "If the governing heading *ārdhadhātuka* were absent when this [suffix] *lopa* applies, then in the case of *cikīrṣati*, there would also be elision of the vowel *a* of the suffix *san*. Having raised this objection—suggesting that even if the vowel *a* of *san* were elided here, the vowel *a* of the suffix *śap* would still be heard—he then provides the resolution: "The governing heading *ārdhadhātuka* exists for the purpose of ensuring that the vowel *a* of *śap* itself is not elided. To this, [the opponent] replies: "This is not a valid purpose."

The activity of the Teacher (Pāṇini) makes it known that there is no elision of the vowel *a* of the *śap* [suffix] by this [rule], since he teaches the *luk*-elision of *śap* after roots beginning with *ad* (A 2.4.72). This is what he states: "not by this. The meaning is: not by the rule "elision of *at*" (A 6.4.48), which falls under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "ārddhadhātuka" suffixes. [Objection: But if there were elision of the vowel *a* of the *śap* in forms such as *vittaḥ* and *mṛṣṭaḥ*, then, by the principle of "characterization by the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), operations such as *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would occur.

Anticipating the objection—"How can this be a *jñāpaka* (indicative proof), since there exists another purpose, namely the prescription of the elision (*luk*) of *śap* for the sake of its cessation?"—he says: "from those ending in long *ā*" (*ākārāntebhyaḥ*). The sense is that if the elision of *śap* were simply the elision of the final *a*, then roots such as *yā* and others ending in long *ā* would be listed only in the *bhūvādi* class and not in the *adādi* class, because there is no difference between *luk* and *lopa* in that regard. Thus ends the sixth chapter.
Now begins the seventh chapter.

But surely, even in cases such as *śaṅkhaḥ* and *śaṇḍhaḥ*, the substitutions *āyan*, etc., would apply; for since suffixes such as *kha* and *ḍha* are prescribed by Uṇādi-sūtras like "from the root *śam*, [the suffix] *kha*" (*śameḥ khaḥ*, Sū.u.sū. 107), these suffixes begin with *kh*, and thus the rule "āyan, ey, īn" (*āyaneyī*) would apply. Anticipating this objection, he says: The prescription of the suffix *īyaṅ* after the root *ṛt* (in Pāṇini 3.1.29: *ṛterīyaṅ*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitutions *āyan*, etc., do not apply to suffixes following verbal roots.

The intended meaning is as follows: *ṛti* is a verbal root found in the Sūtra collection (*sautra-dhātu*) with the sense of "loathing" (*jugupsā*). From that root, the suffix *īyaṅ* is prescribed in its own right by the rule "ṛterīyaṅ" (Pāṇini 3.1.29). Thus, the form *ṛtīyate* is established. In that case, for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*), one could simply have stated "ṛteśchaṅ. Then, by applying the substitution of *īya* for the letter *ch* according to the rule "āyaneyī" (Pāṇini 7.1.2), the desired form *ṛtīya* would indeed be accomplished.

Furthermore, by abandoning the lighter analysis (*nyāsa*) and adopting the heavier one—namely, *ṛterīyaṅ*—it indicates that the substitutions such as *āyan* and so forth do not apply to those suffixes beginning with *ph* that follow a verbal root (*dhātu*). Consequently, when *chaṅ* is prescribed, the substitution of *īya* for the *ch* of the *chaṅ* following a root would not otherwise occur; thus, the prescription of *īyaṅ* is purposeful. By this, in forms such as *śaṅkha*, the rule *āyaneyī* does not apply.

In the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77), the inclusion of the term *ac* indicates that there exists some other principle here besides the *bhak-tva* (the status of being a suffix) for the application of the technical designation *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*. Regarding the rule *ṭhako 'ci vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 5.3.71), the author of the Vārttikas stated that the inclusion of the term *ac* is for the sake of subsequent rules.

In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya raises the objection: "If [the mention of *aj*] were for the sake of the subsequent rule, then he would have placed it right there; what purpose, then, could be stated for its being placed here? Having raised this doubt, he states that the purpose is to prevent the application of *num* in the case of *trapu* and *japu*. He then explains that because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the condition "when followed by an inflectional ending" (*vibhaktau*), the *num* occurs only when an inflectional ending follows. Since the inflectional ending is elided by *luk* in the case of *trapu* and *jatu*, the *num* will not occur simply because the condition of being followed by an inflectional ending is absent; thus, the inclusion of the term *aj* is redundant.

One should not suspect that the status of being followed by an inflection (*vibhaktiparatva*) applies here by virtue of the definition of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Anticipating this objection—that such a suspicion is barred by the prohibition "na lumatāṅgasya"—[the author] states: "In that case, since [the desired result] is already established, the fact that he employs the mention of 'a vowel' (*ajgrahaṇa*) indicates that there exists here another method known as *pratyayalakṣaṇa*. Thus, because [the word] *trapu* and others would otherwise incur the augment *num* due to the status of being followed by an inflection according to the definition of a suffix, the mention of 'a vowel' is made to prevent that."

Thus, the purpose of this indication is that even when the *l* is elided from the vocative case ending in *he trapo*, the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by the rule *hrasvasya guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.108) is established because the condition of being followed by a vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) still applies by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle; so he has stated. He says this with the words: "The mention of *ac* [in the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ*]... Furthermore, the prohibition in the rule *na tisṛcatasṛ* (Pāṇini 6.4.4) indicates that the substitute *rā* does not supersede the augment *nuṭ*.

Regarding the rule *jhrvi.ṭa ṭhastriyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 7.1.96), there is the Vārttika: "The augment *nuṭ* [is applied] by prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) over *num*, *acir*, and *tṛjvadbhāva*. An example of *acir* is *tisṛṇām* and *catasṛṇām*. In both cases—*tisṛ* + *ām* and *catasṛ* + *ām*—the substitution of *r* for the *ṛ* by the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ* (7.2.100) and the introduction of the augment *nuṭ* by the rule *hrasvanadyāpaḥ* (7.1.54) would both apply. However, since the substitution of *r* is taught later in the sequence, it takes precedence; once that substitution has been made, the augment *nuṭ* no longer applies.

Therefore, the intention of the *vārttika* is that, by means of the "prior prohibition" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the substitution of *r* (*rādeśa`) is set aside and the augment *nuṭ* is applied. Immediately following that is another *vārttika*: "Or rather, not so, because there is no prohibition of the substitution of *r* in the domain of *nuṭ*. Its intention is that one must state that the substitution of *r* does not occur in the domain of *nuṭ*; otherwise, just as the substitution of *r* would override the rules for *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and *pūrvasavarṇa*, it would also override the application of *nuṭ*.

Refuting these two *vārttikas*, the author of the *Bhāṣya* demonstrated that since the rule "na tisṛcatasṛ" prohibits the lengthening of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* when followed by a *nām* suffix, the substitution of *r* does not apply in the domain of *nuṭ*; thus, a prohibition of *r* in the domain of *nuṭ* need not be stated, and even the supplementary mention (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of *nuṭ* by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) is unnecessary. Bearing this in mind, he says: "The prohibition 'na tisṛcatasṛ' [is sufficient]."

Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.17: *vibhāṣā bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ*. The separation of this rule (*yogavibhāga*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that when there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) for a particular condition, there is a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) for that same condition. [Objection: But surely two rules—"*āditaśca*" and "*vibhāṣā bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ*"—are recited in the Aṣṭādhyāyī. Among them, regarding the first rule, [it concerns] the niṣṭhā suffixes following a root beginning with the vowel *ā*.

The meaning is that *iṭ* should not occur. *Prasvinnaḥ* is the illustrative example. The meaning of the second rule is that *iṭ* may optionally (*vā*) occur after a root beginning with a vowel when used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) or in the sense of the commencement of an action (*ādikarmaṇi*). In that case, let there be no two rules; instead, let there be only a single rule: *ādito vibhāṣā bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ*. The meaning of this rule is that *iṭ* is optional after a root beginning with a vowel when used in the sense of an abstract action or in the sense of the commencement of an action.

If it is asked how the prohibition of *iṭ* in the active voice (*kartari*) is obtained, it is obtained by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 7.2.15). The meaning of that rule is: for that [root] for which an optional *iṭ* is prescribed anywhere, there shall be no *iṭ* in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). Consequently, since an optional *iṭ* has been stated at the outset for the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the reflexive-passive (*ādikarman*), the prohibition of *iṭ* in the past passive participle in the active voice is established by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā."

Thus, having raised the objection as to why there is a division of rules (*yogavibhāga*)—whereby the first rule is explained as being for the purpose of prohibiting *iṇ*, and the second as being for the purpose of prescribing *veṭ*—[the author] replies: "For this very reason, although [the desired result] is established by a single rule, the making of a division of rules indicates the following principle: 'Where there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) with respect to a particular condition (*upādhi*), there is a prohibition with respect to that same condition. That is to say, a prohibition must apply to exactly the same thing characterized by the same qualifiers for which an option was prescribed."

Furthermore, because an option (*vikalpa*) is prescribed there for the two conditions of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*), the prohibition of the augment *iṭ*—by the rule "for that [root] which has an option regarding the *niṣṭhā* in the sense of the agent"—would not apply. Since neither the option nor the prohibition would be possible for the abstract state or the beginning of an action, the prohibition would not occur. Consequently, the sūtra would become redundant. Therefore, the division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) was made in order to prohibit the augment *iṭ* for the *niṣṭhā* in both the agent and the object, and to prescribe the augment *iṭ* optionally for the abstract state and the beginning of an action.

The purpose of making known that [the suffix] is due to an upapada is as follows: from the verbal root *vid* in the sense of "knowing," the rule *vibhāṣā gamahanavidaviśām* (Pāṇini 7.2.68) prescribes the optional application of the augment *iṭ* to the suffix *vas*. Consequently, one forms both *viditvān* and *vidvān*. However, regarding the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) *vidita*, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15) would have applied. That prohibition is, however, set aside by the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*).

It has been determined in the Bhāṣya and other works that only the root *vidlṛ* in the sense of "obtaining" (*lābhe*) is intended here; since the augment *iṭ* is prescribed for this root optionally, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā" applies only to it and not to the root meaning "to know. Thus, the form *vidita* belonging to the root meaning "to know" is established. With this intention in mind, he says: "by means of a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*)."

And in this regard, Kaiyaṭa’s commentary should also be consulted: "Even though there is co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) with the root *han* for the root *vid*, nevertheless, due to the subsequent rule [of Pāṇini] regarding words (*śabdapara-vipratiṣedha*), the distinction is established such that [the prohibition applies] to *vid*, not to *han*. Regarding the rule *svaratisūti* (Pāṇ. 7.2.44): because of the inclusion of the root *svṛ* in the rule *sanīvantardha* (Pāṇ. 7.2.49), it is known by implication (*jñāpaka*) that this option does not apply within the scope of the prohibition characterized by the suffix *u*.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of *svṛtvā*, there would arise the contingency of optional *iṭ* by the rule *svaratisūtisūyatidhūñūdito vā*.
