Nor should it be argued that there is no possibility of *iṭ* because of the prohibition of *iṭ* after a root ending in a consonant followed by *u* (*ugantāt*) before a *kit* suffix, according to the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11). For, just as the rule *svarati...* acts as an exception (*bādhaka*) to the prohibition of *iṭ* characterized by a single vowel (*ekājlakṣaṇa*)—according to the maxim *yenanāprāptinyāya*—it likewise acts as an exception to the rule *śryukaḥ kiti*; thus, the contingency of *iṭ* is unavoidable. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the case of *sanīvantardha...*" etc.

The intention is as follows: by the rule "sanīvantardhabhrasjadambhuśrisvṛyūrṇubharajñapisanām" (Pāṇini 7.2.49), it is stated that the augment *iṭ* optionally occurs after the suffix *san* when following roots ending in *iv*, as well as the roots beginning with *ṛdh*. The root *svṛ* is also specified therein. Its examples are *susvūrṣati* and *sisvariṣati*.

In this regard, since the optional application of *iṭ* is already established by the rule *svaratisūti* itself, the inclusion of *svṛ* in that rule would otherwise be redundant; being thus purposeful, it indicates that the prohibition characterized by the term *ug* (from the rule *śryukaḥ kiti*) does not apply to the scope of the optional prohibition [stated in] *svaratisūtīti*. Consequently, when the prohibition from the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* would otherwise apply, the inclusion of *svṛ* in the rule *sanīvantardha* is for the purpose of overriding that [prohibition].

And thus, because the optional application of *iṭ* does not occur in this case, there is no possibility of *iṭ* due to the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti*. [Jñāpakasamuddeśa, pāda 8] Regarding the rule *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.117), the inclusion of the word *puṣkarasat* in the *anuśatikādi* group indicates that when the initial vowel (*ādi*) undergoes *vṛddhi*, the *vṛddhi* characterized by the final or penultimate vowel (*antyopadhā*) does not take place.

Objection: In the case of *krauṣṭraḥ* and *jāgataḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the words *kroṣṭṛ* and *jagat* respectively by the rule *tasyedam*, and the vowel-vṛddhi is applied by the rule *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ*. In that situation, since the *ṛ*-vowel is the final sound, the vṛddhi [of the preceding vowel] would apply by the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115). Is this not so?

The rule for *vṛddhi* of the first vowel (*acāmādivṛddhi*) sublates both the *vṛddhi* conditioned by the final letter and the *vṛddhi* conditioned by the penultimate letter (*upadhā*). Therefore, it must be stated that in the words *tath-* [and *tad-*], only the *vṛddhi* of the first vowel occurs. For sublation is to be asserted on the basis of the principle of "that which does not apply otherwise" (*yenanāprāptinyāya*), since [the former] is an exception (*apavāda*). However, this is not the case here. One might object: even where the *vṛddhi* conditioned by the final letter or the penultimate letter is incapable of occurring, there too—such as in *sauśrutaḥ* and similar forms—the sublation is impossible because the *vṛddhi* of the first vowel still finds scope (*sāvakāśatvena*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the *anuśatikādi* group."

The meaning is as follows: in the sense of "the offspring of Puṣkarasat," when the suffix *iñ* is applied to the word *puṣkarasat* by the rule "bāhv-ādibhyaś-ca" (Pāṇini 4.1.96), and the initial *vṛddhi* has been obtained, the word *puṣkarasat* is listed among the *anuśatikādi* group for the sake of *vṛddhi* in both members of the compound. If, even in the case of the *vṛddhi* of the initial vowels (*acāmādi*), there were also *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), then—by the *vṛddhi* of the initial vowel *u* and by the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel *a* of the *sakāra*—the form *pauṣkarasādiḥ* would be established through the *vṛddhi* of both members.

If it were for that purpose, its inclusion in the *anuśatikādi* group would be redundant; yet since it is included there, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned rule. Although the inclusion of the word *puṣkarasāc*—which is otherwise eligible for penultimate vowel strengthening (*upadhāvṛddhi*)—is sufficient to indicate the absence of such strengthening, one should nevertheless understand that, either by way of partial acceptance (*ekadeśānumati*) or by virtue of being an indicator with general scope, it is established that even the strengthening prescribed for the final syllable does not occur.

The prohibition [of *guṇa*] regarding *ciṇ* and *ṇal* in the rule *jāgro 'viciṇṇalṅitsu* (Pāṇini 7.3.85) makes known that *vṛddhi* does not occur for that which has already undergone *guṇa*. [Objection: But surely, when the root *jāgṛ* is followed by the causative suffix *ṇic* and the suffix *laṭ*, as in *jāgarayati*, we have the sequence *jāgṛ-i-ati*. At this stage, since the *ṛ*-vowel undergoes *guṇa* by the rule *jāgro 'viciṇṇalṅitsu* and is subsequently replaced by *ra* (*rapara*), we have *jāgar-i-ati*. Then, by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116), *vṛddhi* would appear to apply. Anticipating this objection, he says: "regarding *ciṇ* and *ṇal*."

In the very sūtra *jāgro 'viciṇṇalṅitsu*, the *guṇa* substitution is prohibited when *ciṇ* or *ṇal* follows. The result of this is that in both cases—*ajāgāri* and *jajāgāra*—the desired forms are established through the application of *vṛddhi* preceded by the non-application of *guṇa*. Even if *guṇa* were applied, at the stage *ajāgar-i* and *jajāgar-a*, the desired forms would still be established by the *vṛddhi* rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*; so what is the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* in those two cases?

Furthermore, the prohibition [of *guṇa*] serves to indicate that the vowel *a* produced by the term *guṇa* does not undergo the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*. Thus, when *guṇa* would apply to *jāgr-* in the case of the suffixes *ciṇ* and *ṇal*, the resulting *a* would not be subject to *vṛddhi*; therefore, the prohibition of *guṇa* for those two suffixes is established. Consequently, in the absence of *guṇa*, the forms *ajāgāri* and *jajāgāra* are derived through the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule *aco ñṇiti*; thus, the prohibition finds its purpose within its own scope.

The purpose of this indication (*jñāpana-prayojana*), however, is that in forms such as *jāgarayati*, the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116) does not apply; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.96): the fact that the suffixes *knū* and *san* are marked with the *kit* designation serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that for roots of this class, the *guṇa* substitution does not take place. [Objection: But then, in the case of the root *bhid* in the forms *bhettṛ* (agentive suffix *tṛc*) and *bhettum* (infinitive suffix *tumun*), the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca* would not be established.

In the forms *bhid-tṛ* and *bhid-tum*, there arises the concern that since the consonants at the end of the root and the beginning of the suffix are immediately adjacent, they form a *saṃyoga* (conjunction). Consequently, by the rule *saṃyoge guru* (Pāṇini 1.4.11), the vowel *i* would receive the designation *guru* (heavy), thereby subverting its *laghu* (light) designation. Because the penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel *i* would thus lack lightness, [the rule for shortening] would not apply. Anticipating this objection, he says: *knusanoh*. In the rule *trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.140), the marker *k* attached to the suffix *knu* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* substitution of the penultimate vowel in forms such as *gṛdhnuḥ*.

In that case as well, since the consonants at the end of a verbal root and the beginning of a suffix are designated as a "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), the designation "heavy" (*guru*) applies to the vowel *ṛ* by the rule "a syllable with a conjunction is heavy. Consequently, because the designation "light" (*laghu*) is sublated, the vowel lacks lightness; thus, since the condition for *guṇa* substitution is absent, the employment of the *kit* marker—which would otherwise serve to prohibit *guṇa*—is rendered purposeless.

Thus, the prescription of *kittva* for the suffix *san* beginning with a *jhal* consonant following a *hal* consonant immediately preceded by an *ic*-vowel—by the rule *halantācca* (Pāṇini 1.2.10)—as in the case of *bhibhitsati* and similar forms, would be rendered useless, as its purpose is to prohibit *guṇa*. This is because, when the *saṃyoga* designation applies to the final *a* of the root and the initial *s* of the suffix, the preceding *i* becomes heavy (*guru*) due to that cluster; and since it lacks lightness (*laghu*), *guṇa* simply does not apply.

And thus, the fact that the *kit* designation for the suffixes *knusa* and *nu* is otherwise redundant serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that for words of this class—where the status of being "heavy" (*guru*) is obtained by taking as the cause the designation of "consonant cluster" (*saṃyoga*) for the final consonant of the root and the initial consonant of the suffix—the vowel *i* undergoes *guṇa*. In this way, the *kit* designation becomes meaningful as it serves to prohibit that *guṇa* which would otherwise apply. The purpose of this indication is the establishment of *guṇa* in forms such as *bhettā* and *bhettum*. This is the intended meaning.

Because of the separate mention of *āp* in the rule *jhrjñā.pa.ṭa ṭhaṅerāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.116), the term *āp* does not receive the designation *nadī*. Furthermore, by the rule *jhrvi.ṭa ṭhayū strayākhyau nadī* (Pāṇini 1.4.3), the designation *nadī* is prescribed for those stems ending in *ī* or *ū* that are always feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*).

In this context, if the term *yū* were not stated, then even words like *khaṭvā* and *mālā*, which are invariably feminine and end in the suffix *ṭāp*, would receive the designation *nadī*. Consequently, in forms such as *khaṭvābandhuḥ* and *mālābandhuḥ*, the rule *nadī bandhuni* (Pāṇini 6.2.109) would incorrectly result in an udātta accent on the final syllable of the first member (*pūrvapada*). However, since *khaṭvā* is derived from the root *khaṭ* with the Uṇādi suffix *kvun*, it lacks the status of ending in *ī* or *ū*; thus, the *nadī* designation does not apply, and the aforementioned fault is avoided. Therefore, the purpose of stating *yū* must be explained.

However, that purpose is untenable, because the designation *nadī* for a word ending in *āP* can be prevented by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). To explain: if a word ending in *āP* were also to receive the designation *nadī*, then in the rule *ṅerāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ*, since the inclusion of words ending in *āP* would already be established by the term *nadī* alone, the separate mention of *āP* would be redundant. Yet, that [separate mention] has been made; thus, it indicates that a word ending in *āP* does not receive the designation *nadī*. This is what he expresses with the words: "thus, separately."

And thus, since the purpose of [the rule] *āpaḥ*—which is to exclude the designation *nadī* for [stems ending in] *āp*—does not apply to *thū*, it must be stated that its result in forms such as *mātre* and *mātuḥ* is precisely the exclusion of the *nadī* designation for the stem ending in *ṛ*. For if that [stem *mātṛ*] were a *nadī*, then by the rule *āṇ nadyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.112), the augment *āṭ* would be applied to the following *ṅit* case-ending; this is established in the Bhāṣya. In the rule *ṛtaśca* (Pāṇini 7.3.110), the use of the long vowel marker *t* (*tapara*) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this [word *ṛtaḥ*] is a qualifier of the *aṅga* (stem).

Now, regarding the rule *ṛtaśca* (Pāṇini 7.4.92), is the term *ṛtaḥ* a qualifier of the *aṅga* (the verbal base) or a qualifier of the *abhyāsa* (the reduplicated syllable)? In the view that it is a qualifier of the *abhyāsa*, the meaning of the rule is that when there is *yaṅluk*, the augment *ruk*, *rik*, or *rīk* should be applied to the reduplicated syllable of a root ending in *ṛ*. In the view that it is a qualifier of the *aṅga*, the meaning of the rule is that the aforementioned augments should be applied to the reduplicated syllable of a root ending in the vowel *ṛ*.

Anticipating the question, "Which of these two positions is logical here?", he states that it is an adjective qualifying the *aṅga* (the base): "an adjective qualifying the *aṅga*. In this sūtra, were it not for the presence of the long vowel *ṝ* (taparakāraṇa), then in the case of the root *kṝ* ("to scatter") with *yaṅ*-luṅ, as in *cākartī*, the augment *rug* and others would undesirably apply to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

When *kṝ* is in the state of *yaṅ-luk* (elision of the *yaṅ* suffix), the rule for reduplication (*dhātoḥ dvitvam*) applies, resulting in *kṝ-kṝ-ti*. When the shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-hrasva*) occurs, the *ṛ* of the reduplicated syllable is replaced by *a* according to the rule *uraṛ*, yielding *kar-kṝ-ti*. After the application of *halādi-śeṣa* and *cutva* (the substitution of *c*), the reduplicated syllable becomes long according to *dīrgho 'kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.83), resulting in *cākṝti*. Then, by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*, the *ṛ* is replaced by its *guṇa* vowel, and the form *cākartī* is established. In this context, if the *ṛ* were intended as a qualifier of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-viśeṣaṇatva-pakṣe*), the inclusion of the *ta*-par (*taparakaraṇa*) would be redundant.

Indeed, the result of that [specification] is the exclusion of the long vowel in the state of *abhyāsa*. For a long vowel cannot occur in the state of *abhyāsa*, because the rule "hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.70) would otherwise apply a short vowel. Thus, the purpose of the marker *t* (in *tapara*) indicates that this [specification] is a qualifier of the *aṅga*.

Furthermore, in the absence of the *tapara* (the long vowel marker) there, since the base (*aṅga*) *kṛ* could potentially end in a long vowel even when the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is short—resulting in forms such as *carkarti*, *carikarti*, and *carīkarti* for the root *kṛ* once the *rug* and other augmentations are applied—the form *cākartī* would be what is desired. Therefore, the *tapara* is employed. The point is that once it is employed, because the base *kṛ* cannot possibly end in a short *ṛ*-vowel, the application of the *rug* and other augments to its reduplicated portion does not occur.

Pāṇini 7.4.93 (*sanvallaghuni*) states that [the rules] apply as if they were *san*-affixes when a light vowel follows. The prescription in 7.4.95 (*atsmṛdṛtvarapra*... to block the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* indicates that the substitution of *i* occurs even for vowels separated by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*). Objection: But according to the rule 7.4.93 (*sanvallaghuni caṅpare 'ṇaglope*), it is stated that when a *ṇi*-stem is followed by *caṅ*, the reduplication undergoes the same treatment as a *san*-affix provided that a light vowel follows the *ṇi*. If this is the case, then in the form *acikṣaṇat*, the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated vowel would not be applicable.

Regarding the form *acakṣaṇiat* derived from the root *kṣaṇa-dhātu* through the addition of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the aorist marker (*laṅ*), the augment (*aṭ*), the reduplication (*caṅ*), the application of *halādiśeṣa*, and the substitution of *c* for *kṣ*, one might raise the following doubt: since the letter *k* (which is part of the technical term *saṃyoga*) intervenes between the short vowel *a* in *kṣa* and the reduplicated syllable, the condition of being "followed by a light [vowel]" does not apply to the reduplication. Anticipating this objection, he says: "for the purpose of overriding the substitution of *it*," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: By the rule *atsmṛdṛtvarapramradastṝspaśām* (Pāṇini 7.4.95), the substitution of *a* for the final vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is prescribed for the roots *smṛ*, *dṛ*, *tvar*, *pramrad*, *stṝ*, and *spaś*, when followed by a *ṇi*-affix that is itself followed by *caṅ*. Examples include *asasmarat* and so forth. [This applies] by the rule *sanvallaghuni*.

By means of this sūtra, the substitution of *a* is prescribed to override the shortening (*itva*) that would otherwise apply through the extension of the *san*-treatment (*sanvadbhāva*). In that case, because the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is separated by the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) consisting of the letters *s* and *m*, the reduplicated syllable lacks the status of being followed by a light vowel (*laghu*) with *caṅ* or *ṇi* following it; consequently, since there is no application of the *san*-treatment due to the absence of such conditions, the shortening (*itva*) does not arise. Thus, the prescription of the substitution of *a*—being otherwise redundant as a means to override that [non-arising] shortening—indicates that shortening (*itva*) occurs even for those [syllables] separated by a conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Therefore, the meaning is that in forms such as *acikṣaṇat*, the shortening (*itva*) is easily obtained. Thus ends the seventh chapter. Now begins the eighth chapter.

Regarding the rule *padasya* (Pāṇini 8.1.16): the inclusion of the word *anta* ("end") in the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (8.2.7) indicates that this genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is a qualifying genitive (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*), not a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). [Objection: But surely the governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*) *padasya* applies to all subsequent rules. Thus, there arises a doubt as to whether the term *padasya* in those rules is a genitive of location or a qualifying genitive; to address this, he says: "In the rule *nalopaḥ*... and so forth.

In the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* ("there is elision of the *n* at the end of a nominal stem"), the term *pada* is also governed. If that [genitive case] were a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), then the mention of *anta* (end) would be redundant. For if that were the case, *prātipadikasya* would be a qualifier of *padasya*. The meaning of the rule would then be: "there is elision of the *n* of a word that is a nominal stem and ends in *n*. In that situation, by the maxim *alo 'ntyaparibhāṣā* ("the substitute replaces the final letter among those [letters] which are qualified by the genitive"), the elision of the *n* at the end of the word would occur anyway; so what is the purpose of mentioning *anta*?

The fact that the word *kṛtam* is used here indicates that this is a genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Consequently, the meaning of the rule is: "there is elision of the *n* which is a constituent part of that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which itself is a constituent part of the word. Since there is no genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) in this context, the paribhāṣā "the [operation applies] to the final [element]" (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*) does not apply; thus, without the mention of the word *anta*, the elision of the final *n* would not be obtained. Therefore, the inclusion of the word *anta* is made for the purpose of ensuring the elision of the final *n*, thereby fulfilling its own specific function.

The purpose of indicating that this is a genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*) elsewhere, however, is as follows: in the rule *udāttasvaritayor yaṇaḥ svarito 'nudāttasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.4), because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the word *padasya*, if that were a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), the meaning of the sūtra would be: "When there is a *yaṇ* substitute for an acute or circumflex vowel, the circumflex accent occurs on the final letter of that *pada* which has an unaccented vowel immediately following it. [To avoid this unintended meaning, the genitive is taken as one of qualification.]

Consequently, that rule would apply only in the case of *kumāryau* and not in the case of *kumāryaḥ*. To explain: when *kumārī au* is present, although the svarita-ness of the final *au* of the word *kumāryau*—which follows the *yaṇ* substituted for the acute *ī* and is itself the grave (*anudātta*) vowel *au*—is established; nevertheless, in the case of *kumārī jas*, there is a grave vowel *j-as* (the *a* of *jas*) following the *yaṇ* substituted for the acute *ī*.

Since there is no absence of the manifestation [of the vowel] here due to the absence of attainment of its own accent (*iṣvaraprāpti*), the condition of being "at the end of a word" (*tadantatva*) does not apply to the *jas* suffix because it ends in *s*. Consequently, the circumflex (*svarita*) accent for the vowel *a* in *kumāryaḥ* would not be established. However, if the term "of the word" (*padasya*) is taken as a genitive of specification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*), the meaning of the sentence becomes: "The circumflex accent applies to that non-accented (*anudātta*) sound which follows a *ṇakāra* (the *n* of *j-as*) that occupies the place of an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) vowel and is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the word."

And in that case, since the low-pitched (*anudātta*) vowel *a*, which is a constituent of the element *jas*, possesses the status of being a constituent of a word (*pada*), its circumflex (*svarita*) nature is established. In this same way, the purpose [of the rule] should also be understood in the rule "A single substitute for an acute and a non-acute is acute" (Pāṇini 8.2.5). Regarding the rule "Everything except at the beginning of a verse-quarter is unaccented" (Pāṇini 8.1.18), because of the prohibition "Not so for the periphrastic future (*luṭ*)" (Pāṇini 8.1.29), there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that even the particle *anu* becomes unaccented.

Because of the prohibition of the *lṛṭ* [future] by the rule *gatyarthaloṭā* (Pāṇini 8.1.51), there is a *jñāpaka* (indicative mark) that even a non-final [verb] becomes unaccented (*anudātta*). The governing rule (*adhikārasūtra*) is: *viṭaṣṭhanudāttaṃ sarvamāpādādau*. In this context, if the term *sarva* ("all") were not employed, then because this rule would also apply to the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (8.1.28), the unaccented status prescribed for a *tiṅ*-ending word following a non-*tiṅ*-ending word would—by the principle *ādeḥ parasya*—"apply only to the first [syllable]."

[If the word *sarva* were not used,] it would not apply to that which is divided at the beginning [of the sentence]. However, it is desired that every constituent part (*avayava*) of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) be unaccented (*anudātta*). Therefore, one must state that the purpose of employing the term *sarva* is for this reason. Furthermore, he states that this purpose is also established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), namely: *na luṭ*. For by the rule *na luṭ*, it is stated that a finite verb ending in *luṭ* (the periphrastic future) following a non-finite verb (*atiṅanta*) is not subject to suppression (i.e., remains accented). And it must be stated that the suppression of the *luṭ* ending is obtained by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*.

If that sūtra were to prescribe the anudātta (unaccented) nature of the very first syllable, then the prohibition of nighāta (elision of accent) for the end of a *luṅ* form would be redundant, because there is no *luṅ* form that is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable). In a *luṅ* form, since the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following the root *tās-* is anudātta, the *tās-* itself becomes udātta. Consequently, in forms such as *kartā* where the *ṭi*-portion is elided, the word is antodātta (accented on the final syllable) by the rule of *udāttanivṛtti-svara*; in forms such as *kartārau*, it is madhyodātta (accented on the middle syllable).

However, there exists no *luṭ* ending which is initially acute (*ādyudātta*) such that its [inherent] *anudātta* status—already applicable by rule—would need to be prohibited. Therefore, the prohibition "not in the case of *luṭ*" (*na luṭ*), being otherwise purposeless, indicates that in the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*, the principle *ādeḥ parasya* ("of what follows, it is the first element") does not apply. And thus:

The meaning is that even for a constituent part of a word (*padāvayava*) that is beginningless (*anādi*), the state of being unaccented (*anudāttatva*) occurs. Consequently, in cases such as *kartā* and *kartārau*, although the unaccented status would apply to both the final and the middle syllables, the rule *na luṭ* (Pāṇini 8.1.29) serves to prohibit that; thus, the inclusion of the word *sarvasya* (in the rule *sarvasya supi* 6.1.191) is unnecessary. Now, one might object: "Even if *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54) does not apply here, by the maxim *alontyaparibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.52), the accent would still fall on the very last syllable alone. Therefore, let the word *sarva* be included to prevent that. To this, he replies: *gatyarthaloṭā*. (This refers to the fact that the prohibition applies to all parts of the word, thereby ensuring the desired result.)

By the rule *gatyarthaloṭā* (Pāṇini 8.1.51), the prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) for that which ends in a *luṅ* (aorist) suffix is enjoined. Since every form ending in a *luṅ* suffix is *madhyodātta* (accented on the middle syllable) due to the general rule that *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are *anudātta*, there is no possibility for *nighāta* to apply in the first place; thus, the prohibition would be purposeless. This purposelessness indicates that the rule *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52)—which prescribes that an operation applies to the final letter—does not operate here. Consequently, since by implication the entire word is understood to be *anudātta*, the sense is that the explicit mention of *sarvam* (the whole) in the rule should have been omitted.

In reality, because the form *bhokṣye*—ending in the suffix *lṛṭ* and having its final syllable udātta—is present, the rule *gatyarthaloṭā* (Pāṇini 8.1.51) finds its application in prohibiting the *anigata* (anudātta) status of that [final syllable] when the rule *alo 'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52) would otherwise apply. Since this [rule *gatyarthaloṭā*] thus serves a specific purpose, it cannot be considered an indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of a general principle]. Therefore, it is clear from the Bhāṣya that the inclusion of the word *sarva* (in the rule *sarvasya dve*) is necessary. Regarding the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.7): the mention of *ahan* (in the rule *ahannarurātra...*), or the addition of *rūpa*, *rātri*, and *sthāntara* as exceptions, serves as an indicator that the elision of *n* does not occur for a non-final [syllable], just as in the case of the suffix *ru*.

One might raise the objection that the elision of *n* prescribed by the rule *ṭan-lopah prātipadika-antasya* would apply even in the form *ahobhyām*. Anticipating this, the author of the Vārttika stated: "There is a prohibition of the elision of *n* after [the suffixes] *aṭ*, *ḍat*, *ḍha*, *ṭa*, and *ḍa*. Now, it may be argued that such a prohibition need not be stated. For in the case of *ahanbhyām*, since the substitution of *ru* (which results in *aho*) takes effect, superseding the elision of *n*, the elision of *n* does not occur there anyway. Nor should it be said that the elision of *n* would still apply because the substitution of *ru* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) when the elision of *n* is to be performed.

Because the *ru* [substitution] would subvert the elision of the *n*, if the *ru* were considered *asiddha* with respect to the elision of the *n*, then the prescription of *ru* would be purposeless. This is because at the time the *ru* is to take effect in the word *ahan*, the elision of the *n* would also be applicable; thus, there would be no word *ahan* that is not already subject to the elision of the *n*. Nor should it be argued that once the *n* is elided in the word *ahan*, the *ru* may be prescribed for the vowel *ā* following the *h*; for in that case, the *ru*—possessing an infinite scope (*anantya-rūpa-avakāśa*)—would not be a subverter of the elision of the *n*.

If the rule *ahan* intended to prescribe the substitution of *r* for a non-final *n*, then, for the sake of brevity, it would have simply stated *aha*. By not doing so, and instead providing the instruction in its form accompanied by the letter *n* (*ahan*), the author indicates that the substitution of *r* is not prescribed for a non-final [nasal] by this rule *ahan*. Consequently, by that rule, the substitution of *r* must be prescribed specifically for the final *n*.

The author of the Bhāṣya demonstrated that the Vārttika—"there is a prohibition of the elision of *n* after *aṅhat*, *aṭṭhat*, *aḍhat*, and *anaḥ*"—is unnecessary; for the elision [of *n*] by the rule "the *n* at the end of a nominal stem (*pratipadika*) is elided" is superseded by the unconditioned (*anavakāśa*) substitution of *ru*. He states this with the words: "the mention of *ahan*. [Objection: But surely the mention of *ahan* is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*), because the sūtra serves a purpose by prescribing the substitution of *ru* in cases such as "he dīrghāho atra" (O long-lived one, here).

For in that case, the elision of *n* is prohibited by the rule "na ṅisaṃbuddhyoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.8). Thus, since there is no scope for the substitution of *ru* to be considered "without scope" (niravakāśa)—as it shares scope with the application of *nalopa*—it cannot sublate the *nalopa*. Consequently, when *nalopa* is to be applied, because the substitution of *ru* is "not established" (*asiddha*) by the principle "pūrvatrāsiddham," the elision of *n* would apply in forms such as *ahobhyām*. Anticipating this objection, he states—with dissatisfaction—the alternative: "Or rather, an addition should be made for *rūpa*, *ratni*, and *rathantara*."

The meaning is as follows: the substitution of *ru* for the word *ahan* is prescribed after [the words] *rūpa*, *rātri*, and *rathantara*. Even in that case, if the substitution of *ru* were to apply to the non-final vowel *a* once the *n* had been elided (*nalopa*), then the rule would have prescribed the letter *r* itself rather than *ru*. Therefore, it is the substitution of *u* for the subsequent *r* that is prescribed by the rule *ato roraplutāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.113).

However, if *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) were applied to the letter *a*, then because that *a* would follow the *h* in the word *ah*, it would not be preceded by a vowel; consequently, *utva* (the substitution of *u*) would not apply. Thus, instead of prescribing *rutva* as the result of *utva*, one should have prescribed the substitution of *repha* (*r*) itself. Since he has prescribed *rutva*, he thereby indicates that *rutva* does not occur for a non-final letter. Consequently, when *rutva* is applied to the final *n* alone, the elision (*lopa*) also applies to that same *n*. Because *rutva*—having no other scope—is more powerful, it sublates the elision of *n*, thereby establishing forms such as *ahorūpam*. In this way, the rule achieves its purpose within its own domain.

The purpose of this indication (*jñāpana*) is that in forms such as *ahobhyām*, there is no elision of the *n* (*nalopa*), but rather the substitution of *ru* (*rutva*) occurs. Furthermore, the rule *āsandīvat* (Pāṇini 7.2.11) and *īvatyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.221) indicate that the suffix *vat* applies in words such as *ahīvat*. Now, an objection: [text fragment]... *nanu* (but surely).

Regarding the rule *saṃjñāyām* "āsandīvad-aṣṭhīvac-cakrīvat-kakṣīvad-drumaṇvad-carmaṇvatī": are these two [rules] part of a single sūtra or distinct sūtras? If they constitute a single sūtra, then for words not listed here—such as *ahīvatī*, *kapīvatī*, and so on—the substitution of *v* for *m* would not apply, because they are not *saṃjñās*. If they are distinct sūtras, it must be stated that by the first sūtra the substitution of *v* for the *m* of the suffix *mat* is effected, and by the second sūtra the forms beginning with *āsandīvat* are established as *nipātas*.

If that were the case, then in examples such as *ikṣumatī* and *drumatī*, the substitution of *vat* would also apply by the first rule because they are technical names (*saṃjñā*). Anticipating this objection, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "Let it be as you wish. In that regard, one might ask: if there is only a single rule, how is the application of *vat* established in cases such as *ahīvatī*? To address this, he says: "of *īvatī*" and so forth. By the rule "*īvatyāḥ*," an udātta accent on the final syllable is prescribed for a word ending in *īvatī*. Examples are *ahīvatī* and *munīvatī*.

If the substitution of *v* (vatva) did not occur in examples such as *ahīvatī*, the very form of the word *īvatī* would be difficult to obtain; consequently, the explanatory reference (*anuvāda*) *īvatyāḥ* would be inconsistent. Thus, the mention of *īvatyāḥ* indicates that the substitution of *v* indeed occurs for words of this class. If it is objected: "But for the sake of forms like *āsandīvat*, [the form] should be *īvatyāḥ*; how then can this serve as an indicator? We say: No.

Regarding this, one should consult the following passage from Kaiyaṭa’s *Pradīpa*: "Because there is no application of these [suffixes] to feminine nouns, and because they lack the word *īvatī* as their final member. Furthermore, the inclusion of the letters *ḍ*, *ḍh*, *ḍh*, *ṭh*, *ḍ*, *n*, and *ī* in Pāṇini’s sūtra 8.2.56 (*anudāttopadeśavanatitanotyādīnām anunāsikalopo jhali kṅiti*) indicates that this grammatical operation applies even when these sounds follow.

JHRVIṬA: Now, regarding the rule *nudavidondatṛtrāghrāhṛṅvṛścaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.56), is the substitution of *na* for the *niṣṭhā*-suffixal *t* following roots such as *nud* prescribed optionally, or is it prohibited optionally? In other words, is this rule (*yoga*) a positive injunction (*vidhi*) or a prohibition (*niṣedha*)? If the position is that it is a positive injunction, then the word *naḥ* must be explicitly stated [in the rule]. Nor can it be argued that the word *naḥ* will be carried over (*anuvartate*) from the preceding rule *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ* (8.2.42).

This is because the *nakāra* has been excluded by rules such as *śuṣaḥ kaḥ* and *paco vaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.51, 52). However, in the view that this is a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), the prohibition of the *nakāra* is established even without the mention of *nakāra*, since that which would otherwise apply to the *niṣṭhā-ta* after roots such as *nud* does not occur. But in this view, the mention of the roots *ḍhauk*, *ḍhauk*, *ṭunau*, and *ṭunau* would be redundant, because the substitution of *na* for the *niṣṭhā-ta* following these roots does not occur anyway.

Since the three beginning with *nud* are subject to the rule *radābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.2.42), and since for *trā* and *ghnā* the rule *saṃyogāderāto dhātoryaṇvataḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.43) applies, it is logical that these [three] should be excluded; however, this does not apply to the root *ḍhauk*. Therefore, raising the doubt as to which alternative should be adopted, the *Bhāṣya* first establishes the positive injunction (*vidhi*) and then adopts the negative prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) as well, stating: "Or rather, let there be a prohibition," and so forth.

In that view, the inclusion of *ḍhaddhaṭhṭhaḍa|nī* is for the purpose of indicating (*jñāpanārtham*) that "the substitution of *n* occurs even for the *t* of a *niṣṭhā* suffix following the roots *ḍhaddhaṭhṭhaḍa|nī*. For a prohibition is not possible regarding what has not been previously applicable; with this intention, he says: "The inclusion of *ḍhaddhaṭhṭhaḍa|nī* [is for the sake of indication]. [Regarding the rule] *nityaṃ samāse* (Pāṇini 8.3.45): the prohibition [contained in the rule] *anuttarapadasthasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.46) serves as an indicator (*jñāpakam*) that there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in a sentence (*vākye*).

Objection: In the rule *nityaṃ samāse 'nuttarapadasthasya*, the phrase *anuttarapadasthasya* ("not standing in the final member of a compound") is employed to prevent the substitution of *ṣ* for the visarga in examples such as *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā*. Even though the absence of *ṣ* is secured by this rule in those cases, the substitution of *ṣ* would still result [in other instances] by the rule *isusoḥ sāmathrye* (Pāṇini 8.3.44).

Nor should it be argued that in that sūtra, only the *sāmarthya* characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) is intended by the word *sāmarthya*; for although the compound *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā* possesses the *sāmarthya* characterized by unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), it lacks the *sāmarthya* characterized by mutual expectancy, and thus the preceding sūtra would not apply. This is because, since the word *sāmarthye* is heard in its general sense in the sūtra, both types of *sāmarthya* can be understood as being included in the preceding rule.

Nor should it be argued that, even so, because the suffixes *is* and *us* are included among those ending in *kṛt* suffixes, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of a suffix applies; thus, although *sarpis* ends in *is*, *paramasarpis* does not end in *is*, and consequently, in the case of *paramasarpiḥ-kuṇḍikā*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* by the preceding rule does not occur.

This being the case, keeping in mind the objection that even in the sentence *paramasarpiṣkaroti*, the optional application of the rule for *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) would be untenable by the preceding sūtra, he says: "There is a prohibition [of ṣatva] when [the word] stands in a non-final position (*anuttarapadastha*). The underlying intention is as follows: in the sūtra *nityaṃ samāse*, the term *isusoḥ* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). In that context, if, in the domain of *is* and *us*...

If the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of an affix (pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā) were to apply here, then in the case of *paramasarpiḥ kuṇḍi*, the substitution of *ṣ* would not occur simply because the word *paramasarpiḥ* lacks the suffix *is*; thus, the rule [Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.47], "of that which stands at the end of a non-final member," would suffice. However, since that [substitution] has indeed been applied in the domain of *is* and *us*, it indicates that the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of an affix does not operate there.

Therefore, because that [paribhāṣā] does not apply even to the preceding rule (*isusoḥ sāmarthye*), the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) is established optionally in the sentence *paramasarpiṣkaroti* as well; this is because the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) does not apply to the rule stating that there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in a sentence (*vākye*). And thus, in order to prevent *ṣatva* in cases such as *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā*, one must rely upon the definition of *sāmarthya* (semantic connection) characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) in the preceding rule; such is the truth of the matter.

In the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.59), the prohibition of *ṣatva* for the suffix *sāt* in the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.111) indicates that *ṣatva* applies even to a portion of a suffix.

In the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, regarding the interpretation where the term *ādeśa* (substitute) and *pratyaya* (suffix) are construed in apposition as "that *sakāra* which is a substitute or a suffix," one might raise the objection that *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) would not apply in forms such as *kariṣyati* and *hariṣyati*. This is because, although the *sakāra* in *sya* is a constituent (*avayava*) of the suffix, it lacks the status of being a suffix itself. Anticipating this objection, the *Bhāṣya* establishes the *ṣatva* of a *sakāra* that is a constituent of a suffix by means of an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence). He states this [in the verse]: *sātpadādyoḥ*.

By the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* for the letter *s* belonging to a prefix (*sa*) or to the beginning of a word is prohibited. In that context, since the *s* belonging to a prefix lacks the status of being an affix (*pratyaya*), the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* does not apply; thus, the prohibition [of *ṣ*] would be redundant. This redundancy serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* applies even to a *s* that is part of an affix.

Consequently, since the *s* that is a constituent of the suffix *sāt* would also be subject to the rule for changing to *ṣ*, the mention of *sāt* is meaningful as it serves to prohibit that change. And thus, the intention is that the change to *ṣ* will be established even in cases such as *kariṣyati*. In that very context, another interpretation has been presented: that the change to *ṣ* applies to the *sakāra* (the letter *s*) which is either a substitute (*ādeśa*) or part of a suffix (*pratyaya*).

In that view, fearing that a compound between the word *ādeśa* ending in the nominative case and the word *pratyaya* ending in the genitive case would be untenable, the *Bhāṣya* provides a justification based on an *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark). It says: the mention of *ghasi* in the rule *ṭhaśāsivasighasīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.60) is the *jñāpaka* that this compound occurs between two words in different case endings. By the rule *ṭhaśāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*, the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of *ghas* is prescribed.

*jakṣatuḥ* is the illustrative example. If it were not the case that [the rule applies] to the *sakāra* which belongs to both the substitute (*ādeśa*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), then the meaning would be: "the *ṣatva* [substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] applies to that *sakāra* which belongs to the substitute. In that case, since the *sakāra* in *ghas* is a part of the substitute for the root *ad*, its *ṣatva* would be established by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* alone; consequently, the mention of *ghasi* [in the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*] would be purposeless.

The meaning of the rule (*sūtra*) is that the substitution of *ṣ* occurs for that *s* which is both an *ādeśa* (substitute) and a constituent part (*avayava*) of a *pratyaya* (suffix). By this, it indicates that the compound *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* consists of two words with different case endings (*nānāvibhakti*), rather than two words with identical case endings (*samānavibhaktika*). Consequently, since the *s* of the root *ghas* is not an *ādeśa*, the rule for *ṣ*-substitution would otherwise not apply; thus, the inclusion of the root *ghas* in the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca* is meaningful, as its purpose is to ensure that *ṣ*-substitution does indeed apply there. This is the intended sense.

In this context, the term *parapratyaya* is a *dvandva* compound consisting of *pratyaya* and *avayava*. Thus, the compound is formed only between two words that possess identical case endings (*samānavibhaktika*). Nevertheless, it should be noted that because the word *pratyaya* here functions as an indicator for the meaning of the word *pratyaya* ending in the genitive case, it is described as having a different case ending (*vyadhikaraṇavibhaktika*).

Nor should it be argued that the inclusion of the term *ghasi* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) only for the principle that the word "substitute" (*ādeśa*) does not refer to a part of a substitute, and not for the aforementioned statement; or alternatively, that it serves as an indicator only for the principle that a compound occurs only between the words "substitute" (*ādeśa*) and "suffix" (*pratyaya*) when they appear with identical case-endings (*samānavibhaktika*). This is because the rule that a compound occurs between two words with identical case-endings is not something to be established by an indicator. In the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), a compound occurs between two words with identical case-endings.

And since, in the present context, the substitution of *ṣ* in forms such as *kariṣyati* would be untenable, it is determined that there is a compound with the word *pratyaya* ending in the genitive case. When the doubt arises—namely, that the word *ādeśa* should also be compounded only with a word having the same case-ending as itself—it is resolved by the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the word *ādeśa* ends in the nominative case; for it follows by implication that this is a compound between two words of different case-endings. [Pāṇini 8.3.110: *jharo jhari savarṇe*].

The inclusion of the word *aśvasani* in the list beginning with *savana* indicates that the substitution of *ṣ* occurs even after a root that does not end in *i*. [Objection: But is it not the case that the reading of the word *aśvasani* in the *savana*-group within the rule prohibiting the substitution of *ṣ*—namely, *na raparasṛpisṛjispṛśispṛhisavanādīnām*—is redundant? Nor can it be argued that if it were not included there, the *s* belonging to its constituent parts would incur the substitution of *ṣ*.

By the rule *sū. 8.3.103*, the occurrence of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) must be stated. Since the term *iṇaḥ* is understood as anuvṛtti (carried over) there, *ṣatva* is prescribed only for a *s* that follows a preceding member ending in *iṇ*. Now, raising the objection that in the word *aśvasani*, the *s* does not follow a preceding member ending in *iṇ* and thus *ṣatva* would not apply, he states the purpose of its inclusion [in the list] as a *jñāpaka* (indicative proof): "In *savanādiṣu*. Thus, it is indicated that in certain cases, *ṣatva* occurs even for a *s* following a preceding member that does not end in *iṇ*.

Therefore, since the substitution of *ṣ* would otherwise apply even in the case of the word *aśvasani*, its inclusion in the list beginning with *savana* is made for the purpose of prohibiting that substitution. However, the purpose of this indication (*jñāpana*) is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya: that the substitution of *ṣ* is established in forms such as *jalāṣāham* and *māṣa*. Regarding the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.41), the prohibition in the rule *toḥ ṣi* (Pāṇini 8.4.43) indicates that here there is no correspondence based on numerical order (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*).

Objection: In the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*, by the rule *yathāsaṃkhyamanudeśaḥ samānām*, the meaning of the sūtra would be that through correspondence according to order, when a *s* is joined with a *ṣ*, a *ṣ* is substituted; and when a *t*-class letter (*tavarga*) is joined with a *ṭ*-class letter (*ṭavarga*), a *ṭ*-class letter is the substitute. Consequently, one might object that in forms such as *rāmaṣṭīkate* and *peṣṭā*, the substitution of *ṣṭu* would not occur. Anticipating this, he says: "There is a prohibition [of this] by the rule *toḥ ṣi*."

By the rule *toḥ ṣi*, the substitution of a *ṣṭu* sound (ṣṭutva) for the dental class (*tavarga*) when followed by a *ṣakāra* is prohibited. An example is *san ṣaṣṭhaḥ*. If, however, there were a sequential correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) in the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*, then that rule would apply only when the dental class is joined with the retroflex class (*ṭavarga*), and not with a *ṣakāra*; consequently, since the *ṭavarga* would not apply in cases such as *san ṣaṣṭhaḥ*, the rule *toḥ ṣi* would be rendered useless.

That rule was formulated [in the *Śikṣā*] to indicate that, in the rule "ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ," there is no application according to the respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyānvaya*). Therefore, forms such as *rāmaṣṭīkate* are established; this is the intended meaning. Thus ends the first supplement on the collection of indicators (*jñāpaka*).
